segments.label: §16, de source block1
segments.text: In jeder Sprache wiederholt sich unläugbar derselbe geistige Process; Kräfte, Mittel und Erfolge sind einander so gleich und ungleich, als die menschlichen körperlichen und geistigen Sprachanlagen Verschiedenartigkeit innerhalb der von der Natur gesteckten Gränzen erlauben.

segments.label: §16, de source block2
segments.text: Wo man nun einzelne Sprachen zu schildern versucht, muss man von dem allgemeinen Typus dieses Processes ausgehen und dahin zurückkehren, weil es sonst durchaus an dem nothwendigen Vergleichungspunkt fehlen würde.

segments.label: §16, de source block3
segments.text: Die Allgemeinheit dieses Typus besteht darin, dass Alles, was von ihm auszusagen ist, nur durch den reinen Begriff der Sprache bedingt und von allen andren Umständen abgesehen wird, die, aus den übrigen menschlichen Anlagen und den auf sie einwirkenden Verhältnissen entspringend, in der Wirklichkeit den allgemeinen Typus individualisiren.

segments.label: §16, codex source block1
segments.text: The same mental process undeniably recurs in every language; its powers, means and results resemble and differ from one another as much as the diversity of human bodily and mental dispositions for language permits within the limits set by nature.

segments.label: §16, codex source block2
segments.text: Whenever one attempts to describe particular languages, one must therefore start from the general type of this process and return to it, since otherwise the necessary point of comparison would be entirely lacking.

segments.label: §16, codex source block3
segments.text: The generality of this type consists in everything that can be said of it being determined solely by the pure concept of language, with all other circumstances left aside: circumstances which arise from the other human dispositions and the conditions acting upon them, and which in reality individualise the general type.

segments.label: §16, muse source block1
segments.text: In every language the same mental process undeniably repeats itself; powers, means and results are as like and unlike one another as the human bodily and mental dispositions for language permit diversity within the limits set by nature.

segments.label: §16, muse source block2
segments.text: Where one now attempts to describe individual languages, one must start from the general type of this process and return to it, because otherwise the necessary point of comparison would be entirely lacking.

segments.label: §16, muse source block3
segments.text: The generality of this type consists in this, that everything that is to be asserted of it is conditioned only by the pure concept of language and that abstraction is made from all other circumstances which, arising from the remaining human dispositions and from the conditions acting upon them, individualize the general type in reality.

segments.label: §16, astra source block1
segments.text: The same mental process undeniably recurs in every language; its powers, means and results resemble and differ from one another to the extent that human bodily and mental dispositions for language permit diversity within the limits set by nature.

segments.label: §16, astra source block2
segments.text: When attempting to describe individual languages, we must therefore begin with the general type of this process and return to it, since otherwise we would entirely lack the necessary point of comparison.

segments.label: §16, astra source block3
segments.text: The generality of this type consists in everything that can be said of it being determined solely by the pure concept of language, while all other circumstances are disregarded: circumstances that arise from the remaining human dispositions and the conditions acting upon them, and that individualize the general type in reality.

segments.label: §17, de source block1
segments.text: Was man bisher in diesem Sinn, unter dem Namen der allgemeinen Grammatik, ausgearbeitet hat, erschöpft den Begriff bei weitem nicht, sondern bleibt bei einem kleinen Theile desselben stehn.

segments.label: §17, de source block2
segments.text: Diese Wissenschaft, von der wir leider noch nicht wissen, ob sie schon bei den Indischen Grammatikern Fortschritte gemacht hatte, die aber von den Griechischen in einigen Punkten zu einer Vollendung gebracht war, die wenig mehr hinzuzufügen erlaubte, beschäftigt sich eigentlich nur mit der logischen Zergliederung der Rede und der Untersuchung der zur Verknüpfung der Gedanken in dieser nöthigen Wortformen ; also zunächst mit einem Erzeugniss der Sprache und daher nur mit einem Theile von dieser.

segments.label: §17, de source block3
segments.text: Man hat zwar hie und da dem Begriff der allgemeinen Grammatik eine grössere Ausdehnung gegeben, nirgends aber, soviel mir bekannt ist, hat man, wie hier gefordert wird, eine Analyse des Verfahrens der Sprache in seinem ganzen Zusammenwirken versucht.

segments.label: §17, de source block4
segments.text: Da sie sich auch vorzüglich mit der Betrachtung der grammatischen Formen, als der Bestandtheile der Rede, im Einzelnen beschäftigt, so fällt sie, nach der hier versuchten ganz andren Eintheilung der Sprachanalyse, grossentheils in den folgenden Abschnitt, und kann auf keine Weise uns des Geschäftes überheben, das Allgemeine, was zur Vergleichung des Besondren erfordert wird, aus eigner Ideenentwicklung hier von neuem aufzustellen, so viel besser es auch wäre, sich, bei der Schilderung einer Gattung bestimmter Sprachen, auf ein schon anderwärts aufgeführtes, und bewährtes allgemeines Lehrgebäude der Sprache beziehen zu können.

segments.label: §17, codex source block1
segments.text: What has so far been developed in this sense under the name of general grammar falls far short of exhausting the concept, stopping instead at a small part of it.

segments.label: §17, codex source block2
segments.text: This discipline, which we unfortunately do not yet know whether the Indian grammarians had already advanced, but which the Greek grammarians brought in some respects to a perfection that left little to add, is actually concerned only with the logical analysis of discourse and the investigation of the word forms needed to connect thoughts within it; thus, in the first instance, with a product of language, and consequently with only a part of language.

segments.label: §17, codex source block3
segments.text: Here and there, admittedly, the concept of general grammar has been given a wider scope; but nowhere, to my knowledge, has anyone attempted what is required here: an analysis of the procedure of language in the full interplay of its operations.

segments.label: §17, codex source block4
segments.text: Since general grammar is also chiefly concerned with examining grammatical forms individually as the components of discourse, it falls largely within the following section under the quite different division of linguistic analysis attempted here, and can in no way relieve us of the task of establishing afresh, through the development of our own ideas, the general principles needed to compare particulars, however much better it would be, when describing a class of particular languages, to be able to refer to an established and tested general system of linguistic doctrine already constructed elsewhere.

segments.label: §17, muse source block1
segments.text: What has hitherto been worked out in this sense, under the name of general grammar, by no means exhausts the concept, but stops at a small part of it.

segments.label: §17, muse source block2
segments.text: This science, of which we unfortunately do not yet know whether it had already made progress among the Indian grammarians, but which had been brought by the Greek grammarians in some points to a perfection that allowed little more to be added, is really concerned only with the logical analysis of speech and with the investigation of the word-forms necessary in it for connecting thoughts; thus in the first instance with a product of language and therefore only with a part of language.

segments.label: §17, muse source block3
segments.text: A greater extension has indeed here and there been given to the concept of general grammar, but nowhere, so far as I know, has an analysis of the procedure of language in its whole joint working been attempted, as is required here.

segments.label: §17, muse source block4
segments.text: Since it is also chiefly concerned in detail with considering the grammatical forms as the constituents of speech, it falls, according to the wholly different division of the analysis of language attempted here, for the most part into the following section, and can in no way relieve us of the task of setting up anew here, from our own development of ideas, the general element required for comparison of the particular, however much better it would be, in describing a genus of determinate languages, to be able to refer to a general system of doctrine concerning language already erected and proved elsewhere.

segments.label: §18, de source block1
segments.text: Es wird also jetzt zunächst nothwendig seyn, den allgemeinen Sprachtypus wenigstens in seinen Grundzügen zu entwerfen, und dann zu prüfen, welche Eintheilung der ganzen in diesem Kapitel abzuhandlenden Materie sich aus demselben ergeben dürfte.

segments.label: §18, codex source block1
segments.text: Our immediate task must therefore be to sketch the general type of language, at least in its basic features, and then to examine what division of the whole subject matter to be treated in this chapter might follow from it.

segments.label: §18, muse source block1
segments.text: It will therefore now first be necessary to sketch the general type of language at least in its fundamental features, and then to examine what division of the whole material to be treated in this chapter is likely to result from it.

segments.text: Our first task must therefore be to sketch the general type of language, at least in its main features, and then to examine what division of all the material to be treated in this chapter might follow from it.

segments.text: Our first task must therefore be to sketch the general type of language, at least in outline, and then to examine what division of all the material to be treated in this chapter might follow from it.

segments.label: §19, de source block1
segments.text: Der geistige Process der Sprache wird hier in seiner weitesten Ausdehnung genommen, nicht bloss in der Beziehung derselben auf die Rede und den Vorrath ihrer Wortelemente, sondern auch in der Beziehung auf ihren Einfluss auf das Denk- und Empfindungsvermögen.

segments.label: §19, de source block2
segments.text: Der ganze Gang kommt in Betrachtung, auf dem sie, von dem Geiste ausgehend, auf den Geist zurückwirkt, im Individuum, in dem jedesmal lebenden Geschlecht und in der Nation durch mehrere Geschlechter hindurch.

segments.label: §19, codex source block1
segments.text: The mental process of language is taken here in its widest scope, not merely in language's relation to discourse and its stock of word elements, but also in relation to its influence on the capacities for thinking and feeling.

segments.label: §19, codex source block2
segments.text: We consider the entire course by which language, proceeding from the mind, acts back upon the mind: in the individual, in the generation living at any given time, and in the nation across several generations.

segments.label: §19, muse source block1
segments.text: The mental process of language is taken here in its widest extension, not merely in the relation of language to speech and to the stock of its word-elements, but also in its relation to its influence on the faculty of thought and feeling.

segments.label: §19, muse source block2
segments.text: The whole course comes into consideration along which it, proceeding from the mind, reacts upon the mind, in the individual, in the generation living at any given time and in the nation through several generations.

segments.label: §20, de source block1
segments.text: Denn es ist schon sonst dargethan, und kann wohl, als unbestritten, angenommen werden, dass die Sprache nicht bloss die Bezeichnung des, unabhängig von ihr geformten Gedanken, sondern selbst das bildende Organ des Gedanken ist.

segments.label: §20, de source block2
segments.text: Die intellectuelle Thätigkeit, durchaus geistig, durchaus innerlich, und gewissermassen spurlos vorübergehend, wird durch den Ton in der Rede äusserlich und wahrnehmbar für die Sinne, und erhält durch die Schrift einen bleibenden Körper.

segments.label: §20, de source block3
segments.text: Das auf diese Weise Erzeugte ist das Gesprochene und Aufgezeichnete aller Art, die Sprache aber der Inbegriff der Laute, welche die bestimmte intellectuelle Thätigkeit, welcher sie angehört, auf diesem Wege hervorzubringen vermag, und der nach Gesetzen (die wiederum aus der Natur der intellectuellen Thätigkeit und des ihr entsprechenden Tonsystems hervorgehn) möglichen Verbindungen und Umgestaltungen derselben.

segments.label: §20, de source block4
segments.text: Die intellectuelle Thätigkeit und die Sprache sind daher Eins und unzertrennlich von einander; man kann nicht einmal schlechthin die erstere als das Erzeugende, die andre als das Erzeugte ansehen.

segments.label: §20, de source block5
segments.text: Denn obgleich das jedesmal Gesprochene allerdings ein Erzeugniss des Geistes ist, so wird es doch, indem es zu der schon vorher vorhandenen Sprache gehört, ausser der Thätigkeit des Geistes, durch die Laute und Gesetze der Sprache bestimmt, und wirkt, indem es gleich wieder in die Sprache überhaupt übergeht, wieder bestimmend auf den Geist zurück.

segments.label: §20, de source block6
segments.text: Die intellectuelle Thätigkeit ist an die Nothwendigkeit geknüpft, eine Verbindung mit dem Ton einzugehen, das Denken kann sonst nicht zur Deutlichkeit gelangen, die Vorstellung nicht zum Begriff werden.

segments.label: §20, de source block7
segments.text: Den Ton erzeugt sie aus freiem Entschluss und formt ihn durch ihre Kraft, denn vermöge ihrer Durchdringung wird er zum articulirten Laut (wenn es möglich wäre, einen Anfang aller Sprache zu denken), begründet ein Gebiet solcher Laute, das selbständig, bestimmend und beschränkend, auf sie zurückwirkt.

segments.label: §20, codex source block1
segments.text: For it has already been demonstrated elsewhere, and may surely be accepted as undisputed, that language is not merely the designation of thought formed independently of it, but is itself the formative organ of thought.

segments.label: §20, codex source block2
segments.text: Intellectual activity, wholly mental, wholly inward, and in a sense passing without a trace, becomes outward and perceptible to the senses through sound in speech, and acquires an enduring body through writing.

segments.label: §20, codex source block3
segments.text: What is produced in this way is everything spoken and recorded; language, however, is the totality of the sounds that the particular intellectual activity to which it belongs can produce by this means, together with their possible combinations and transformations according to laws which in turn arise from the nature of intellectual activity and its corresponding sound system.

segments.label: §20, codex source block4
segments.text: Intellectual activity and language are therefore one and inseparable from each other; one cannot even regard the former simply as what produces and the latter as what is produced.

segments.label: §20, codex source block5
segments.text: For although what is spoken on any occasion is certainly a product of the mind, it nevertheless belongs to a language already in existence, and is therefore determined not only by the mind's activity but also by the sounds and laws of that language; and as it immediately passes back into language as a whole, it acts back upon the mind, determining it in turn.

segments.label: §20, codex source block6
segments.text: Intellectual activity is bound by the necessity of entering into a connection with sound; otherwise thinking cannot attain distinctness, nor can a representation become a concept.

segments.label: §20, codex source block7
segments.text: It produces sound by a free decision and shapes it through its power, for sound becomes articulated sound through being permeated by intellectual activity; and it establishes a domain of such sounds which acts back upon it independently, determining and limiting it—if it were possible to conceive of a beginning of all language.

segments.label: §20, muse source block2

segments.text: It produces sound by a free decision and shapes it through its power, for sound becomes articulated sound through being permeated by intellectual activity; and (if it were possible to conceive a beginning of all language) it establishes a domain of such sounds that independently acts back upon the activity, determining and limiting it.

segments.label: §21, de source block1
segments.text: Dasjenige, wessen das Denken in der Sprache bedarf, ist nicht eigentlich das dem Ohre wirklich Vernehmbare, oder um es anders auszudrücken, wenn man den articulirten Laut in die Articulation und das Geräusch zerlegt, nicht dieses, sondern nur jene.

segments.label: §21, de source block2
segments.text: Die Articulation beruht auf der Gewalt des Geistes über die Sprachwerkzeuge, sie zu einer Behandlung des Tons zu nöthigen, welche der Form seines Wirkens entspricht.

segments.label: §21, de source block3
segments.text: Dasjenige, worin sich diese Form und die Articulation, wie in einem verknüpfenden Mittel begegnen, ist, dass beide ihr Gebiet in Grundtheile zerlegen, deren Zusammenfügung lauter solche Ganze bildet, welche das Streben in sich tragen, Theile neuer Ganze zu werden.

segments.label: §21, de source block4
segments.text: Ausser jener Gewalt ist aber auch in dem Geiste ein, sich den Sprachwerkzeugen selbst mittheilender Drang, von ihnen einen solchen Gebrauch zu machen, und auf jener Gewalt und diesem Drange beruht die Erzeugung der Sprache sogar unabhängig von dem Ohre vernehmbarem Geräusch.

segments.label: §21, de source block5
segments.text: Dass die Sprache wirklich ganz innerlich ist, und auch ohne Lauthervorbringung und Vernehmung möglich bleibt, lehrt das Beispiel der Taubstummen.

segments.label: §21, de source block6
segments.text: Durch das Ohr ist jeder Zugang zu ihnen verschlossen, sie lernen aber das Gesprochene an der Bewegung der Sprachwerkzeuge des Redenden und an der Schrift verstehen, sie sprechen selbst, indem man die Lage und Bewegung ihrer Sprachwerkzeuge lenkt.

segments.label: §21, de source block7
segments.text: Dies kann nur durch das, auch ihnen beiwohnende Articulationsvermögen geschehen, indem sie durch den Zusammenhang ihres Denkens mit ihren Sprachwerkzeugen im Andern aus dem einen Gliede, der Bewegung seiner Sprachwerkzeuge, das andre, sein Denken, errathen lernen.

segments.label: §21, de source block8
segments.text: Der Ton, den wir hören, offenbart sich ihnen durch die Lage und Bewegung der Organe, sie vernehmen seine Articulation ohne sein Geräusch.

segments.label: §21, de source block9
segments.text: Es mag diesem auch in ihnen etwas Sinnliches, vielleicht etwas von ihrer Phantasie dem Mangelnden untergeschobenes entsprechen, wovon wir keinen Begriff haben, aber immer geht bei ihnen eine merkwürdige Zerlegung des articulirten Lautes vor.

segments.label: §21, de source block10
segments.text: Sie verstehen wirklich die Sprache, da sie alphabetisch lesen und schreiben, und selbst reden lernen, nicht bloss den Gedanken durch Zeichen oder Bilder.

segments.label: §21, de source block11
segments.text: Sie erlernen dies, nicht bloss dadurch, dass sie Vernunft, wie andre Menschen, sondern ganz eigentlich dadurch, dass sie auch Sprachfähigkeit besitzen, Uebereinstimmung ihres Denkens mit ihren Sprachwerkzeugen, und Drang beide zusammenwirken zu lassen, das eine und das andre wesentlich gegründet in der menschlichen, wenn auch von einer Seite verstümmelten Natur.

segments.label: §21, codex source block1
segments.text: What thinking requires in language is not, strictly speaking, what is actually audible to the ear; or, to put it differently, if articulated sound is divided into articulation and noise, it requires only the former, not the latter.

segments.label: §21, codex source block2
segments.text: Articulation rests on the mind's power over the organs of speech, compelling them to handle sound in a way corresponding to the form of its own operation.

segments.label: §21, codex source block3
segments.text: The point at which this form and articulation meet, as in a connecting medium, is that both divide their domain into basic parts whose combination produces nothing but wholes that carry within themselves the striving to become parts of new wholes.

segments.label: §21, codex source block4
segments.text: Besides this power, however, the mind also contains an impulse to make such use of the organs of speech, an impulse which communicates itself to those organs; and the production of language rests on this power and this impulse even independently of noise audible to the ear.

segments.label: §21, codex source block5
segments.text: The example of deaf-mute people teaches us that language really is wholly inward and remains possible even without the production and perception of sound.

segments.label: §21, codex source block6
segments.text: Every avenue of access to them through the ear is closed, yet they learn to understand what is spoken through the movements of the speaker's organs of speech and through writing; they themselves speak when the position and movement of their organs of speech are guided.

segments.label: §21, codex source block7
segments.text: This can happen only through the capacity for articulation that they too possess: because of the connection between their thinking and their organs of speech, they learn to infer in another person one member of the connection, his thinking, from the other, the movement of his organs of speech.

segments.label: §21, codex source block8
segments.text: The sound we hear reveals itself to them through the position and movement of the organs; they perceive its articulation without its noise.

segments.label: §21, codex source block9
segments.text: Something sensory of which we have no conception may correspond to this noise in them too, perhaps something their imagination supplies in place of what is missing; but in any event, a remarkable separation of the components of articulated sound takes place in them.

segments.label: §21, codex source block10
segments.text: They really understand language, since they learn to read and write alphabetically and even to speak, rather than merely understanding thought through signs or pictures.

segments.label: §21, codex source block11
segments.text: They learn this not merely because they possess reason like other human beings, but quite specifically because they also possess a capacity for language: a correspondence between their thinking and their organs of speech, and an impulse to make the two work together, both essentially grounded in human nature, even though it is mutilated in one respect.

segments.label: §21, muse source block1
segments.text: That of which thinking has need in language is not really what is actually audible to the ear, or, to express it differently, if one resolves articulated sound into articulation and noise, it is not the latter, but only the former.

segments.label: §21, muse source block2
segments.text: Articulation rests on the power of the mind over the organs of speech, compelling them to a treatment of tone which corresponds to the form of its working.

segments.label: §21, muse source block3
segments.text: That in which this form and articulation meet, as in a connecting means, is that both resolve their domain into fundamental parts whose joining together forms nothing but wholes of such a kind as carry within themselves the striving to become parts of new wholes.

segments.label: §21, muse source block4
segments.text: Besides that power, however, there is also in the mind an urge, communicating itself to the organs of speech themselves, to make such use of them, and on that power and this urge rests the production of language even independently of noise audible to the ear.

segments.label: §21, muse source block5
segments.text: That language is really wholly inward, and remains possible even without the production and hearing of sound, is taught by the example of deaf-mutes.

segments.label: §21, muse source block6
segments.text: Every access to them through the ear is closed; but they learn to understand what is spoken from the movement of the organs of speech of the person speaking and from writing, and they themselves speak when the position and movement of their organs of speech are guided.

segments.label: §21, muse source block7
segments.text: This can happen only through the faculty of articulation dwelling in them also, in that, through the connexion of their thinking with their organs of speech, they learn in another person to divine the one member, his thinking, from the other member, the movement of his organs of speech.

segments.label: §21, muse source block8
segments.text: The tone that we hear reveals itself to them through the position and movement of the organs; they perceive its articulation without its noise.

segments.label: §21, muse source block9
segments.text: Something sensible may also correspond to the latter in them, perhaps something supplied by their imagination in place of what is lacking, of which we have no concept, but always a remarkable resolution of articulated sound takes place in them.

segments.label: §21, muse source block10
segments.text: They really understand language, since they read and write alphabetically and themselves learn to speak, not merely thought through signs or pictures.

segments.label: §21, muse source block11
segments.text: They learn this not merely because they possess reason, like other human beings, but quite properly because they also possess a capacity for language, a correspondence of their thinking with their organs of speech, and an urge to let both work together, the one and the other essentially grounded in human nature, even if mutilated on one side.

segments.label: §22, de source block1
segments.text: Die Articulation (deren Begriff ich hier nur nach ihrer Wirkung, als diejenige Gestaltung des Lautes nehme, welche ihn zum Träger von Gedanken macht) ist jedoch im Vorigen nur nach ihrer logischen, oder wenigstens nur nach ihrer intellectuellen Natur geschildert worden.

segments.label: §22, de source block2
segments.text: In ihrer wesentlichen hängt sie aber gerade von dem Ton, als Geräusch, oder vielmehr von derjenigen Lufterschütterung ab, durch welche die Sprachwerkzeuge in die Ferne wirken.

segments.label: §22, de source block3
segments.text: Sie lässt sich daher auch nie unmittelbar auf andre Sinne, als das Ohr, anwenden, und wie man es versuchte, würde man immer nur Zeichen von Tönen, nicht unmittelbar von elementarisch zerlegbaren Wörtern hervorbringen.

segments.label: §22, de source block4
segments.text: Dies beruht darauf, dass gerade die einem fremden Ohre vernehmbare Lufterschütterung durch die, von dem Gedanken bestimmten Organe mit der menschlichen Natur unzertrennlich, und nothwendig zu ihrer Entwicklung, verbunden ist.

segments.label: §22, codex source block1
segments.text: In the foregoing, however, articulation—whose concept I take here only in terms of its effect, as the shaping of sound that makes it a vehicle of thoughts—has been described only in its logical, or at least only in its intellectual, nature.

segments.label: §22, codex source block2
segments.text: In its essential nature, however, it depends precisely on sound as noise, or rather on the vibration of the air through which the organs of speech act at a distance.

segments.label: §22, codex source block3
segments.text: It can therefore never be applied directly to any sense other than hearing; however one attempted this, one would always produce only signs of sounds, not direct signs of words divisible into elementary parts.

segments.label: §22, codex source block4
segments.text: This rests on the fact that precisely the vibration of the air, audible to another's ear and produced by organs determined by thought, is inseparably connected with human nature and necessary to its development.

segments.text: In its essential nature, however, it depends precisely on tone as noise, or rather on that vibration of the air through which the organs of speech act at a distance.

segments.label: §22, muse source block3

segments.label: §22, muse source block4
segments.text: This rests on the fact that precisely the vibration of the air, audible to another person's ear, through the organs determined by thought is inseparably connected with human nature, and is necessary to its development.

segments.label: §23, de source block1
segments.text: Es liegt aber hierin dreierlei: der Drang des Gedanken nach Aeusserung, das Bedürfniss der Empfindung zum thierischen Schrei, und die Nothwendigkeit der gesellschaftlichen Wechselwirkung zur Ausbildung des Gedanken.

segments.label: §23, de source block2
segments.text: Jedes dieser Stücke führt einzeln zur Hervorbringung des Tons, und die Sprache vereinigt alle im articulirten Laut.

segments.label: §23, codex source block1
segments.text: Three things are involved here: thought's impulse towards expression, feeling's need to issue in an animal cry, and the necessity of social interaction for the development of thought.

segments.label: §23, codex source block2
segments.text: Each of these leads separately to the production of sound, and language unites them all in articulated sound.

segments.label: §23, muse source block1
segments.text: But herein lie three things: the urge of thought towards utterance, the need of feeling for the animal cry, and the necessity of social interaction for the formation of thought.

segments.label: §23, muse source block2
segments.text: Each of these items leads singly to the production of tone, and language unites all of them in articulated sound.

segments.label: §24, de source block1
segments.text: Das Denken ist eine geistige Handlung, wird aber durch sein Bedürfniss nach Sprache ein Antrieb zu einer körperlichen.

segments.label: §24, de source block2
segments.text: Es ist ein fortschreitendes Entwicklen, eine blosse innere Bewegung, in der nichts Bleibendes, Stätiges, Ruhendes angenommen werden kann, und zugleich eine Sehnsucht aus dem Dunkel nach dem Licht, aus der Beschränkung nach der Unendlichkeit.

segments.label: §24, de source block3
segments.text: In dem, aus zwiefacher Natur in Eins zusammengeschmolzenen menschlichen Wesen geht dies Streben auch nach aussen, und findet, durch die Vermittlung der Sprachwerkzeuge, in der Luft, dem feinsten und am leichtesten bewegbaren aller Elemente, dessen scheinbare Unkörperlichkeit dem Geiste auch sinnlich entspricht, einen ihm wundervoll angemessenen Stoff, in dem, bei der menschlichen aufrechten Stellung, die Rede frei und ruhig von den Lippen zum Ohre strömt, der das Licht der Gestirne herbeiführt, und sich, ohne sichtbare Schranken, in die Unendlichkeit ausdehnt.

segments.label: §24, codex source block1
segments.text: Thinking is a mental act, but through its need for language it becomes an impulse towards a bodily act.

segments.label: §24, codex source block2
segments.text: It is a progressive unfolding, a purely inward movement in which nothing enduring, constant or at rest can be assumed, and at the same time a longing to pass from darkness into light, from limitation into infinity.

segments.label: §24, codex source block3
segments.text: In the human being, whose twofold nature is fused into one, this striving also turns outwards and, through the mediation of the organs of speech, finds a material wonderfully suited to it in air, the finest and most easily moved of all the elements, whose apparent incorporeality corresponds to the mind even in sensory terms: a material in which, given the human upright posture, speech flows freely and calmly from the lips to the ear, which brings us the light of the stars, and which extends without visible bounds into infinity.

segments.label: §24, synthesis source block2
segments.text: It is a progressive unfolding, a purely inward movement in which nothing lasting, steady or at rest can be assumed, and at the same time a longing to pass from darkness into light, from limitation into infinity.

segments.label: §24, synthesis source block3
segments.text: In the human being, whose twofold nature is fused into one, this striving also turns outwards. Through the mediation of the organs of speech, it finds in air—the finest and most easily moved of all the elements, whose apparent incorporeality corresponds to the mind even at the sensory level—a material wonderfully suited to it: a material in which, given the upright human posture, discourse flows freely and calmly from lips to ear, which carries to us the light of the heavenly bodies, and which extends into infinity without visible bounds.

segments.label: §24, revised source block1
segments.text: Thinking is a mental act, but through its need for language it becomes an impulse towards a bodily act.

segments.label: §25, de source block1
segments.text: Indem auf diese Weise das geistige Streben sich Bahn durch die Lippen bricht, kehrt das Erzeugniss desselben zum eignen Ohre zurück; die subjective innere Handlung wird als äussres Object wieder aufgenommen.

segments.label: §25, de source block2
segments.text: Dadurch theilt und befördert die Sprache das innerste Wesen des Denkens, das beständige Uebergehen des Subjects und Objects in einander.

segments.label: §25, de source block3
segments.text: Denn keine Gattung der Vorstellungen kann als ein reines Beschauen eines schon vorhandenen Gegenstandes betrachtet werden.

segments.label: §25, de source block4
segments.text: Die Thätigkeit der Sinne muss sich mit der inneren Handlung des Geistes synthetisch verbinden, und aus dieser Verbindung reisst sich die Vorstellung los, wird, der subjectiven Kraft gegenüber, zum Object, und kehrt, als solches aufs neue wahrgenommen, in jene zurück.

segments.label: §25, de source block5
segments.text: Ohne daher irgend auf die Mittheilung zwischen Menschen und Menschen zu sehn, ist das Sprechen eine nothwendige Bedingung des Denkens des Einzelnen in abgeschlossener Einsamkeit.

segments.label: §25, de source block6
segments.text: In der Erscheinung entwickelt sich jedoch die Sprache nur gesellschaftlich.

segments.label: §25, de source block7
segments.text: Denn der Mensch versteht sich selbst nur, indem er die Verstehbarkeit seiner Worte an Andren versuchend geprüft hat.

segments.label: §25, codex source block1
segments.text: As mental striving thus breaks a path through the lips, its product returns to one's own ear; the subjective inward act is received again as an outward object.

segments.label: §25, codex source block2
segments.text: Language thereby shares in and furthers the innermost essence of thinking: the constant passage of subject and object into each other.

segments.label: §25, codex source block3
segments.text: For no kind of representation can be regarded as the mere contemplation of an object already present.

segments.label: §25, codex source block4
segments.text: The activity of the senses must unite synthetically with the inward act of the mind; the representation breaks free from this union, becomes an object confronting the subjective power, and returns to that power when perceived anew as such an object.

segments.label: §25, codex source block5
segments.text: Thus, quite apart from any communication between one human being and another, speaking is a necessary condition of the individual's thinking in secluded solitude.

segments.label: §25, codex source block6
segments.text: In its actual manifestation, however, language develops only socially.

segments.label: §25, codex source block7
segments.text: For a human being understands himself only after experimentally testing the intelligibility of his words on others.

segments.label: §25, muse source block2

segments.label: §25, muse source block3

segments.text: Without therefore looking at all to communication between human being and human being, speaking is a necessary condition of the thinking of the individual in secluded solitude.

segments.label: §25, muse source block7
segments.text: For man understands himself only in that he has tried and tested the intelligibility of his words on others.

segments.label: §26, de source block1
segments.text: Wenn der unarticulirte Laut, wie immer bei den Thieren, und bisweilen beim Menschen, die Stelle der Sprache vertritt, so entpresst ihn entweder, wie bei widrigen Empfindungen, die Noth, oder es liegt ihm Absicht zum Grunde, indem er lockt, warnt, zur Hülfe herbeiruft, oder er entströmt, ohne Noth und Absicht, dem frohen Gefühle des Daseyns, dem Gefallen am Schmettern der Töne.

segments.label: §26, de source block2
segments.text: Das Letzte ist das Poetische, ein aufglimmender Funke in der thierischen Dumpfheit.

segments.label: §26, de source block3
segments.text: Diese verschiedenen Arten der Laute sind unter den mehr oder minder stummen und klangreichen Geschlechtern der Thiere sehr ungleich vertheilt, und verhältnissmässig wenigen ist die höhere und freudigere Gattung geworden.

segments.label: §26, de source block4
segments.text: Es wäre auch für die Sprache belehrend, aber vielleicht unmöglich, zu ergründen, woher diese Verschiedenheit stammt.

segments.label: §26, de source block5
segments.text: Dass die Vögel allein den Gesang besitzen, liesse sich vielleicht daraus erklären, dass sie freier, als alle andre Thiere, in dem Elemente des Tons, und in seinen reineren Regionen leben, wenn nicht so viele Gattungen derselben, gleich den auf der Erde wandelnden Thieren, an wenige einförmige Laute gebunden wären.

segments.label: §26, codex source block1
segments.text: When unarticulated sound takes the place of language, as it always does in animals and sometimes in human beings, either distress forces it out, as with painful feelings; or it has an intention behind it, as when it lures, warns or calls for help; or, without distress or intention, it pours forth from the joyful feeling of existence, from pleasure in the pealing of sounds.

segments.label: §26, codex source block2
segments.text: The last is the poetic element, a spark flaring up in animal dullness.

segments.label: §26, codex source block3
segments.text: These different kinds of sound are distributed very unequally among the more or less silent or richly vocal kinds of animal, and comparatively few have been granted the higher and more joyful kind.

segments.label: §26, codex source block4
segments.text: To discover the source of this difference would be instructive for language too, but perhaps impossible.

segments.label: §26, codex source block5
segments.text: The fact that birds alone possess song might perhaps be explained by their living more freely than all other animals in the element of sound, and in its purer regions, were it not that so many kinds of bird, like the animals that walk on the earth, are restricted to a few monotonous sounds.

segments.label: §26, muse source block1
segments.text: When unarticulated sound takes the place of language, as always in animals and sometimes in man, either need wrings it out, as in adverse feelings, or intention underlies it, in that it lures, warns or calls hither for help, or it streams forth, without need and intention, from the glad feeling of existence, from delight in the loud ringing out of tones.

segments.label: §26, muse source block2
segments.text: The last is the poetic element, a spark glimmering up in animal dullness.

segments.label: §26, muse source block3
segments.text: These different kinds of sounds are very unequally distributed among the more or less mute and richly sounding genera of animals, and to relatively few has the higher and more joyful kind fallen.

segments.label: §26, muse source block4
segments.text: It would also be instructive for language, but perhaps impossible, to fathom whence this diversity stems.

segments.label: §26, muse source block5
segments.text: That birds alone possess song could perhaps be explained from the fact that they live more freely than all other animals in the element of tone and in its purer regions, if so many genera of them were not, like the animals that walk on the earth, bound to a few uniform sounds.

segments.label: §27, de source block1
segments.text: In die Sprache gehen dieselben antreibenden Ursachen über: Noth, Absicht und Gefallen an der Rede.

segments.label: §27, de source block2
segments.text: Aber das letzte bezieht sich in ihr auch, und hauptsächlich, auf den Gedanken, und dadurch kommt eine vierte Ursach hinzu, das Bedürfniss der Mittheilung und Entwicklung der Ideen und Empfindungen durch Gespräch.

segments.label: §27, de source block3
segments.text: Es gehört gewiss zu den irrigsten Behauptungen, die Entstehung der Sprachen vorzugsweise dem Bedürfniss gegenseitiger Hülfsleistung zuzuschreiben.

segments.label: §27, de source block4
segments.text: Der Mensch im Naturstande ist nicht so bedürftig, und dazu hätten, wie man an den Thieren sieht, unarticulirte Laute ausgereicht.

segments.label: §27, de source block5
segments.text: Die Sprache ist, auch in ihren Anfängen, durchaus menschlich.

segments.label: §27, de source block6
segments.text: Auch die Sprachen der sogenannten Wilden, und gerade sie, besitzen eine überall über das Bedürfniss überschiessende Fülle und Mannigfaltigkeit von Ausdrücken, und es giebt wohl in keiner Einöde eine wandernde Familie, die nicht ihre Lieder besässe, denn der Mensch, als Thiergattung, ist wesentlich ein singendes Geschöpf, nur Ideen mit den Tönen verbindend.

segments.label: §27, de source block7
segments.text: Der viel wesentlichere Entstehungsgrund der Sprache ist das Gefallen am Sprechen, und daher ist es auf die Bildung der Sprachen von so wichtigem Einfluss, wie schweigsam oder geschwätzig ein Volk ist.

segments.label: §27, codex source block1
segments.text: The same impelling causes pass into language: distress, intention and pleasure in discourse.

segments.label: §27, codex source block2
segments.text: But in language the last also refers, and chiefly, to thought, and this adds a fourth cause: the need to communicate and develop ideas and feelings through conversation.

segments.label: §27, codex source block3
segments.text: It is surely among the most erroneous assertions to attribute the origin of languages chiefly to the need for mutual assistance.

segments.label: §27, codex source block4
segments.text: Human beings in the state of nature are not so needy, and unarticulated sounds would have sufficed for that purpose, as we see in animals.

segments.label: §27, codex source block5
segments.text: Language, even in its beginnings, is thoroughly human.

segments.label: §27, codex source block6
segments.text: Even the languages of the so-called savages—indeed, precisely those languages—possess an abundance and variety of expressions everywhere exceeding need, and there is probably no wandering family in any wilderness that does not possess its songs; for the human being, considered as an animal species, is essentially a singing creature, only one that connects ideas with sounds.

segments.label: §27, codex source block7
segments.text: The much more essential ground of language's origin is pleasure in speaking, and this is why the degree to which a people is taciturn or talkative has so important an influence on the formation of languages.

segments.text: The far more essential ground of the origin of language is delight in speaking, and hence it is of such important influence on the formation of languages how silent or talkative a people is.

segments.label: §28, de source block1
segments.text: Man muss den Menschen, auch in seinen edelsten Bestrebungen, immer in seiner ganzen Natur, deren eine Seite er mit der Thierheit theilt, betrachten, und daher auch in der Sprache nicht das blosse Tönen übersehen, wodurch gleichsam der thierische Laut in den articulirten übergeht.

segments.label: §28, de source block2
segments.text: Hierbei ist nun zunächst das Verhältniss dieses Tönens zur Ideenbezeichnung bemerkbar.

segments.label: §28, de source block3
segments.text: Es kann dies mit dem Colorit in der Malerei verglichen werden.

segments.label: §28, de source block4
segments.text: Die Sprachen sind darin bald reicher, bald dürftiger, bald freier von schmetterndem Geräusch, bald mehr damit überladen.

segments.label: §28, de source block5
segments.text: Es geschieht aber auch, dass Sprachen überhaupt, oder auf gewissen Bildungsstufen mehr oder weniger ideenloses Schmettern der wirklichen Sprache beimischen, Sylben und selbst Wörter gebrauchen ohne bestimmte Einwirkung auf den Sinn, fast nur zur Ausfüllung des Tones.

segments.label: §28, de source block6
segments.text: Ein gewisses Gefühl mag sich freilich mit allen dieser Art verbinden, dies aber ist auch bei dem unarticulirten Laute möglich.

segments.label: §28, de source block7
segments.text: Durch die Cultur der Sprache fallen nun entweder diese blossen Ausfüllungsworte hinweg, oder werden im günstigeren Falle, durch künstlichere Bearbeitung, Zeichen feiner Nuancen der Ideen oder ihrer Verbindungen.

segments.label: §28, codex source block1
segments.text: Even in their noblest endeavours, human beings must always be considered in their whole nature, one side of which they share with animality; hence we must not overlook in language the mere sounding through which animal sound passes, as it were, into articulated sound.

segments.label: §28, codex source block2
segments.text: What first deserves attention here is the relation of this sounding to the designation of ideas.

segments.label: §28, codex source block3
segments.text: It may be compared with colouring in painting.

segments.label: §28, codex source block4
segments.text: Languages are sometimes richer, sometimes poorer in it, sometimes freer from pealing noise, sometimes more overloaded with it.

segments.label: §28, codex source block5
segments.text: But languages also sometimes, either generally or at certain stages of development, mix more or less thoughtless pealing into actual language, using syllables and even words without any definite effect on the meaning, almost solely to fill out the sound.

segments.label: §28, codex source block6
segments.text: Some feeling may admittedly attach to everything of this kind, but that is possible with unarticulated sound too.

segments.label: §28, codex source block7
segments.text: As language is cultivated, these mere filler words either disappear or, in the more favourable case, become signs of fine nuances of ideas or their connections through more skilful elaboration.

segments.label: §28, muse source block1
segments.text: Man must always be considered, even in his noblest endeavours, in his whole nature, one side of which he shares with animality, and hence in language too one must not overlook the mere sounding through which, as it were, the animal sound passes over into the articulated sound.

segments.label: §28, muse source block2
segments.text: Here the relation of this sounding to the designation of ideas is now first noteworthy.

segments.label: §28, muse source block3
segments.text: This can be compared with colouring in painting.

segments.label: §28, muse source block4
segments.text: Languages are in this respect now richer, now poorer, now freer from blaring noise, now more overloaded with it.

segments.label: §28, muse source block5
segments.text: But it also happens that languages in general, or at certain stages of formation, mix more or less idea-less blaring into real language, use syllables and even words without determinate effect on the sense, almost only for filling out the tone.

segments.label: §28, muse source block6
segments.text: A certain feeling may indeed combine with all things of this kind, but this is also possible in the case of unarticulated sound.

segments.label: §28, muse source block7
segments.text: Through the cultivation of language these mere filling-out words now either fall away, or, in the more favourable case, become through more artful elaboration signs of finer nuances of ideas or of their combinations.

segments.label: §28, astra source block1
segments.text: Even in their noblest strivings, human beings must always be considered in their whole nature, one side of which they share with animality; hence in language too we must not overlook the mere sounding through which, as it were, animal sound passes into articulated sound.

segments.label: §28, astra source block2
segments.text: The first thing to observe here is the relation of this sounding to the designation of ideas.

segments.label: §28, astra source block3
segments.text: It may be compared with colouring in painting.

segments.label: §28, astra source block4
segments.text: Languages are sometimes richer in it, sometimes poorer, sometimes freer of resounding noise, sometimes more overloaded with it.

segments.label: §28, astra source block5
segments.text: It also happens, however, that languages, either generally or at certain stages of development, mix more or less ringing devoid of ideas into actual language, using syllables and even words without any definite effect on the sense, almost solely to fill out the sound.

segments.label: §28, astra source block6
segments.text: A certain feeling may admittedly attach to all expressions of this kind, but that is also possible with unarticulated sound.

segments.label: §28, astra source block7
segments.text: Through the cultivation of language, these mere filler words either disappear or, in the more favourable case, become, through more artful elaboration, signs of fine nuances of ideas or of their connections.

segments.label: §29, de source block1
segments.text: In der Natur des Tones, als solchen, liegt endlich allein die wahre Individualitaet jeder Sprache.

segments.label: §29, de source block2
segments.text: Was man thun und versuchen mag, ihre Eigenthümlichkeiten zu schildern, so bestimmt man nur immer näher und näher die Gattung, welcher sie angehört ;als diese und keine andere Sprache spricht sie sich nur selbst vor dem Ohre aus.

segments.label: §29, de source block3
segments.text: Obgleich das Alphabet der ganzen Menschheit von gewissen, nicht einmal sehr weiten Gränzen umschlossen ist, so hat doch jedes Volk mit eigner Sprache auch sein eignes Lautsystem in der Ausschliessung gewisser Töne, der Vorliebe für andre, der Bestimmung der verschiedenen zur Bezeichnung verschiedener Begriffe, der Behandlung der Töne in ihren Verbindungen u. s. f.

segments.label: §29, de source block4
segments.text: Man kann dies mit dem verschiedenartigen Geschrei und den Tonarten der Thiergattungen vergleichen.

segments.label: §29, de source block5
segments.text: Es ist darin, wenn auch die fortschreitende Entwicklung viel abschliesst, doch etwas Festes, Stammartiges, tief in den Modificationen der Sprachwerkzeuge und dem Tongefühle Gegründetes.

segments.label: §29, de source block6
segments.text: Es unterscheidet aber noch mehr die Stämme, als die Sprachen, da in derselben Sprache einzelne Stämme von allen übrigen durchaus abweichende Töne haben, wie z. B. die Florentiner den hauchenden Kehllaut.

segments.label: §29, de source block7
segments.text: Allein abgesehen von solchen Einzelnheiten, die für die Sprache an sich zufällig erscheinen, hat das Lautsystem auf die wesentlichsten Theile einer jeden den bedeutendsten Einfluss; es ist das erste, worin man sich durchaus fest setzen muss.

segments.label: §29, de source block8
segments.text: Freilich führt dies in eine mühvolle, oft ins Kleinliche gehende Elementaruntersuchung, es sind aber auch lauter in sich kleinliche Einzelnheiten, auf welchen der Totaleindruck der Sprachen beruht, und nichts ist mit dem Studium derselben so unverträglich, als bloss in ihnen das Grosse, Geistige, Vorherrschende aufsuchen zu wollen.

segments.label: §29, de source block9
segments.text: Genaues Eingehen in jede grammatische Subtilitaet, und Spalten der Wörter in ihre Elemente ist durchaus nothwendig, wenn man sich nicht in allen Urtheilen über den Bau und selbst über die Abstammung Irrthümern blossstellen will.

segments.label: §29, codex source block1
segments.text: Ultimately, the true individuality of each language lies solely in the nature of sound as such.

segments.label: §29, codex source block2
segments.text: Whatever one does or attempts in describing its peculiarities, one only defines more and more closely the class to which it belongs; as this language and no other, it expresses itself only by sounding itself before the ear.

segments.label: §29, codex source block3
segments.text: Although the alphabet of all humanity is confined within certain limits, which are not even very wide, every people with a language of its own nevertheless also has its own sound system: in excluding certain sounds, preferring others, assigning different sounds to designate different concepts, handling sounds in their combinations, and so forth.

segments.label: §29, codex source block4
segments.text: This may be compared with the different cries and vocal modes of the kinds of animal.

segments.label: §29, codex source block5
segments.text: Although progressive development brings much to completion, there is nevertheless something fixed and characteristic of a stock in this, deeply grounded in modifications of the organs of speech and in the feeling for sound.

segments.label: §29, codex source block6
segments.text: It distinguishes stocks even more than languages, however, since within the same language particular stocks have sounds entirely different from those of all the others, as the Florentines, for example, have their aspirated guttural.

segments.label: §29, codex source block7
segments.text: Yet apart from such details, which seem accidental to language in itself, the sound system has the most significant influence on the most essential parts of every language; it is the first thing in which one must establish a thoroughly firm footing.

segments.label: §29, codex source block8
segments.text: Admittedly, this leads into laborious elementary investigation, often descending to minutiae; but the total impression of languages rests entirely on details that are minute in themselves, and nothing is more incompatible with studying languages than wanting to seek in them only what is great, mental and predominant.

segments.label: §29, codex source block9
segments.text: Close attention to every grammatical subtlety, and the splitting of words into their elements, are absolutely necessary if one is to avoid exposing every judgement about structure, and even about descent, to error.

segments.label: §29, muse source block1
segments.text: In the nature of tone as such there finally lies alone the true individuality of every language.

segments.label: §29, muse source block2
segments.text: Whatever one may do and attempt to describe its peculiarities, one only ever determines more and more closely the genus to which it belongs; as this and no other language it utters itself only itself before the ear.

segments.label: §29, muse source block3
segments.text: Although the alphabet of the whole of mankind is enclosed by certain limits that are not even very wide, yet every people with a language of its own also has its own system of sounds in the exclusion of certain tones, preference for others, determination of the different ones for the designation of different concepts, treatment of the tones in their combinations, and so forth.

segments.label: §29, muse source block4
segments.text: One can compare this with the diverse crying and the kinds of tone of the animal genera.

segments.label: §29, muse source block5
segments.text: There is in it, even if progressive development rounds much off, something firm, tribal in kind, deeply grounded in the modifications of the organs of speech and in the feeling for tone.

segments.label: §29, muse source block6
segments.text: It distinguishes, however, tribes even more than languages, since in the same language individual tribes have tones wholly deviating from all the rest, as for example the Florentines have the breathing guttural sound.

segments.label: §29, muse source block7
segments.text: But apart from such details, which appear accidental for language in itself, the system of sounds has the most significant influence on the most essential parts of every language; it is the first thing in which one must establish oneself thoroughly.

segments.label: §29, muse source block8
segments.text: This does indeed lead into a laborious elementary investigation often descending into the petty, but it is also nothing but details petty in themselves on which the total impression of languages rests, and nothing is so incompatible with the study of them as wanting to seek out in them merely what is great, mental and predominant.

segments.label: §29, muse source block9
segments.text: Exact attention to every grammatical subtlety, and splitting words into their elements, is thoroughly necessary if one does not want to expose oneself to errors in all judgements about structure and even about descent.

segments.label: §30, de source block1
segments.text: Die wichtigste Ursach, aus welcher die Sprache, vermittelst des Tones, der Wirkung nach aussen bedarf, ist die Geselligkeit, zu welcher der Mensch durch seine Natur unbedingt hingewiesen wird.

segments.label: §30, de source block2
segments.text: Es liegt in derselben aber ein zwiefaches, obgleich in einem dritten Höheren eng Verbundenes: einmal dass alle menschlichen Kräfte sich nur gesellschaftlich vollkommen entwickeln, dass es etwas Gemeinsames in dem ganzen menschlichen Geschlechte giebt, von dem jeder Einzelne eine, das Verlangen nach Vervollständigung durch die andren in sich tragende Bestimmung besitzt.

segments.label: §30, de source block3
segments.text: Beides ist gerade bei der Sprache besonders wichtig.

segments.label: §30, de source block4
segments.text: Denn je grösser und bewegter das gesellige Zusammenwirken auf sie ist, je mehr gewinnt sie unter übrigens gleichen Umständen, und auf jenem eben erwähnten Gemeinsamen beruht die Möglichkeit alles Verständnisses.

segments.label: §30, codex source block1
segments.text: The most important reason why language needs to act outwards through sound is sociability, towards which human beings are unconditionally directed by their nature.

segments.label: §30, codex source block2
segments.text: Sociability contains two things, though they are closely connected in a third, higher one: first, that all human powers develop fully only in society; and second, that there is something common to the whole human race, of which each individual possesses a particular determination carrying within it the desire to be completed by the others.

segments.label: §30, codex source block3
segments.text: Both are especially important precisely in language.

segments.label: §30, codex source block4
segments.text: For the greater and more animated the social interplay acting upon language, the more it gains, other circumstances being equal; and the possibility of all understanding rests on the common element just mentioned.

segments.label: §30, muse source block1
segments.text: The most important cause from which language, by means of tone, needs outward effect is sociability, to which man is unconditionally directed by his nature.

segments.label: §30, muse source block2
segments.text: But in it there lies a twofold element, although closely united in a third and higher one: first, that all human powers develop perfectly only socially; that there is something common in the whole human race of which every individual possesses a determination carrying within itself the desire for completion through the others.

segments.label: §30, muse source block3
segments.text: Both are especially important precisely in the case of language.

segments.label: §30, muse source block4
segments.text: For the greater and more animated the social co-operation upon it is, the more it gains, other circumstances being equal, and on that common element just mentioned rests the possibility of all understanding.

segments.label: §31, de source block1
segments.text: Auch die Geselligkeit lässt sich ohne Einseitigkeit nicht aus dem blossen Bedürfniss ableiten.

segments.label: §31, de source block2
segments.text: Sie beruht nicht einmal in den Thieren darauf.

segments.label: §31, de source block3
segments.text: Keines ist leicht so sich in seiner Stärke alleingenügend, als der gerade vorzugsweise in Heerden lebende Elephant.

segments.label: §31, de source block4
segments.text: Auch in den Thieren entspringt daher die bei einigen Gattungen grössere, bei andren geringere Neigung zur Geselligkeit aus viel tiefer in ihrem Wesen liegenden Ursachen.

segments.label: §31, de source block5
segments.text: Es ist nur uns unmöglich, dieselben zu ergründen, weil wir uns gar keinen Begriff von der doch nicht abzuläugnenden Fähigkeit der Thiere machen können, wahrzunehmen, zu empfinden und Wahrnehmungen zu verknüpfen.

segments.label: §31, de source block6
segments.text: Im Menschen aber ist das Denken wesentlich an gesellschaftliches Daseyn gebunden, und der Mensch bedarf, abgesehen von allen körperlichen und Empfindungsbeziehungen, zum blossen Denken eines dem Ich entsprechenden Du , der Begriff erreicht seine Bestimmtheit und Klarheit erst durch das Zurückstrahlen aus einer fremden Denkkraft.

segments.label: §31, de source block7
segments.text: Er wird erzeugt, indem er sich aus der bewegten Masse des Vorstellens losreisst, und dem Subject gegenüber zum Object bildet.

segments.label: §31, de source block8
segments.text: Es genügt jedoch nicht, dass diese Spaltung in dem Subjecte allein vorgeht, die Objectivität ist erst vollendet, wenn der Vorstellende den Gedanken wirklich ausser sich erblickt, was nur in einem andren, gleich ihm vorstellenden und denkenden Wesen möglich ist.

segments.label: §31, de source block9
segments.text: Zwischen Denkkraft und Denkkraft aber ist die einzige Vermittlerin die Sprache, und so entsteht auch hier ihre Nothwendigkeit zur Vollendung des Gedanken.

segments.label: §31, de source block10
segments.text: Es liegt aber auch in der Sprache selbst ein unabänderlicher Dualismus, und alles Sprechen ist auf Anrede und Erwiederung gestellt.

segments.label: §31, de source block11
segments.text: Das Wort ist kein Gegenstand, vielmehr den Gegenständen gegenüber etwas Subjectives, nun aber soll es im Geiste des Denkenden doch ein Object, von ihm erzeugt und auf ihn zurückwirkend seyn.

segments.label: §31, de source block12
segments.text: Damit es sich nun von einem blossen Scheinobjecte, einem Traumbilde, unterscheide, muss es Wesenheit in einem Hörenden und Erwiedernden gewinnen.

segments.label: §31, de source block13
segments.text: Diesen Urtypus aller Sprachen drückt das Pronomen durch die Unterscheidung der zweiten Person von der dritten aus.

segments.label: §31, de source block14
segments.text: Ich und Er sind wirklich verschiedne Gegenstände, und mit ihnen ist eigentlich Alles erschöpft, denn sie heissen mit andren Worten Ich und Nichtich.

segments.label: §31, de source block15
segments.text: Du aber ist ein dem Ich gegenübergestelltes Er.

segments.label: §31, de source block16
segments.text: Indem Ich und Er auf innrer und äusserer Wahrnehmung beruhen, liegt in dem Du Spontaneitaet der Wahl.

segments.label: §31, de source block17
segments.text: Es ist auch ein Nicht-Ich, aber nicht, wie das Er, in der Sphäre aller Wesen, sondern in einer andren, der eines durch Einwirkung gemeinsamen Handelns.

segments.label: §31, de source block18
segments.text: In dem Er selbst liegt nun dadurch, ausser dem Nicht-Ich, auch ein Nicht-Du, und es ist nicht bloss einem von ihnen, sondern beiden entgegengesetzt.

segments.label: §31, de source block19
segments.text: Dass dieselbe Pronominalform durch alle Sprachen durchgeht, zeigt, dass, nach dem Gefühl aller Völker, das Sprechen in seinem Wesen voraussetzt, dass der Sprechende, sich gegenüber, einen Angeredeten von allen Andren unterscheidet.

segments.label: §31, de source block20
segments.text: In mehreren Amerikanischen Sprachen zeigt sich sogar darin eine besondre Sorgfalt die zweite Person herauszuheben, dass sie auch in der ersten des Plurals durch verschiedene Formen andeuten, ob der Angeredete darunter begriffen, oder ausgeschlossen ist.

segments.label: §31, codex source block1
segments.text: Sociability too cannot be derived from mere need without one-sidedness.

segments.label: §31, codex source block2
segments.text: It does not rest on need even in animals.

segments.label: §31, codex source block3
segments.text: Scarcely any animal is so self-sufficient in its strength as the elephant, which nevertheless lives predominantly in herds.

segments.label: §31, codex source block4
segments.text: Thus in animals too, the greater inclination towards sociability in some kinds and the lesser inclination in others arise from causes lying much deeper in their being.

segments.label: §31, codex source block5
segments.text: It is simply impossible for us to fathom these causes, because we can form no conception at all of animals' nevertheless undeniable ability to perceive, to feel and to connect perceptions.

segments.label: §31, codex source block6
segments.text: In human beings, however, thinking is essentially bound to social existence; quite apart from all bodily relations and relations of feeling, a human being needs, simply in order to think, a You corresponding to the I: a concept attains its definiteness and clarity only by being reflected back from another power of thought.

segments.label: §31, codex source block7
segments.text: It is produced by breaking free from the moving mass of representation and forming itself into an object confronting the subject.

segments.label: §31, codex source block8
segments.text: Yet it is not enough for this division to take place within the subject alone; objectivity is complete only when the person forming representations actually sees the thought outside himself, which is possible only in another being that forms representations and thinks as he does.

segments.label: §31, codex source block9
segments.text: But language is the sole mediator between one power of thought and another, and so here too its necessity for the completion of thought becomes apparent.

segments.label: §31, codex source block10
segments.text: There is also an unalterable dualism within language itself, and all speaking is directed towards address and reply.

segments.label: §31, codex source block11
segments.text: The word is not a thing; rather, in relation to things it is something subjective, yet in the mind of the thinker it is nevertheless to be an object, produced by him and acting back upon him.

segments.label: §31, codex source block12
segments.text: To distinguish itself from a merely apparent object, a dream image, it must acquire substantial reality in someone who hears and replies.

segments.label: §31, codex source block13
segments.text: The pronoun expresses this original type of all languages by distinguishing the second person from the third.

segments.label: §31, codex source block14
segments.text: I and He are genuinely different objects, and in fact they exhaust everything, for in other words they mean I and Not-I.

segments.label: §31, codex source block15
segments.text: You, however, is a He placed opposite the I.

segments.label: §31, codex source block16
segments.text: Whereas I and He rest on inward and outward perception, You involves spontaneity of choice.

segments.label: §31, codex source block17
segments.text: It too is a Not-I, but unlike He it lies not in the sphere of all beings, but in another sphere, that of action made common through influence.

segments.label: §31, codex source block18
segments.text: He itself thereby comes to contain, besides Not-I, also Not-You, and is opposed not merely to one of them but to both.

segments.label: §31, codex source block19
segments.text: The fact that the same pronominal form runs through all languages shows that, according to the feeling of all peoples, speaking essentially presupposes that the speaker distinguishes, opposite himself, an addressee from everyone else.

segments.label: §31, codex source block20
segments.text: Several American languages even show particular care in singling out the second person by indicating, through different forms in the first-person plural as well, whether the addressee is included or excluded.

segments.label: §31, muse source block1
segments.text: Sociability too cannot without one-sidedness be derived from mere need.

segments.label: §31, muse source block2
segments.text: It does not even in animals rest on that.

segments.label: §31, muse source block3
segments.text: No animal is easily so sufficient to itself in its strength as the elephant, which lives precisely pre-eminently in herds.

segments.label: §31, muse source block4
segments.text: In animals too, therefore, the inclination to sociability, greater in some genera and lesser in others, arises from causes lying much deeper in their being.

segments.label: §31, muse source block5
segments.text: It is only impossible for us to fathom them, because we can form no concept at all of the capacity of animals, which is nevertheless not to be denied, to perceive, to feel and to combine perceptions.

segments.label: §31, muse source block6
segments.text: In man, however, thinking is essentially bound to social existence, and man needs, apart from all bodily and feeling relations, for mere thinking a Thou corresponding to the I; the concept attains its determinateness and clarity only through being reflected back from a foreign power of thought.

segments.label: §31, muse source block7
segments.text: It is produced in that it tears itself loose from the moved mass of representing and forms itself, over against the subject, into an object.

segments.label: §31, muse source block8
segments.text: It is not sufficient, however, that this division takes place in the subject alone; objectivity is only completed when the representing person really beholds the thought outside himself, which is possible only in another being representing and thinking like him.

segments.label: §31, muse source block9
segments.text: Between power of thought and power of thought, however, the sole mediatress is language, and so here too its necessity for the completion of thought arises.

segments.label: §31, muse source block10
segments.text: But there also lies in language itself an unalterable dualism, and all speaking is set upon address and reply.

segments.label: §31, muse source block11
segments.text: The word is not an object; rather, over against objects, it is something subjective, but now in the mind of the thinking person it is nevertheless to be an object, produced by him and reacting upon him.

segments.label: §31, muse source block12
segments.text: In order that it may now distinguish itself from a mere apparent object, a dream-image, it must gain real being in a person hearing and replying.

segments.label: §31, muse source block13
segments.text: The pronoun expresses this original type of all languages through the distinction of the second person from the third.

segments.label: §31, muse source block14
segments.text: I and He are really different objects, and with them everything is really exhausted, for in other words they are called I and Non-I.

segments.label: §31, muse source block15
segments.text: Thou, however, is a He placed over against the I.

segments.label: §31, muse source block16
segments.text: Whereas I and He rest on inner and outer perception, in the Thou there lies spontaneity of choice.

segments.label: §31, muse source block17
segments.text: It too is a Non-I, but not, like He, in the sphere of all beings, but in another sphere, that of a common acting through mutual influence.

segments.label: §31, muse source block18
segments.text: In the He itself there now thereby lies, besides the Non-I, also a Non-Thou, and it is opposed not merely to one of them, but to both.

segments.label: §31, muse source block19
segments.text: That the same pronominal form runs through all languages shows that, according to the feeling of all peoples, speaking in its essence presupposes that the speaker distinguishes, over against himself, a person addressed from all others.

segments.label: §31, muse source block20
segments.text: In several American languages a special care to single out the second person even shows itself in this, that they also indicate in the first person of the plural through different forms whether the person addressed is included under it or excluded from it.

segments.label: §32, de source block1
segments.text: Was sich auf diese Weise ergiebt, wenn man den einfachen Act des Denkens zu zergliedern versucht, das wiederholt sich im geistigen Leben des Menschen unaufhörlich; die gesellige Mittheilung gewährt ihm Ueberzeugung und Anregung.

segments.label: §32, de source block2
segments.text: Die Denkkraft bedarf etwas ihr Gleiches und doch von ihr Geschiedenes.

segments.label: §32, de source block3
segments.text: Durch das Gleiche wird sie entzündet, durch das von ihr Geschiedne erhält sie einen Prüfstein der Wesenheit ihrer innern Erzeugungen.

segments.label: §32, de source block4
segments.text: Denn der Mensch kann in seiner veränderlichen Beschränktheit die Wahrheit, als das schrankenlos Feste, nur als ausser sich Liegendes ansehn, und sein ganzes geistiges Streben ist ein Anringen an sie, und das mächtigste Mittel ihr nahe zu kommen, seinen Abstand von ihr zu messen, ist die gesellige Vereinigung.

segments.label: §32, de source block5
segments.text: So ist die Sprache ein nothwendiges Erforderniss zur ersten Erzeugung des Gedanken, und zur fortschreitenden Ausbildung des Geistes.

segments.label: §32, codex source block1
segments.text: What emerges in this way when we attempt to analyse the simple act of thinking repeats itself unceasingly in human mental life; social communication affords conviction and stimulation.

segments.label: §32, codex source block2
segments.text: The power of thought needs something like itself and yet distinct from itself.

segments.label: §32, codex source block3
segments.text: It is kindled by what is like itself, while what is distinct from it supplies a touchstone for the substantial reality of its inward productions.

segments.label: §32, codex source block4
segments.text: For in his changeable limitation, the human being can regard truth, as what is boundlessly fixed, only as something lying outside himself; all his mental striving is a struggle towards it, and social association is the most powerful means of approaching it and measuring his distance from it.

segments.label: §32, codex source block5
segments.text: Language is thus a necessary requirement both for the first production of thought and for the progressive development of the mind.

segments.label: §32, muse source block1
segments.text: What results in this way when one attempts to analyse the simple act of thinking repeats itself incessantly in the mental life of man; social communication affords him conviction and stimulation.

segments.label: §32, muse source block2
segments.text: The power of thought needs something equal to it and yet separated from it.

segments.label: §32, muse source block3
segments.text: Through what is equal it is kindled; through what is separated from it it receives a touchstone of the real being of its inner productions.

segments.label: §32, muse source block4
segments.text: For man in his changeable limitation can regard truth, as what is fixed without bounds, only as lying outside himself, and his whole mental striving is a wrestling towards it, and the mightiest means of coming near to it, of measuring his distance from it, is social union.

segments.label: §32, muse source block5
segments.text: Thus language is a necessary requirement for the first production of thought and for the progressive formation of the mind.
