segments.label: §33, de source block1
segments.text: Die geistige Mittheilung setzt, von dem Einen zum Andren übergehend, in diesem etwas ihm mit jenem Gemeinsames voraus.

segments.label: §33, de source block2
segments.text: Man versteht das gehörte Wort nur, weil man es selbst hätte sagen können.

segments.label: §33, de source block3
segments.text: Es kann in der Seele nichts, als durch eigne Thätigkeit vorhanden seyn, und das Verstehen ist ebensowohl, als das Sprechen, selbst eine Anregung der Sprachkraft, nur in ihrer innern Empfänglichkeit, wie dieses in seiner äusseren Thätigkeit, daher es dem Menschen auch so natürlich ist, das eben Verstandene gleich wieder auszusagen.

segments.label: §33, de source block4
segments.text: Es liegt daher in jedem Menschen die Sprache in ihrem ganzen Umfange, was aber nichts anders sagen will, als dass jeder ein durch eine bestimmt modificirte Kraft, anstossend und beschränkend, geregeltes Streben besitzt, die ganze Sprache, wie es äussere oder innere Veranlassung herbeiführt, nach und nach hervorzubringen, oder hervorgebracht zu verstehen.

segments.label: §33, de source block5
segments.text: Diese Kraft ist, wie jede, natürlich eine individuelle, aber nach allen den Gattungsbegriffen individualisirt, vermöge welcher jede Gattung gegen eine allgemeinere höhere als Individuum genommen werden kann.

segments.label: §33, de source block6
segments.text: Sie ist mithin die allgemeine Sprachkraft, bestimmt durch den Völkerstamm, die Nation, die Mundart, dann in ihren Lautzeichen feststehend, in der Art des Gebrauches bestimmt durch alle so mächtig auf das Gemüth einwirkenden inneren Beschaffenheiten und äusseren Zufälligkeiten, dass die Wirkung in der Sprache fühlbar wird, endlich durch die in keine allgemeinere Kategorie mehr zu bringende Individualität.

segments.label: §33, de source block7
segments.text: Jede dieser bis zum Allgemeinsten aufsteigenden Stufen bildet eine Sprachsphäre, die durch das allem unter ihr Begriffenen Gemeinsame, und durch das von dem ausser ihr Befindlichen Verschiedne bestimmt wird.

segments.label: §33, de source block8
segments.text: Bei jeder allgemeinen Sprachuntersuchung wird es daher zur nothwendigen Aufgabe, bei den verschiedenen in Betrachtung kommenden Punkten, z. B. beim Alphabet, die Gränzen der menschlichen Sprache überhaupt aufzusuchen, in diesem weiten Gebiete die kleineren, wieder in einander begriffenen der einzelnen Sprachgattungen abzusondern, und überall dahin zu sehen, ob diese den Begriff, von welchem aus die Eintheilung gemacht ist, erfüllen, mithin in ihrem geschichtlichen Daseyn ein durch die Idee gegebenes Ganzes bilden.

segments.label: §33, codex source block1
segments.text: Mental communication, in passing from one person to another, presupposes in the latter something he has in common with the former.

segments.label: §33, codex source block2
segments.text: We understand a word we hear only because we could have said it ourselves.

segments.label: §33, codex source block3
segments.text: Nothing can be present in the soul except through its own activity, and understanding, just as much as speaking, is itself a stimulation of the power of language, only in its inward receptivity, as speaking is in its outward activity; hence it is also so natural for human beings immediately to say again what they have just understood.

segments.label: §33, codex source block4
segments.text: Language therefore lies within every human being in its entire extent; but this means nothing other than that everyone possesses a striving, regulated through the prompting and limiting action of a specifically modified power, gradually to produce the whole language, or to understand it when produced, as inward or outward occasions arise.

segments.label: §33, codex source block5
segments.text: Like every power, this is naturally an individual one, but it is individualised according to all those concepts of classes by virtue of which each class can be taken as an individual in relation to a higher, more general class.

segments.label: §33, codex source block6
segments.text: It is thus the general power of language, determined by the ethnic stock, the nation and the dialect; then, with its sound signs fixed, determined in its manner of use by all the inward qualities and outward contingencies that act upon the mind so powerfully that their effect becomes perceptible in language; and finally determined by the individuality that can no longer be brought under any more general category.

segments.label: §33, codex source block7
segments.text: Each of these levels, ascending to the most general, forms a linguistic sphere determined by what is common to everything included within it and by what distinguishes it from everything outside it.

segments.label: §33, codex source block8
segments.text: In every general investigation of language it therefore becomes necessary, at the various points under consideration—for example, the alphabet—to seek the limits of human language in general, to distinguish within this wide domain the smaller, again mutually nested domains of particular classes of language, and everywhere to consider whether these fulfil the concept from which the division was made, and thus form in their historical existence a whole given by the idea.

segments.label: §33, muse source block1
segments.text: Mental communication, passing over from the one to the other, presupposes in the latter something common to him with the former.

segments.label: §33, muse source block2
segments.text: One understands the heard word only because one could oneself have said it.

segments.label: §33, muse source block3
segments.text: Nothing can be present in the soul except through its own activity, and understanding is just as much as speaking itself a stimulation of the power of language, only in its inner receptivity, as speaking is in its outer activity, hence it is also so natural for man at once to utter again what he has just understood.

segments.label: §33, muse source block4
segments.text: Hence there lies in every human being language in its whole extent, which, however, means nothing else than that everyone possesses a striving, regulated by a determinately modified power impelling and limiting, gradually to produce the whole language, as outer or inner occasion brings it about, or to understand it when produced.

segments.label: §33, muse source block5
segments.text: This power is, like every power, naturally an individual one, but individualized according to all the generic concepts by virtue of which every genus can be taken, in relation to a more general and higher one, as an individual.

segments.label: §33, muse source block6
segments.text: It is therefore the general power of language, determined by the tribal stock, the nation, the dialect, then fixed in its sound-signs, determined in the manner of use by all inner qualities and outer accidents acting so powerfully on the inner mind that the effect becomes perceptible in language, and finally by the individuality that can no longer be brought under any more general category.

segments.label: §33, muse source block7
segments.text: Each of these stages, ascending to the most general, forms a sphere of language, which is determined by what is common to everything comprised under it and by what is different from what is situated outside it.

segments.label: §33, muse source block8
segments.text: In every general investigation of language it therefore becomes a necessary task, at the various points coming into consideration, for example in the alphabet, to seek out the limits of human language in general, in this wide domain to separate off the smaller domains, again comprised within one another, of the individual genera of language, and everywhere to see whether these fulfil the concept from which the division is made, and thus in their historical existence form a whole given through the idea.

segments.label: §33, astra source block1
segments.text: Mental communication, in passing from one person to another, presupposes in the latter something common to both.

segments.label: §33, astra source block2
segments.text: We understand a word we hear only because we could have said it ourselves.

segments.label: §33, astra source block3
segments.text: Nothing can be present in the soul except through its own activity, and understanding, just as much as speaking, is itself an activation of linguistic power: understanding activates its inward receptivity, as speaking activates its outward activity. Hence it is also so natural for a person immediately to say again what has just been understood.

segments.label: §33, astra source block4
segments.text: Language therefore lies within every human being in its full extent; but this means only that everyone possesses a striving, regulated through the impulse and limitation supplied by a power modified in a particular way, gradually to produce the whole language, or to understand it when produced, as external or internal occasions call for it.

segments.label: §33, astra source block5
segments.text: This power, like every power, is naturally an individual one, but it is individualized according to all those generic concepts by virtue of which each genus can be taken as an individual in relation to a higher, more general genus.

segments.label: §33, astra source block6
segments.text: It is thus the general linguistic power, determined by the ethnic stock, the nation and the dialect; then, with its sound signs established, determined in its manner of use by all the inner qualities and external contingencies that act so powerfully on the inner life that their effect becomes perceptible in language; and finally determined by the individuality that can no longer be brought under any more general category.

segments.label: §33, astra source block7
segments.text: Each of these stages, ascending to the most general, forms a linguistic sphere determined by what is common to everything included within it and by what differs from everything outside it.

segments.label: §33, astra source block8
segments.text: Every general investigation of language must therefore, for each of the various points under consideration—for example, the alphabet—seek out the limits of human language in general, distinguish within this broad domain the smaller, mutually nested domains of the particular classes of languages, and everywhere examine whether these fulfil the concept from which the division proceeds, and thus form in their historical existence a whole given by the idea.

segments.label: §34, de source block1
segments.text: Jede Vielfachheit des in sich Gleichartigen führt diese Aufgabe mit sich, und vorzugsweise bei Untersuchungen, die, wie die die Sprache betreffenden, nicht bloss historisch zu erkennen und darzustellen, sondern teleologisch auf die Sprache und den Menschen bildend zurückzuwirken geführt werden.

segments.label: §34, de source block2
segments.text: Den allgemeinen Zusammenhang der Sprachen erklärt nun zwar allerdings die Gleichartigkeit der menschlichen Natur, in der ähnliche Kräfte nach gleichen Gesetzen wirken.

segments.label: §34, de source block3
segments.text: Eine tiefere Untersuchung und vollere Würdigung der Sprache scheint mir aber noch viel weiter und auf einen Punkt zu führen, zu dem ich bis jetzt nur durch leichtere Betrachtungen den Weg habe bahnen wollen, und auf dem keine weitere Erklärung möglich ist, wie denn keine metaphysische d. h. auf die Ergründung des Seyns an sich gegründete Untersuchung weiter als an das Ende des zu Erklärenden zu leiten vermag.

segments.label: §34, de source block4
segments.text: Mir nun — denn ich spreche dies lieber in dem Tone innerer Ueberzeugung, als mit der Zuversicht allgemeiner Behauptung aus — scheint das Wesen der Sprache verkannt, der geistige Process ihrer Entstehung (nicht der an sich, sondern auch der im jedesmaligen Sprechen und Verstehen) nur scheinbar erklärt, und ihre mächtige Einwirkung auf das Gemüth unrichtig gewürdigt zu werden, wenn man das Menschengeschlecht als zahllose zu derselben Gattung gehörende Naturen, und nicht vielmehr als Eine in zahllose Individuen zerspaltene betrachtet, eine Ansicht, zu der man auch in ganz andren Beziehungen, als in der der Sprache, und von ganz anderen Punkten aus gelangt.

segments.label: §34, de source block5
segments.text: Die Verschiedenheit der beiden einander gegenüber gestellten Behauptungen ist einleuchtend, da die innere Verwandtschaft des Menschengeschlechts nach der letzteren auf der Einheit des Wesens desselben, nach der ersteren nur auf der Einheit der Idee beruht, welche dasselbe, betrachtend oder schaffend, zusammenfasst.

segments.label: §34, codex source block1
segments.text: Every multiplicity of things alike in kind brings this task with it, especially in investigations which, like those concerning language, are conducted not merely to gain and present historical knowledge, but teleologically to act back formatively upon language and human beings.

segments.label: §34, codex source block2
segments.text: The general interconnectedness of languages is certainly explained by the likeness in kind of human nature, in which similar powers operate according to the same laws.

segments.label: §34, codex source block3
segments.text: Yet a deeper investigation and fuller appreciation of language seem to me to lead much further, to a point towards which I have so far sought to prepare the way only through less demanding reflections, and at which no further explanation is possible; for no metaphysical investigation—that is, one grounded in fathoming being in itself—can lead beyond the point where what is to be explained ends.

segments.label: §34, codex source block4
segments.text: To me—for I prefer to express this in the tone of inward conviction rather than with the assurance of a universal assertion—the essence of language seems to be misunderstood, the mental process of its genesis—not that in itself, but also that in each act of speaking and understanding—only seemingly explained, and its powerful influence on the mind incorrectly appreciated, if the human race is regarded as countless natures belonging to the same species, rather than as one nature divided into countless individuals: a view reached in quite other connections than that of language, and from quite different starting points.

segments.label: §34, codex source block5
segments.text: The difference between the two opposed assertions is evident, since on the latter view the inward kinship of the human race rests on the unity of its being, whereas on the former it rests only on the unity of the idea that encompasses it, whether in contemplation or in creation.

segments.label: §34, muse source block1
segments.text: Every multiplicity of what is in itself of the same kind brings this task with it, and pre-eminently in investigations which, like those concerning language, are conducted not merely in order historically to know and present, but teleologically so as to react formatively upon language and man.

segments.label: §34, muse source block2
segments.text: The general connexion of languages is indeed explained by the sameness of kind of human nature, in which similar powers act according to the same laws.

segments.label: §34, muse source block3
segments.text: A deeper investigation and fuller appreciation of language seems to me, however, to lead much further, and to a point to which I have hitherto wished only to clear the way through easier considerations, and at which no further explanation is possible, just as no metaphysical investigation, that is, one grounded on fathoming being in itself, can lead further than to the end of what is to be explained.

segments.label: §34, muse source block4
segments.text: Now to me — for I utter this preferably in the tone of inner conviction rather than with the confidence of general assertion — the essence of language seems to be misconceived, the mental process of its origin (not that in itself, but also that in each act of speaking and understanding) only apparently explained, and its powerful effect on the inner mind incorrectly appreciated, if one regards the human race as countless natures belonging to the same genus, and not rather as One nature split into countless individuals, a view to which one also arrives in wholly other relations than that of language, and from wholly other points.

segments.label: §34, muse source block5
segments.text: The difference between the two assertions placed opposite each other is evident, since the inner relationship of the human race according to the latter rests on the unity of its being, according to the former only on the unity of the idea which, contemplating or creating, comprehends it.

segments.label: §34, astra source block1
segments.text: Every multiplicity of things alike in kind brings this task with it, especially in investigations such as those concerning language, which are undertaken not merely to gain and present historical knowledge, but teleologically, to act back upon language and human beings in a formative way.

segments.label: §34, astra source block2
segments.text: The general interconnectedness of languages is indeed explained by the similarity in kind of human nature, in which similar powers operate according to the same laws.

segments.label: §34, astra source block3
segments.text: But a deeper investigation and fuller appreciation of language seem to me to lead much further, to a point towards which I have so far sought to prepare the way only through less demanding reflections, and at which no further explanation is possible. For no metaphysical investigation—that is, one grounded in an inquiry into being in itself—can lead beyond the endpoint of what is to be explained.

segments.label: §34, astra source block4
segments.text: To me, then—for I prefer to express this in the tone of inner conviction rather than with the assurance of a general assertion—it seems that the essence of language is misconceived, the mental process of its emergence only apparently explained—not just its emergence as such, but also its emergence in each act of speaking and understanding—and its powerful influence on the inner life wrongly assessed, if humanity is regarded as countless natures belonging to the same species, rather than as one nature divided into countless individuals. This latter view is also reached in contexts quite different from language, and from entirely different starting points.

segments.label: §34, astra source block5
segments.text: The difference between these two opposed assertions is evident: according to the latter, humanity's inner kinship rests on the unity of its essence; according to the former, it rests only on the unity of the idea that comprehends humanity, whether in contemplation or in creation.

segments.label: §35, de source block1
segments.text: In der Art dieser Verwandtschaft liegt das Geheimniss der menschlichen Individualität verschlossen, das man zugleich als das des menschlichen Daseyns ansehen kann.

segments.label: §35, de source block2
segments.text: Es ist der Punkt, in dem sich in einem auf den irdischen folgenden Zustande vorzüglich eine Verschiedenheit erwarten lässt, die dann, wenn Bewusstseyn beide Zustände verknüpfte, zugleich eine durchgängige Umänderung aller bisherigen Ansichten hervorbringen würde.

segments.label: §35, de source block3
segments.text: Erklären und ergründen lässt sich dies Geheimniss nicht, aber zur richtigen Erklärung der Erscheinungen und zur Richtung des intellectuellen Strebens muss man sich hüten, das wahre Wesen jener Verwandtschaft der menschlichen Individualität zu verkennen, es bloss aus logischen und discursiven Begriffen [zu] schöpfen, und es nicht vielmehr aus der Tiefe des inneren Gefühls, und in einem die Untersuchung bis zu ihren Endpunkten verfolgenden Nachdenken aufzufassen.

segments.label: §35, de source block4
segments.text: Man gewinnt daher schon, wenn man die im Vorigen als die richtige angegebene Ansicht auch nur als geahndete Möglichkeit stehen lässt, sich nicht in die entgegengesetzte zu verschliessen.

segments.label: §35, codex source block1
segments.text: The nature of this kinship holds the secret of human individuality, which may also be regarded as the secret of human existence.

segments.label: §35, codex source block2
segments.text: This is the point at which one might especially expect a difference in a state following earthly life, a difference which, if consciousness linked the two states, would at the same time bring about a complete transformation of all previous views.

segments.label: §35, codex source block3
segments.text: This secret cannot be explained or fathomed; but to explain phenomena correctly and give direction to intellectual striving, we must guard against misunderstanding the true essence of that kinship of human individuality, against deriving it merely from logical and discursive concepts, rather than grasping it from the depths of inward feeling and through reflection that pursues the investigation to its furthest points.

segments.label: §35, codex source block4
segments.text: Something is therefore already gained if we leave the view identified above as correct standing even as a dimly apprehended possibility, so as not to shut ourselves within the opposite view.

segments.label: §35, muse source block1
segments.text: In the manner of this relationship lies locked the mystery of human individuality, which can at the same time be regarded as the mystery of human existence.

segments.label: §35, muse source block2
segments.text: It is the point at which, in a state following the earthly one, a difference may pre-eminently be expected, which then, if consciousness connected both states, would at the same time produce a thoroughgoing alteration of all previous views.

segments.label: §35, muse source block3
segments.text: This mystery cannot be explained and fathomed, but for the correct explanation of appearances and for the direction of intellectual striving one must beware of misconceiving the true being of that relationship of human individuality, of drawing it merely from logical and discursive concepts, and of not rather apprehending it from the depth of inner feeling and in a reflection that pursues the investigation to its end-points.

segments.label: §35, muse source block4
segments.text: One therefore already gains if one lets the view indicated in what precedes as the correct one stand even only as a divined possibility, and does not shut oneself up in the opposite view.

segments.label: §35, astra source block1
segments.text: The secret of human individuality, which may also be regarded as the secret of human existence, lies enclosed in the nature of this kinship.

segments.label: §35, astra source block2
segments.text: This is the point at which a difference might especially be expected in a state following the earthly one, a difference that, if consciousness connected the two states, would also bring about a thorough transformation of all previous views.

segments.label: §35, astra source block3
segments.text: This secret cannot be explained or fathomed; but to explain appearances correctly and give direction to intellectual striving, we must take care not to misconceive the true nature of that kinship of human individuality, not [to] derive it solely from logical and discursive concepts, but rather to grasp it from the depths of inner feeling and through reflection that pursues the investigation to its furthest limits.

segments.label: §35, astra source block4
segments.text: It is therefore already a gain to leave standing, even as no more than an intuited possibility, the view indicated above as correct, and so avoid shutting oneself within the opposite view.

segments.label: §36, de source block1
segments.text: Was für mich am überzeugendsten gegen diese spricht, ist das oben Gesagte: dass auch das Verstehen ganz auf der inneren Selbstthätigkeit beruht, und das Sprechen mit einander nur ein gegenseitiges Wecken der im Hörenden befindlichen Sprachkraft ist.

segments.label: §36, de source block2
segments.text: Das Begreifen von Worten ist durchaus etwas Andres, als das Verstehen unarticulirter Laute, und fasst weit mehr in sich, als das blosse gegenseitige Hervorrufen des Lauts und des angedeuteten Gegenstandes.

segments.label: §36, de source block3
segments.text: Das Wort kann allerdings auch als untheilbares Ganzes genommen werden, wie man auch in der Schrift wohl den Sinn einer Wortgruppe erkennt, ohne noch ihrer alphabetischen Zusammensetzung gewiss zu seyn, und es wäre möglich, dass die Seele des Kindes in den ersten Anfängen des Verstehens so verführe.

segments.label: §36, de source block4
segments.text: So wie aber nicht bloss das thierische Empfindungsvermögen, sondern die menschliche Sprachkraft angeregt wird (und es mag wohl auch im Kinde keinen Moment geben, wo dies, wenn auch noch so schwach, nicht der Fall wäre), so wird auch das Wort, als articulirt, vernommen.

segments.label: §36, de source block5
segments.text: Nun aber ist dasjenige, was die Articulation dem blossen Hervorrufen seiner Bedeutung (welches natürlich auch durch sie in höherer Vollkommenheit geschieht) hinzufügt, dass sie das Wort unmittelbar durch seine Form als einen Theil eines unendlichen Ganzen, einer Sprache, darstellt.

segments.label: §36, de source block6
segments.text: Denn es ist durch sie, auch in einzelnen Wörtern, die Möglichkeit gegeben, aus den Elementen dieser eine wirklich bis ins Unendliche gehende Anzahl anderer Wörter nach bestimmenden Gefühlen und Regeln zu bilden, und dadurch unter allen Wörtern eine Verwandtschaft, entsprechend der Verwandtschaft der Begriffe, zu stiften.

segments.label: §36, de source block7
segments.text: Die Seele würde aber von diesem künstlichen Mechanismus gar keine Ahndung erhalten, die Articulation ebensowenig, als der Blinde die Farbe, begreifen, wenn ihr nicht eine Kraft beiwohnte, jene Möglichkeit zur Wirklichkeit zu bringen.

segments.label: §36, de source block8
segments.text: Das Sprechenlernen der Kinder ist nicht ein Zumessen von Wörtern, Niederlegen im Gedächtniss, und Wiedernachlallen mit den Lippen, sondern ein Wachsen des Sprachvermögens durch Alter und Uebung.

segments.label: §36, de source block9
segments.text: Das Gehörte thut mehr, als bloss sich mitzutheilen, es schickt die Seele an, auch das noch nicht Gehörte leichter zu verstehen, macht längst Gehörtes, aber damals halb oder gar nicht Verstandenes, indem die Gleichartigkeit mit dem eben Vernommenen der seitdem schärfer gewordenen Kraft plötzlich einleuchtet, klar, und schärft den Drang und das Vermögen, aus dem Gehörten immer mehr und schneller in das Verständniss hinüberzuziehen, immer weniger davon als blossen Klang vorüberrauschen zu lassen.

segments.label: §36, de source block10
segments.text: Die Fortschritte geschehen daher auch nicht, wie etwa beim Vocabellernen, in gleichmässigem, nur durch die verstärkte Uebung des Gedächtnisses wachsendem Verhältniss, sondern in beständig sich selbst steigerndem, da die Erhöhung der Kraft und die Gewinnung des Stoffs sich gegenseitig verstärken und erweitern.

segments.label: §36, de source block11
segments.text: Dass bei den Kindern nicht ein mechanisches Lernen der Sprache, sondern eine Entwicklung der Sprachkraft vorgeht, beweist auch, dass allen menschlichen Kräften ein gewisser Zeitpunkt im Lebensalter zu ihrer Entwicklung angewiesen ist, und dass unter den verschiedenartigsten Umständen alle Kinder ungefähr in demselben, nur innerhalb eines kurzen Zeitraums schwankenden Alter sprechen und verstehen.

segments.label: §36, de source block12
segments.text: Wie aber könnte der Hörende bloss durch das Wachsen seiner sich entwickelnden Kraft eine solche Stärke gewinnen, sich des Gesprochenen zu bemeistern, wenn nicht in dem Sprechenden und Hörenden dasselbe, nur individuel und einander angemessen getrennte Wesen wäre, so dass ein so feines, aber gerade aus der tiefsten und vollsten Natur desselben geschöpftes Zeichen, wie der articulirte Laut ist, hinreicht, beide auf übereinstimmende Weise, vermittelnd, anzuregen ?

segments.label: §36, codex source block1
segments.text: What speaks most convincingly against that opposite view for me is what was said above: that understanding too rests entirely on inward self-activity, and speaking with one another is merely a mutual awakening of the power of language present in the hearer.

segments.label: §36, codex source block2
segments.text: Comprehending words is something entirely different from understanding unarticulated sounds, and involves far more than the mere reciprocal evocation of the sound and the object indicated.

segments.label: §36, codex source block3
segments.text: A word can certainly also be taken as an indivisible whole, just as in writing one may recognise the sense of a group of words without yet being sure of its alphabetic composition; and it would be possible for a child's soul to proceed in this way in the earliest beginnings of understanding.

segments.label: §36, codex source block4
segments.text: But as soon as not merely the animal capacity for feeling but the human power of language is stimulated—and there may well be no moment even in the child when this is not the case, however faintly—the word is also perceived as articulated.

segments.label: §36, codex source block5
segments.text: What articulation adds to the mere evocation of the word's meaning—which it naturally also accomplishes more perfectly—is that through its form it immediately presents the word as part of an infinite whole, a language.

segments.label: §36, codex source block6
segments.text: For articulation provides, even in individual words, the possibility of forming from their elements a number of other words that genuinely extends to infinity, according to determining feelings and rules, and thereby of establishing among all words a kinship corresponding to the kinship of concepts.

segments.label: §36, codex source block7
segments.text: The soul would have no inkling of this skilfully contrived mechanism, and would comprehend articulation no more than a blind person comprehends colour, unless it possessed a power to turn that possibility into actuality.

segments.label: §36, codex source block8
segments.text: Children's learning to speak is not a matter of words being portioned out, deposited in memory and babbled back with the lips, but a growth of the capacity for language through age and practice.

segments.label: §36, codex source block9
segments.text: What is heard does more than merely communicate itself: it prepares the soul to understand more easily even what has not yet been heard; it clarifies things heard long ago but then understood only partly or not at all, as their likeness in kind to what has just been perceived suddenly becomes evident to a power that has since grown more acute; and it sharpens the impulse and ability to draw ever more of what is heard, and ever more quickly, into understanding, allowing ever less of it to rush past as mere sound.

segments.label: §36, codex source block10
segments.text: Progress therefore does not occur, as in learning vocabulary, at a steady rate increasing only through greater exercise of memory, but at a rate that constantly increases of itself, since the enhancement of the power and the acquisition of material mutually strengthen and extend each other.

segments.label: §36, codex source block11
segments.text: That children undergo a development of the power of language rather than mechanically learning language is also shown by the fact that all human powers are assigned a certain period of life for their development, and that under the most varied circumstances all children speak and understand at approximately the same age, varying only within a short span.

segments.label: §36, codex source block12
segments.text: But how could the hearer, merely through the growth of his developing power, acquire such strength to master what is spoken, unless the same being were present in speaker and hearer, divided only individually and in ways suited to each other, so that a sign as subtle as articulated sound, yet drawn precisely from the deepest and fullest nature of that being, suffices to mediate between them and stimulate both in a corresponding manner?

segments.label: §36, muse source block1
segments.text: What speaks most convincingly for me against the latter view is what was said above: that understanding too rests wholly on inner self-activity, and speaking with one another is only a mutual awakening of the power of language present in the hearer.

segments.label: §36, muse source block2
segments.text: The conceiving of words is thoroughly different from the understanding of unarticulated sounds, and comprehends far more in itself than the mere mutual evoking of sound and indicated object.

segments.label: §36, muse source block3
segments.text: The word can indeed also be taken as an indivisible whole, just as in writing one may well recognize the sense of a group of words without yet being certain of its alphabetical composition, and it would be possible that the child's soul proceeded in this way in the first beginnings of understanding.

segments.label: §36, muse source block4
segments.text: But as soon as not merely the animal faculty of feeling but the human power of language is stimulated (and there may well be no moment even in the child at which this, however weakly, is not the case), the word is also perceived as articulated.

segments.label: §36, muse source block5
segments.text: Now what articulation adds to the mere evoking of its meaning (which naturally also takes place through it in higher perfection) is that it presents the word immediately through its form as a part of an infinite whole, a language.

segments.label: §36, muse source block6
segments.text: For through it the possibility is given, even in individual words, of forming from their elements a number of other words really extending to infinity, according to determining feelings and rules, and thereby establishing among all words a relationship corresponding to the relationship of the concepts.

segments.label: §36, muse source block7
segments.text: The soul would, however, receive no divination at all of this artful mechanism, and would conceive articulation as little as the blind man conceives colour, if a power to bring that possibility into actuality did not dwell in it.

segments.label: §36, muse source block8
segments.text: Children's learning to speak is not a measuring out of words, laying them down in the memory and repeating them babblingly with the lips, but a growth of the faculty of language through age and practice.

segments.label: §36, muse source block9
segments.text: What is heard does more than merely communicate itself; it disposes the soul to understand more easily also what has not yet been heard, makes clear things heard long ago but then half or not at all understood, in that their sameness of kind with what has just been perceived suddenly becomes evident to the power that has since become sharper, and sharpens the urge and the faculty of drawing ever more and more quickly from what is heard over into understanding, of letting ever less of it rush past as mere sound.

segments.label: §36, muse source block10
segments.text: Progress therefore also does not take place, as for instance in learning vocabulary, in a uniform proportion growing only through strengthened practice of memory, but in a constantly self-intensifying one, since the heightening of power and the gaining of material mutually strengthen and extend each other.

segments.label: §36, muse source block11
segments.text: That in children not a mechanical learning of language but a development of the power of language takes place is also proved by the fact that to all human powers a certain point in age is assigned for their development, and that under the most diverse circumstances all children speak and understand at approximately the same age, varying only within a short period.

segments.label: §36, muse source block12
segments.text: But how could the hearer, merely through the growth of his developing power, gain such strength as to master what is spoken, if there were not in the speaker and the hearer the same being, only individually and mutually appropriately separated, so that so fine a sign, yet drawn precisely from the deepest and fullest nature of that being, as articulated sound is, suffices, mediatingly, to stimulate both in concordant manner?

segments.label: §37, de source block1
segments.text: Wenn dies richtig ist, so wird zugleich klar, wie Absonderung und Vermischung der Nationen die Ursache der Verschiedenheit ihrer Sprachen werden.

segments.label: §37, de source block2
segments.text: Denn je weiter die Menschen dadurch aus einander weichen, desto mehr tritt die Trennung der Individualität der Einheit des Wesens entgegen, obschon sich die Einheit der menschlichen Natur überhaupt auch darin beweist, dass Kinder jedes Volks, vom Mutterschoosse in jedes fremde versetzt, ihr Sprachvermögen in dessen Sprache entwickeln.

segments.label: §37, de source block3
segments.text: Diese Erscheinung kann zwar auch gerade umgekehrt dafür angeführt werden, dass das Sprechen bloss ein Wiedergeben des Gehörten ist, und, ohne Rücksicht auf Einheit oder Verschiedenheit des Wesens, von dem Umgange abhängt.

segments.label: §37, de source block4
segments.text: So viel man aber der sogar vorherrschenden Gewalt der umgebenden Laute beimessen muss, so würde es willkührlich seyn, den Einfluss der Abstammung, der in diesen ausserordentlichen Fällen nur unterdrückt wird, abläugnen zu wollen.

segments.label: §37, de source block5
segments.text: Sie übt schon einen unläugbaren auf die Stimmwerkzeuge aus, die doch individuell, und natürlich der Sprache der Väter gemäss, modificirt seyn müssen, und nun, im Aneignen und Widerstreben, diese Modification jeder Wirkung auf sie beimischen.

segments.label: §37, de source block6
segments.text: Nichts aber steht so vereinzelt im Menschen, und auch das intellectuelle Sprachvermögen kennt gewiss eine eben solche stammartige Anlage.

segments.label: §37, de source block7
segments.text: Dass die vaterländische Sprache für den Gebildeten und Ungebildeten eine viel grössere Stärke und Innigkeit besitzt, als eine fremde, dass sie das Ohr nach langer Entbehrung mit einer Art plötzlichen Zaubers begrüsst, und in der Ferne mit Sehnsucht berührt, dass dies gar nicht auf dem Geistigen in derselben, dem ausgedrückten Gedanken oder Gefühle, sondern gerade auf dem Unerklärlichen, dem individuellsten, auf ihrem Laute beruht, möchte wohl auch für jene wirkliche Einheit des Wesens sprechen.

segments.label: §37, de source block8
segments.text: Es ist, als ob man mit dem heimischen Laute einen Theil seines Selbst aus dem Andren vernähme.

segments.label: §37, de source block9
segments.text: Es lassen sich auch, wenn man nur auf Erscheinungen dieser Art hinlänglich achtet, in dem feinsten und geistigsten Gebrauche der Sprache, in der Literatur der Nationen, Individuen aufweisen, die, von Kindheit an ihrer Sprache, die sie gar nicht erlernten, entfremdet, doch immer dem Gebrauche der angeeigneten etwas beimischten, wodurch sich zeigte, dass ihre ursprüngliche Bestimmung zu einer andren Sprache, gegen die Natur ihres Wesens, zufällig verrückt worden war.

segments.label: §37, codex source block1
segments.text: If this is correct, it also becomes clear how the separation and intermingling of nations cause the diversity of their languages.

segments.label: §37, codex source block2
segments.text: For the further human beings diverge through these processes, the more the separation of individuality opposes the unity of being, although the unity of human nature in general is also demonstrated by the fact that children of any people, transferred from the womb into any foreign people, develop their capacity for language in that people's language.

segments.label: §37, codex source block3
segments.text: This phenomenon can admittedly also be cited in support of the exact opposite position: that speaking is merely a reproduction of what is heard and depends on social intercourse, irrespective of unity or diversity of being.

segments.label: §37, codex source block4
segments.text: But however much must be attributed to the power, even the predominant power, of the surrounding sounds, it would be arbitrary to deny the influence of descent, which in these exceptional cases is merely suppressed.

segments.label: §37, codex source block5
segments.text: Descent already exercises an undeniable influence on the vocal organs, which must be individually modified, naturally in accordance with the language of the fathers, and which now, in accommodating and resisting, mingle this modification into every influence acting upon them.

segments.label: §37, codex source block6
segments.text: Nothing in a human being is so isolated, however, and the intellectual capacity for language certainly also possesses a similar disposition characteristic of the stock.

segments.label: §37, codex source block7
segments.text: The fact that the native language possesses much greater force and intimacy than a foreign one for educated and uneducated people alike; that after long deprivation it greets the ear with a kind of sudden enchantment and, far from home, touches one with longing; and that this rests not at all on its mental content, the thought or feeling expressed, but precisely on what is inexplicable and most individual, its sound—this too might well speak for that actual unity of being.

segments.label: §37, codex source block8
segments.text: It is as though in the familiar sound one heard a part of oneself coming from the other person.

segments.label: §37, codex source block9
segments.text: If only sufficient attention is paid to phenomena of this kind, one can also point out, in the finest and most intellectual use of language, in the literatures of nations, individuals who, estranged from childhood from their own language, which they never learnt at all, nevertheless always mingled something into their use of the language they acquired that showed how their original destination for another language had been accidentally displaced, contrary to the nature of their being.

segments.label: §37, muse source block1
segments.text: If this is correct, it at the same time becomes clear how separation and mixing of nations become the cause of the diversity of their languages.

segments.label: §37, muse source block2
segments.text: For the further human beings diverge from one another thereby, the more the separation of individuality sets itself against the unity of being, although the unity of human nature in general also proves itself in this, that children of every people, transferred from the mother's lap into any foreign one, develop their faculty of language in the language of the latter.

segments.label: §37, muse source block3
segments.text: This appearance can indeed also be adduced in precisely the opposite direction, to show that speaking is merely a reproducing of what is heard and depends on intercourse without regard to unity or diversity of being.

segments.text: But however much one must attribute to the even predominant power of the surrounding sounds, it would be arbitrary to want to deny the influence of descent, which in these extraordinary cases is only suppressed.

segments.label: §37, muse source block5
segments.text: It already exerts an undeniable influence on the vocal organs, which must indeed be individually modified, and modified naturally in accordance with the language of the fathers, and now, in appropriating and resisting, mix this modification into every effect upon them.

segments.label: §37, muse source block6
segments.text: But nothing stands so isolated in man, and the intellectual faculty of language too certainly knows just such a tribal disposition.

segments.label: §37, muse source block7
segments.text: That the language of one's fatherland possesses for the educated and the uneducated a far greater strength and intimacy than a foreign one, that after long deprivation it greets the ear with a kind of sudden magic and in distant places touches it with longing, and that this rests not at all on the mental element in it, the expressed thought or feeling, but precisely on the inexplicable, most individual element, on its sound, might well also speak for that real unity of being.

segments.label: §37, muse source block8
segments.text: It is as if with the native sound one perceived a part of one's self from the other person.

segments.label: §37, muse source block9
segments.text: If one only pays sufficient attention to appearances of this kind, individuals can also be shown, in the finest and most mental use of language, in the literature of nations, who, estranged from childhood from their language, which they did not learn at all, nevertheless always mixed something into the use of the appropriated language by which it showed itself that their original determination for another language had, against the nature of their being, been accidentally displaced.

segments.label: §37, astra source block8
segments.text: It is as though, in the native sound, one heard a part of oneself coming from the other person.

segments.label: §37, astra source block9
segments.text: If sufficient attention is paid to phenomena of this kind, individuals can also be identified in the finest and most intellectual use of language, in the literature of nations, who were estranged from childhood from their own language, which they never learned, yet always mixed something into their use of the language they acquired that showed how their original orientation towards another language had been accidentally displaced, contrary to the nature of their being.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block1
segments.text: If this is correct, it also becomes clear how the separation and mixture of nations become the cause of differences between their languages.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block2
segments.text: For the further human beings diverge through these processes, the more the separation of individuality stands opposed to the unity of essence; although the unity of human nature in general is also demonstrated by the fact that children of any people, taken from birth and placed among any foreign people, develop their capacity for language in that people's language.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block3
segments.text: This phenomenon can admittedly also be cited in support of precisely the opposite view: that speaking is merely a reproduction of what has been heard and depends on social contact, irrespective of unity or difference of essence.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block4
segments.text: But however much must be attributed to the even predominant power of the surrounding sounds, it would be arbitrary to deny the influence of descent, which is merely suppressed in these exceptional cases.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block5
segments.text: Descent already exerts an undeniable influence on the vocal organs, which must be individually modified, naturally in accordance with the language of the fathers, and which now, in appropriation and resistance, mingle this modification with every influence exerted upon them.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block6
segments.text: Nothing in a human being stands so isolated, however, and the intellectual capacity for language certainly also possesses a similar disposition characteristic of a stock.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block7
segments.text: The fact that the language of one's homeland has far greater force and intimacy for educated and uneducated alike than a foreign language; that after a long deprivation it greets the ear with a kind of sudden enchantment, and touches it with longing when one is far away; and that this rests not at all on its mental content, the thought or feeling expressed, but precisely on what is inexplicable and most individual, its sound—this too might well speak for that real unity of essence.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block8
segments.text: It is as though, in the native sound, one heard a part of oneself coming from the other person.

segments.label: §37, synthesis source block9
segments.text: If sufficient attention is paid to phenomena of this kind, individuals can also be identified in the finest and most intellectual use of language, in the literature of nations, who were estranged from childhood from their own language, which they never learned, yet always mixed something into their use of the language they acquired that showed how their original determination for another language had been accidentally displaced, contrary to the nature of their being.

segments.label: §38, de source block1
segments.text: Indess entstehen, auch ohne allen Einfluss der Abstammung, bloss durch den Umgang und gemeinsames Leben eigene Mundarten.

segments.label: §38, de source block2
segments.text: Dies findet sich vorzüglich innerhalb des Kreises wirklicher Nationalsprachen bei einzelnen Classen des Volks, und die, besonders in den Amerikanischen Sprachen so häufigen eignen Mundarten der Weiber, so wie die der verschiedenen Stände im Malayischen sind von dieser Art.

segments.label: §38, de source block3
segments.text: Es kann aber auch gemeinsame Abstammung hinzutreten, wie in der Sprache der Incas, die zugleich Familien und Standessprache war.

segments.label: §38, de source block4
segments.text: In allen diesen Fällen ist, wie bei der Sprachbildung überhaupt, das Princip Gemeinschaft, die sich, zufällig oder absichtlich, absondert.

segments.label: §38, codex source block1
segments.text: Nevertheless, distinctive dialects arise even without any influence of descent, merely through intercourse and shared life.

segments.label: §38, codex source block2
segments.text: This is found especially among particular classes of the people within the sphere of actual national languages; the distinctive dialects of women, so frequent particularly in American languages, and those of the different social ranks in Malay are of this kind.

segments.label: §38, codex source block3
segments.text: Common descent may also be added, however, as in the language of the Incas, which was both a family language and the language of a social rank.

segments.label: §38, codex source block4
segments.text: In all these cases, as in the formation of language generally, the principle is a community that separates itself, accidentally or deliberately.

segments.label: §38, muse source block1
segments.text: Meanwhile, even without any influence of descent, peculiar dialects arise merely through intercourse and common life.

segments.label: §38, muse source block2
segments.text: This is found pre-eminently within the circle of real national languages among individual classes of the people, and the peculiar dialects of women, so frequent especially in the American languages, as well as those of the different estates in Malay, are of this kind.

segments.label: §38, muse source block3
segments.text: But common descent can also be added, as in the language of the Incas, which was at the same time a family language and a language of estate.

segments.label: §38, muse source block4
segments.text: In all these cases the principle is, as in language-formation in general, community that separates itself off, accidentally or intentionally.

segments.label: §38, astra source block4

segments.label: §39, de source block1
segments.text: Wir haben im Vorigen, die Sprache als Organ des Denkens darstellend, den articulirten Laut, der ihr Wesen ausmacht, nach seiner doppelten Natur, als Articulation (21.) und als Laut (22 — 38.) betrachtet.

segments.label: §39, de source block2
segments.text: Wenden wir uns nun zu dem durch das Sprechen, oder vielmehr durch das Denken in Sprache Erzeugten, so finden wir auch da, dass die Vorstellungsart, die Sprache bezeichne bloss die wahrgenommenen Gegenstände, deren Gesammtmasse wir die Welt nennen, weit entfernt ist, ihren tiefen und vollen Gehalt zu erschöpfen.

segments.label: §39, de source block3
segments.text: Ebensowenig als ein Begriff ohne sie möglich ist, ebensowenig kann es für die Seele ein Gegenstand seyn, da ja jeder äussere Gegenstand nur vermittelst des Begriffes für sie Wesenheit erhält.

segments.label: §39, de source block4
segments.text: In die Bildung und den Gebrauch der Sprache geht nothwendig die ganze Art der subjectiven Wahrnehmung der Gegenstände über.

segments.label: §39, de source block5
segments.text: Denn das Wort entsteht ja aus dieser Wahrnehmung, und ist nicht ein Abdruck des Gegenstandes an sich, sondern des von diesem in der Seele erzeugten Bildes.

segments.label: §39, de source block6
segments.text: Da aller objectiven Wahrnehmung unvermeidlich Subjectivitaet beigemischt ist, so kann man schon unabhängig von der Sprache jede menschliche Individualität als einen eignen Standpunkt der Weltansicht betrachten.

segments.label: §39, de source block7
segments.text: Sie wird aber noch viel mehr dazu durch die Sprache, da das Wort sich, der Seele gegenüber, auch wieder selbst zum Object macht, und eine neue, vom Subject sich absondernde Eigenthümlichkeit hinzubringt, so dass nunmehr in dem Begriffe ein Dreifaches liegt, der Eindruck des Gegenstandes, die Art der Aufnahme desselben im Subject, die Wirkung des Worts, als Sprachlaut.

segments.label: §39, de source block8
segments.text: In dieser letzten herrscht in derselben Sprache nothwendig eine durchgehende Analogie, und da nun auch auf die Sprache in derselben Nation eine gleichartige Subjectivitaet einwirkt, so liegt in jeder Sprache eine eigenthümliche Weltansicht.

segments.label: §39, de source block9
segments.text: Dieser Ausdruck überschreitet auf keine Weise das Mass der einfachen Wahrheit.

segments.label: §39, de source block10
segments.text: Denn der Zusammenhang aller Theile der Sprache unter einander, und der ganzen Sprache mit der Nation ist so enge, dass, wenn einmal diese Wechselwirkung eine bestimmte Richtung angiebt, daraus nothwendig durchgängige Eigenthümlichkeit hervorgehen muss.

segments.label: §39, de source block11
segments.text: Weltansicht aber ist die Sprache nicht bloss, weil sie, da jeder Begriff soll durch sie erfasst werden können, dem Umfange der Welt gleichkommen muss, sondern auch deswegen, weil erst die Verwandlung, die sie mit den Gegenständen vornimmt, den Geist zur Einsicht des von dem Begriff der Welt unzertrennlichen Zusammenhanges fähig macht.

segments.label: §39, de source block12
segments.text: Der Mensch lebt auch hauptsächlich mit den Gegenständen, so wie sie ihm die Sprache zuführt, und da Empfinden und Handeln in ihm von seinen Vorstellungen abhängt, sogar ausschliesslich so.

segments.label: §39, de source block13
segments.text: Durch denselben Act, vermöge welches der Mensch die Sprache aus sich heraus spinnt, spinnt er sich in dieselbe ein, und jede Sprache zieht um die Nation, welcher sie angehört, einen Kreis, aus dem es nur insofern hinauszugehen möglich ist, als man zugleich in den Kreis einer andren Sprache hinübertritt.

segments.label: §39, de source block14
segments.text: Die Erlernung einer fremden Sprache, auf die richtige Art benutzt, ist daher die Gewinnung eines neuen Standpunkts in der bisherigen Weltansicht, da jede das ganze Gewebe der Begriffe und der Vorstellungsweise eines Theils der Menschheit enthält.

segments.label: §39, codex source block1
segments.text: In presenting language above as the organ of thinking, we considered articulated sound, which constitutes its essence, in its twofold nature: as articulation (21) and as sound (22–38).

segments.label: §39, codex source block2
segments.text: If we now turn to what is produced through speaking, or rather through thinking in language, we find here too that the view that language merely designates perceived objects, whose totality we call the world, is far from exhausting its deep and full content.

segments.label: §39, codex source block3
segments.text: Just as no concept is possible without language, neither can any object exist for the soul without it, since every external object acquires substantial reality for the soul only through the concept.

segments.label: §39, codex source block4
segments.text: The entire manner of the subjective perception of objects necessarily enters into the formation and use of language.

segments.label: §39, codex source block5
segments.text: For the word arises from this perception and is an imprint not of the object in itself, but of the image produced by it in the soul.

segments.label: §39, codex source block6
segments.text: Since subjectivity is inevitably mingled into every objective perception, each human individuality can already be regarded, independently of language, as a distinctive standpoint for a view of the world.

segments.label: §39, codex source block7
segments.text: Language makes it so to a much greater degree, however, since the word in turn makes itself an object confronting the soul and adds a new peculiarity that separates itself from the subject; the concept thus now contains three things: the impression of the object, the manner in which the subject receives it, and the effect of the word as a speech sound.

segments.label: §39, codex source block8
segments.text: Within the same language, a pervasive analogy necessarily governs this last effect; and since a subjectivity alike in kind also acts upon language within the same nation, each language contains a distinctive view of the world.

segments.label: §39, codex source block9
segments.text: This expression in no way exceeds the measure of plain truth.

segments.label: §39, codex source block10
segments.text: For the connection of all the parts of language with one another, and of the whole language with the nation, is so close that once this interaction takes a definite direction, a pervasive distinctive character must necessarily follow.

segments.label: §39, codex source block11
segments.text: Language is a view of the world not merely because, since every concept must be capable of being grasped through it, it must equal the world in scope, but also because only the transformation it performs upon objects enables the mind to apprehend the interconnectedness inseparable from the concept of the world.

segments.label: §39, codex source block12
segments.text: Human beings also live chiefly with objects as language presents them to them, and, since their feeling and acting depend on their representations, indeed exclusively so.

segments.label: §39, codex source block13
segments.text: Through the very act by which the human being spins language out of himself, he spins himself into it; and every language draws a circle around the nation to which it belongs, a circle that can be left only to the extent that one simultaneously passes into the circle of another language.

segments.label: §39, codex source block14
segments.text: Learning a foreign language, when put to proper use, is therefore the acquisition of a new standpoint within one's previous view of the world, since each language contains the entire fabric of concepts and manner of representation of a portion of humanity.

segments.label: §39, muse source block1
segments.text: In what precedes, presenting language as the organ of thinking, we have considered articulated sound, which constitutes its essence, according to its twofold nature, as articulation (21.) and as sound (22 — 38.).

segments.label: §39, muse source block2
segments.text: If we now turn to what is produced through speaking, or rather through thinking in language, we find there too that the mode of representation according to which language merely designates perceived objects, whose total mass we call the world, is far removed from exhausting its deep and full content.

segments.label: §39, muse source block3
segments.text: Just as little as a concept is possible without it, just as little can there be an object for the soul without it, since every external object receives real being for it only by means of the concept.

segments.label: §39, muse source block4

segments.label: §39, muse source block5
segments.text: For the word arises precisely from this perception, and is not an impression of the object in itself, but of the image produced by the latter in the soul.

segments.label: §39, muse source block6
segments.text: Since subjectivity is unavoidably mixed into all objective perception, every human individuality can already, independently of language, be regarded as a peculiar standpoint of the view of the world.

segments.label: §39, muse source block7
segments.text: It becomes so, however, far more through language, since the word, over against the soul, also makes itself in turn into an object and brings in a new peculiarity separating itself off from the subject, so that now in the concept there lies a threefold element: the impression of the object, the manner of the reception of it in the subject, and the effect of the word as a language-sound.

segments.label: §39, muse source block8
segments.text: In this last element there necessarily reigns in the same language a thoroughgoing analogy, and since now a subjectivity of the same kind also acts upon language in the same nation, there lies in every language a peculiar view of the world.

segments.label: §39, muse source block9
segments.text: This expression in no way exceeds the measure of simple truth.

segments.label: §39, muse source block10
segments.text: For the connexion of all parts of language with one another, and of the whole language with the nation, is so close that, if once this interaction indicates a determinate direction, thoroughgoing peculiarity must necessarily arise from it.

segments.label: §39, muse source block11
segments.text: But language is a view of the world not merely because it, since every concept is to be capable of being grasped through it, must equal the extent of the world, but also because only the transformation that it undertakes with objects makes the mind capable of insight into the connexion inseparable from the concept of the world.

segments.label: §39, muse source block12
segments.text: Man also lives chiefly with objects as language supplies them to him, and, since feeling and acting in him depend on his representations, he lives even exclusively so.

segments.label: §39, muse source block13
segments.text: Through the same act by virtue of which man spins language out of himself, he spins himself into it, and every language draws around the nation to which it belongs a circle from which it is possible to go out only in so far as one at the same time steps over into the circle of another language.

segments.label: §39, muse source block14
segments.text: The learning of a foreign language, used in the right manner, is therefore the gaining of a new standpoint in the previous view of the world, since every language contains the whole web of concepts and of the mode of representation of a part of mankind.

segments.label: §39, revised source block10
segments.text: For the connection among all the parts of language, and between the whole language and the nation, is so close that once this interaction establishes a definite direction, a distinctive character extending throughout must necessarily result.

segments.label: §39, revised source block11
segments.text: Language is a view of the world not merely because, since every concept is to be graspable through it, it must equal the world in extent, but also because only the transformation it performs upon objects enables the mind to discern the interconnectedness inseparable from the concept of the world.

segments.label: §39, revised source block12
segments.text: Human beings also live principally with objects as language presents those objects to them—and, since their feeling and action depend on their representations, indeed exclusively in this way.

segments.label: §39, revised source block13
segments.text: In the very act by which human beings spin language out of themselves, they spin themselves into it; and every language draws around the nation to which it belongs a circle that can be left only insofar as one simultaneously passes into the circle of another language.

segments.label: §39, revised source block14
segments.text: Learning a foreign language, when put to the right use, is therefore the acquisition of a new standpoint within one's previous view of the world, since every language contains the entire fabric of the concepts and manner of representation of a part of humanity.

segments.label: §40, de source block1
segments.text: Ich habe bisher mehr von dem Sprechen, als von der Sprache gehandelt, und hauptsächlich die Erzeugung und das Verstehen der Rede, und den Einfluss, den sie auf die Seele ausübt, geschildert.

segments.label: §40, de source block2
segments.text: Aus dem Sprechen aber erzeugt sich die Sprache, ein Vorrath von Wörtern und System von Regeln, und wächst, sich durch die Folge der Jahrtausende hinschlingend, zu einer von dem jedesmal Redenden, dem jedesmaligen Geschlecht, der Nation, ja zuletzt selbst von der Menschheit in gewisser Art unabhängigen Macht an.

segments.label: §40, de source block3
segments.text: Wir sind im Vorigen darauf aufmerksam geworden, dass der in Sprache aufgenommene Gedanke für die Seele zum Object wird, und eine ihr insofern als etwas Fremdes zukommende Wirkung auf sie ausübt.

segments.label: §40, de source block4
segments.text: Aber wir haben das Object vorzüglich als aus dem Subject entstanden, die Wirkung als aus demjenigen, worauf sie zurückwirkt, hervorgegangen betrachtet.

segments.label: §40, de source block5
segments.text: Jetzt tritt die entgegengesetzte Ansicht ein, nach welcher die Sprache wirklich ein fremdes Object, ihre Wirkung wirklich aus etwas andrem, als worauf sie wirkt, hervorgegangen ist.

segments.label: §40, de source block6
segments.text: Denn die Sprache muss nothwendig (31.) zweien angehören, und gehört in der That dem ganzen Menschengeschlecht an, da sie nun auch in der Schrift den schlummernden Gedanken dem Geiste erweckbar erhält, so bildet sie sich ein eigenthümliches Daseyn, das zwar immer nur in jedesmaligem Denken Geltung erhalten kann, aber in seiner Totalitaet von diesem unabhängig ist.

segments.label: §40, de source block7
segments.text: Die beiden hier angeregten, einander entgegengesetzten Ansichten, dass die Sprache der Seele fremd und ihr angehörend, von ihr unabhängig und abhängig ist, verbinden sich wirklich in ihr, und machen die Eigenthümlichkeit ihres Wesens aus.

segments.label: §40, de source block8
segments.text: Es muss dieser Widerstreit auch nicht so gelöst werden, dass sie zum Theil fremd und unabhängig und zum Theil beides nicht sey.

segments.label: §40, de source block9
segments.text: Die Sprache ist gerade insofern Object und selbständig, als sie Subject und abhängig ist.

segments.label: §40, de source block10
segments.text: Denn sie hat nirgends, auch in der Schrift nicht, eine bleibende Stätte, sondern muss immer im Denken aufs neue erzeugt werden, und folglich ganz in das Subject übergehen; es liegt aber in dem Act dieser Erzeugung, sie gerade ebenso zum Object zu machen; sie erfährt auf diesem Wege jedesmal die ganze Einwirkung des Individuums, aber diese Einwirkung ist schon in sich durch das, was sie wirkt und gewirkt hat, gebunden.

segments.label: §40, de source block11
segments.text: Die wahre Lösung jenes Gegensatzes liegt in der oben (34.) angeführten Einheit der menschlichen Natur.

segments.label: §40, de source block12
segments.text: Was aus dem stammt, was eigentlich mit mir Eins ist, darin gehen die Begriffe des Subjects und Objects, der Abhängigkeit und Unabhängigkeit in einander über.

segments.label: §40, de source block13
segments.text: Die Sprache gehört mir an, weil ich sie hervorbringe.

segments.label: §40, de source block14
segments.text: Sie gehört mir nicht an, weil ich sie nicht anders hervorbringen kann, als ich thue, und da der Grund hiervon in dem Sprechen und Gesprochenhaben aller Menschengeschlechter liegt, soweit Sprachmittheilung ohne Unterbrechung unter ihnen gewesen seyn mag, so ist es die Sprache selbst, von der ich diese Einschränkung erfahre.

segments.label: §40, codex source block1
segments.text: So far I have dealt more with speaking than with language, chiefly describing the production and understanding of discourse and the influence it exercises on the soul.

segments.label: §40, codex source block2
segments.text: Yet language is produced from speaking, a stock of words and a system of rules, and, winding its way through successive millennia, grows into a power in some respects independent of the particular speaker, the particular generation, the nation, and ultimately even humanity itself.

segments.label: §40, codex source block3
segments.text: We noted above that thought taken up into language becomes an object for the soul and exercises an effect upon it which, in this respect, comes to it as something alien.

segments.label: §40, codex source block4
segments.text: But we considered the object chiefly as arising from the subject, and the effect as proceeding from that upon which it acts back.

segments.label: §40, codex source block5
segments.text: The opposite view now comes into play, according to which language really is an alien object and its effect really does proceed from something other than that upon which it acts.

segments.label: §40, codex source block6
segments.text: For language must necessarily belong to two people (31), and in fact belongs to the whole human race; since in writing it also preserves slumbering thought so that the mind can awaken it, it forms for itself a distinctive existence which can admittedly become effective only in particular acts of thinking, but which in its totality is independent of them.

segments.label: §40, codex source block7
segments.text: The two opposed views raised here—that language is alien to the soul and belongs to it, is independent of it and dependent upon it—really are united in language and constitute the peculiarity of its essence.

segments.label: §40, codex source block8
segments.text: Nor should this conflict be resolved by saying that language is partly alien and independent and partly neither.

segments.label: §40, codex source block9
segments.text: Language is an object and self-subsistent precisely insofar as it is a subject and dependent.

segments.label: §40, codex source block10
segments.text: For it has no permanent abode anywhere, not even in writing, but must always be produced anew in thinking and consequently pass wholly into the subject; yet the very act of producing it involves making it equally an object; in this way it receives the individual's full influence on each occasion, but that influence is already inherently constrained by what language does and has done.

segments.label: §40, codex source block11
segments.text: The true resolution of this opposition lies in the unity of human nature mentioned above (34).

segments.label: §40, codex source block12
segments.text: In what proceeds from that which is actually one with me, the concepts of subject and object, dependence and independence, pass into one another.

segments.label: §40, codex source block13
segments.text: Language belongs to me because I produce it.

segments.label: §40, codex source block14
segments.text: It does not belong to me because I cannot produce it otherwise than I do; and since the ground of this lies in the speaking and past speaking of all human generations, insofar as linguistic communication may have continued uninterrupted among them, it is language itself that imposes this restriction upon me.

segments.label: §40, muse source block8

segments.label: §40, muse source block9
segments.text: Language is object and independent precisely in so far as it is subject and dependent.

segments.text: For it has nowhere, not even in writing, an enduring place, but must always be produced anew in thinking and consequently pass wholly into the subject; but it lies in the act of this production to make it precisely just as much into an object; on this path it experiences each time the whole influence of the individual, but this influence is already in itself bound by what language effects and has effected.

segments.label: §41, de source block1
segments.text: Der fremde Einfluss, welchem der Mensch im Gebrauche der Sprache unterliegt, ist aber, ausser dem eben erwähnten der Sprache, bei dem engen Zusammenhange dieser mit seinem ganzen übrigen Wesen auch noch der, welchen Abstammung, umgebende Lage, und Art des gemeinsamen Lebens auf dieses ausüben.

segments.label: §41, de source block2
segments.text: Dies ist bei geschichtlichen Sprachuntersuchungen vorzüglich wichtig, da man sich auf der einen Seite hüten muss, eine Sprache ganz aus den auf die Nation einwirkenden Umständen zu erklären, und auf der andren nicht vergessen darf, dass auch eine geschichtlich unläugbar überkommene Sprache durch die Nation unglaublich scheinende Abänderungen erleiden kann.

segments.label: §41, de source block3
segments.text: Mit dieser zwiefachen Reihe verketteter Wirkungen hat man es bei Sprachuntersuchungen überall zu thun.

segments.label: §41, de source block4
segments.text: Denn wie alle das Menschengeschlecht geschichtlich betreffende, versetzen sie immer nur in eine Mitte der Dinge, und einen Anfang sich denken, oder gar erklären zu wollen, würde auf leere Voraussetzungen führen.

segments.label: §41, de source block5
segments.text: Auch da, wo weder Geschichte noch Ueberlieferung von einem früheren Zustand Kenntniss geben, und einen allgemeineren Zusammenhang zeigen, muss man es daher doch immer als eine Aufgabe für die überall hin gerichtete Aufmerksamkeit ansehen, irgend einen zu finden.

segments.label: §41, codex source block1
segments.text: Besides the influence of language just mentioned, the alien influence to which human beings are subject in using language also includes, given its close connection with the whole of their remaining being, the influence exercised upon that being by descent, surrounding circumstances and the manner of shared life.

segments.label: §41, codex source block2
segments.text: This is especially important in historical investigations of language, since on the one hand we must guard against explaining a language entirely from the circumstances acting upon the nation, and on the other must not forget that even a language undeniably handed down in history can undergo seemingly incredible modifications through the nation.

segments.label: §41, codex source block3
segments.text: Everywhere in linguistic investigations we have to deal with this twofold series of interconnected effects.

segments.label: §41, codex source block4
segments.text: For, like all investigations concerning the human race historically, they always place us only in the midst of things; to try to conceive of a beginning, let alone explain one, would lead to empty suppositions.

segments.label: §41, codex source block5
segments.text: Even where neither history nor tradition gives knowledge of an earlier state or reveals a wider connection, we must therefore always regard finding some such connection as a task for an attention directed everywhere.

segments.label: §41, muse source block1
segments.text: The foreign influence to which man is subject in the use of language is, however, besides that of language just mentioned, given the close connexion of language with his whole remaining being, also that which descent, surrounding situation and manner of common life exert upon that being.

segments.label: §41, muse source block2
segments.text: This is pre-eminently important in historical investigations of language, since on the one side one must beware of explaining a language wholly from the circumstances acting upon the nation, and on the other side must not forget that even a language historically and undeniably handed down can suffer through the nation alterations that seem incredible.

segments.label: §41, muse source block3
segments.text: It is with this twofold series of linked effects that one has to do everywhere in investigations of language.

segments.label: §41, muse source block4
segments.text: For, like all things historically concerning the human race, they always place one only in a middle of things, and wanting to think a beginning, or even to explain one, would lead to empty presuppositions.

segments.label: §41, muse source block5
segments.text: Even there, therefore, where neither history nor tradition gives knowledge of an earlier state and shows a more general connexion, one must always regard it as a task for attention directed everywhere to find some such connexion.

segments.label: §41, astra source block1
segments.text: Yet the foreign influence to which human beings are subject in using language includes, besides the influence of language just mentioned, the influence that descent, surrounding circumstances and the manner of shared life exert upon the rest of their being, given language's close connection with that being as a whole.

segments.label: §41, astra source block2
segments.text: This is especially important in historical investigations of language: on the one hand, we must guard against explaining a language entirely through the circumstances acting upon the nation; on the other, we must not forget that even a language undeniably inherited in historical terms can undergo changes through the nation that seem incredible.

segments.label: §41, astra source block3
segments.text: Investigations of language everywhere deal with this twofold series of linked effects.
