segments.label: §42, de source block1
segments.text: Wenn man bedenkt, wie auf die jedesmalige Generation in einem Volk Alles das bindend einwirkt, was die Sprache desselben alle vorigen Jahrhunderte hindurch erfahren hat, und wie damit nur die Kraft der einzelnen Generation in Berührung tritt, und diese nicht einmal rein, da das aufwachsende und abtretende Geschlecht untermischt neben einander leben, so wird klar, wie gering eigentlich die Kraft des Einzelnen gegen die Macht der Sprache ist.

segments.label: §42, de source block2
segments.text: Nur durch die ungemeine Bildsamkeit der Sprache, durch die Möglichkeit, von der ich weiter unten reden werde, ihre Formen, dem allgemeinen Verständniss unbeschadet, auf sehr verschiedene Weise aufzunehmen, und durch die Gewalt, welche alles lebendig Geistige über das todt Ueberlieferte ausübt, wird das Gleichgewicht wieder einigermassen hergestellt.

segments.label: §42, de source block3
segments.text: Doch ist es immer die Sprache, in welcher jeder Einzelne fühlt, dass er nichts als ein Ausfluss des ganzen Menschengeschlechts ist.

segments.label: §42, de source block4
segments.text: Nur weil doch jeder einzeln und unaufhörlich auf sie zurückwirkt, bringt doch jede Generation eine Veränderung in ihr hervor, die sich nur in vielen der Beobachtung entzieht.

segments.label: §42, de source block5
segments.text: Denn die Veränderung kann eine zwiefache seyn, eine in den Wörtern und Formen selbst, und eine in dem anders modificirten Gebrauche derselben, und dies letztere ist, wo Schrift und Literatur mangeln, theils geringer, theils schwieriger wahrzunehmen.

segments.label: §42, codex source block1
segments.text: If we consider how everything a people's language has experienced throughout all preceding centuries acts constrainingly upon each successive generation, and how only the power of the single generation comes into contact with this—and not even that in isolation, since the rising and departing generations live intermingled alongside one another—it becomes clear how small the individual's power really is beside the power of language.

segments.label: §42, codex source block2
segments.text: The balance is restored to some degree only through language's extraordinary plasticity, through the possibility, which I shall discuss below, of taking its forms in very different ways without impairing general understanding, and through the power that everything mentally alive exercises over what is handed down dead.

segments.label: §42, codex source block3
segments.text: Yet it is always in language that each individual feels himself to be nothing but an outflow of the whole human race.

segments.label: §42, codex source block4
segments.text: Nevertheless, because everyone individually and unceasingly acts back upon language, each generation produces a change in it, which only in many cases escapes observation.

segments.label: §42, codex source block5
segments.text: For change can be of two kinds: a change in the words and forms themselves, and a change in their differently modified use; where writing and literature are absent, the latter is both less extensive and harder to perceive.

segments.label: §42, muse source block1
segments.text: If one considers how everything that the language of a people has experienced through all preceding centuries acts bindingly upon the generation at any given time in that people, and how only the power of the individual generation comes into contact with it, and this not even purely, since the rising and the departing generation live intermixed beside each other, it becomes clear how small the power of the individual really is against the might of language.

segments.label: §42, muse source block2
segments.text: Only through the uncommon pliability of language, through the possibility, of which I shall speak further below, of taking up its forms in very different ways without detriment to general understanding, and through the power which everything living and mental exerts over what is handed down dead, is the equilibrium to some extent restored again.

segments.label: §42, muse source block3
segments.text: Yet it is always language in which every individual feels that he is nothing but an outflow of the whole human race.

segments.label: §42, muse source block4
segments.text: Only because everyone nevertheless individually and incessantly reacts upon it does every generation nevertheless produce a change in it, which in many cases evades observation.

segments.label: §42, muse source block5
segments.text: For the change can be twofold, one in the words and forms themselves and one in the differently modified use of them, and the latter is, where writing and literature are lacking, partly smaller and partly more difficult to perceive.

segments.label: §42, astra source block1
segments.text: Consider how everything a people's language has undergone throughout all preceding centuries acts as a constraint upon the generation living at any given time, and how only the power of that single generation comes into contact with it—and not even that power in isolation, since the rising and departing generations live intermingled alongside one another. It then becomes clear how slight the individual's power really is beside the power of language.

segments.label: §42, astra source block2
segments.text: The balance is restored to some extent only through language's extraordinary malleability, through the possibility, which I shall discuss below, of taking up its forms in very different ways without impairing general understanding, and through the power that everything mentally alive exerts over the lifeless legacy handed down.

segments.label: §42, astra source block3
segments.text: Yet it is always in language that every individual feels himself to be nothing but an outflow of the whole human race.

segments.label: §42, astra source block4
segments.text: Only because everyone nevertheless acts back upon language individually and unceasingly does every generation nevertheless produce a change in it, though in many cases this merely escapes observation.

segments.label: §42, astra source block5
segments.text: For the change can be twofold: a change in the words and forms themselves, and a change in the differently modified use of them; where writing and literature are absent, this latter change is both smaller and harder to perceive.

segments.label: §43, de source block1
segments.text: Da immer nur das Vorhandene, und immer nur von einer einzelnen, gegen eine unendliche Masse anringenden Kraft verändert wird, so folgt hieraus schon von selbst, dass jede Veränderung in der Sprache und auch die Entstehung neuer Sprachen nur allmählich geschieht.

segments.label: §43, de source block2
segments.text: Auch die Nationen, die durch den Wechsel der Jahrhunderte hindurch Hand in Hand mit den Sprachen gehn, entstehen auf keine andere Weise, und die Mittel, durch welche alle neue Sprachen (soviel wir sie zu erkennen vermögen) gebildet werden, sind Entfremdung und Beimischung.

segments.label: §43, de source block3
segments.text: Ein Haufen eines Stammes zweigt sich ab, und setzt sich fest, wo er entweder noch niemanden antrift, oder sich mit einem andren Stamme vermischt.

segments.label: §43, de source block4
segments.text: Von Erfindung einer Sprache kann im Gebiete geschichtlicher Sprachuntersuchung nicht die Rede seyn, und die Ausdrücke, dass ein Volk seine Sprache schafft, dass sie aus seiner Individualitaet hervorgeht, selbst dass sie ihm ausschliesslich angehört, bedürfen der Vorsicht, um mit Richtigkeit gebraucht zu werden.

segments.label: §43, de source block5
segments.text: Ebendies ist der Fall mit der Anwendung des Begriffes der Abstammung auf die Sprachen, der nie so genommen werden darf, als könnte eine in ihrer Totalitaet aus einer andren hervorgehn, sondern nur so, dass sich die angebliche Muttersprache in dem Munde von Generationen, die sich absonderten und mit fremden vermischten, in eine Tochtersprache verwandelt hat.

segments.label: §43, de source block6
segments.text: Da aber auf diese Weise mehrere Sprachen in eine neue übergehen, so misleitet die Anwendung dieses Begriffes schon darin, dass sie nach einer Stammsprache suchen lässt, da alle verschiedenen Stoffe der zu untersuchenden Sprache gesondert werden sollten.

segments.label: §43, de source block7
segments.text: Die Nationen selbst sind eben so wenig rein von einander geschieden, sondern fliessen auch in einander über, und bilden sich allmählich durch das zusammenwirkende Princip der Absonderung und des Zusammenhaltens; nur wird die so entspringende Eigenthümlichkeit erst nach vollendeter Bildung in einem gewissen Punkte sichtbar.

segments.label: §43, codex source block1
segments.text: Since only what already exists is ever changed, and always only by a single power struggling against an infinite mass, it follows of itself that every change in language, and the emergence of new languages too, occurs only gradually.

segments.label: §43, codex source block2
segments.text: Nations too, which go hand in hand with languages through the changing centuries, arise in no other way; and the means by which all new languages are formed, insofar as we can discern them, are estrangement and admixture.

segments.label: §43, codex source block3
segments.text: A group branches off from a stock and settles where it either encounters no one as yet or intermingles with another stock.

segments.label: §43, codex source block4
segments.text: Within historical investigation of language there can be no question of the invention of a language; and the expressions that a people creates its language, that language proceeds from its individuality, even that language belongs exclusively to it, require caution if they are to be used correctly.

segments.label: §43, codex source block5
segments.text: The same applies to using the concept of descent for languages: it must never be taken to mean that one language could proceed in its totality from another, but only that the supposed mother language has been transformed into a daughter language in the mouths of generations that separated themselves and intermingled with foreign ones.

segments.label: §43, codex source block6
segments.text: But since in this way several languages pass into a new one, applying this concept already misleads by prompting a search for one ancestral language, when all the different materials of the language under investigation ought to be distinguished.

segments.label: §43, codex source block7
segments.text: Nations themselves are no more cleanly separated from one another, but likewise flow into one another and gradually form through the conjoint principle of separation and holding together; only at a certain point, once formation is complete, does the distinctive character arising in this way become visible.

segments.label: §43, muse source block1
segments.text: Since what exists is always changed, and always only by an individual power wrestling against an infinite mass, it already follows from this of itself that every change in language, and also the origin of new languages, takes place only gradually.

segments.label: §43, muse source block2
segments.text: Nations too, which through the change of centuries go hand in hand with languages, arise in no other way, and the means through which all new languages (in so far as we can recognize them) are formed are estrangement and admixture.

segments.label: §43, muse source block3
segments.text: A body of a tribe branches off and settles where it either encounters no one as yet, or mixes with another tribe.

segments.label: §43, muse source block4
segments.text: There can be no talk of invention of a language in the domain of historical investigation of language, and the expressions that a people creates its language, that it proceeds from its individuality, even that it belongs to it exclusively, need caution in order to be used correctly.

segments.label: §43, muse source block5
segments.text: The very same is the case with the application of the concept of descent to languages, which must never be taken as if one language in its totality could proceed from another, but only in the sense that the alleged mother language has, in the mouth of generations that separated themselves off and mixed with foreign ones, transformed itself into a daughter language.

segments.label: §43, muse source block6
segments.text: But since in this way several languages pass over into a new one, the application of this concept already misleads in this respect, that it makes one seek a parent language, whereas all the different materials of the language to be investigated ought to be separated.

segments.label: §43, muse source block7
segments.text: Nations themselves are just as little purely separated from one another, but also flow over into one another and form themselves gradually through the co-operating principle of separation and holding together; only the peculiarity thus arising becomes visible at a certain point only after formation is completed.

segments.label: §43, astra source block1

segments.label: §43, astra source block5
segments.text: The same applies to the use of the concept of descent for languages.* It must never be understood as meaning that one language could emerge in its totality from another, but only that the supposed mother language has changed into a daughter language in the mouths of generations that separated themselves and mixed with foreign ones.

segments.text: But since several languages pass into a new one in this way, applying this concept is already misleading in that it prompts a search for a single ancestral language, whereas all the different materials of the language under investigation should be distinguished.

segments.label: §44, de source block1
segments.text: Alle Sprachen von Völkern, zwischen denen jemals irgend eine Verbindung obgewaltet hat, müssen daher als Eine, nur durch Entfremdung und Vermischung zu mannigfaltigen Unterarten umgeänderte Sprache angesehen werden.

segments.label: §44, de source block2
segments.text: Dies ist ein Hauptgrundsatz bei jeder Sprachuntersuchung, gleich wichtig um etymologisch die Gleichartigkeit der Sprachen zu prüfen, und philosophisch die Art darzustellen, wie die Sprache sich über das Menschengeschlecht verbreitet.

segments.label: §44, de source block3
segments.text: Er beruht aber auf der einfachen, und nicht abzuleugnenden Thatsache, dass wo Menschen, die bisher ganz getrennt wohnten, einander besuchen, oder sich mit einander verbinden, [sie] nach und nach ihr ursprüngliches Reden abändern, und in ein neues, auf welches sie sich vereinigen, umwandeln, meist beide, bisweilen jedoch auch nur einer, von dem andern erst körperlich, dann geistig überwältigter.

segments.label: §44, de source block4
segments.text: Selbst wenn das ursprüngliche Reden geschieden bleibt, gehen doch einzelne Wörter und Formen gegenseitig über.

segments.label: §44, de source block5
segments.text: Man hat daher etymologisch die verschiedenen Elemente der Sprache und ihr Verhältniss aufzusuchen.

segments.label: §44, de source block6
segments.text: Nur wenn alle Elemente gleichartig, und mit der Sprache eines andren Volks übereinstimmend wären, das heisst, wenn die Sprache bloss durch Abzweigung, ohne alle Mischung, entstanden wäre, könnte der Begriff der Abstammung passen.

segments.label: §44, de source block7
segments.text: Da er aber immer zugleich früheres und späteres Daseyn in sich schliesst, so lässt sich über ihn fast niemals aus der Sprache allein entscheiden.

segments.label: §44, de source block8
segments.text: Philosophisch kommt es nun darauf an, nachzuforschen, woran in der Sprache der Mensch am festesten hält, und in welche Verschiedenartigkeit er leichter und schwerer eingeht.

segments.label: §44, codex source block1
segments.text: All the languages of peoples between whom any connection has ever existed must therefore be regarded as one language, modified into manifold varieties only through estrangement and intermingling.

segments.label: §44, codex source block2
segments.text: This is a fundamental principle in every investigation of language, equally important for examining the likeness in kind of languages etymologically and for presenting philosophically the manner in which language spreads across the human race.

segments.label: §44, codex source block3
segments.text: It rests, however, on the simple and undeniable fact that where people who previously lived entirely apart visit or join with one another, [they] gradually modify their original speaking and transform it into a new manner of speaking on which they converge—usually both parties do so, though sometimes only one, overcome by the other first physically and then mentally.

segments.label: §44, codex source block4
segments.text: Even where the original manners of speaking remain separate, individual words and forms nevertheless pass back and forth.

segments.label: §44, codex source block5
segments.text: We must therefore seek out etymologically the different elements of the language and their relation to one another.

segments.label: §44, codex source block6
segments.text: Only if all the elements were alike in kind and agreed with the language of another people—that is, if the language had arisen solely through branching off, without any mixture—could the concept of descent fit.

segments.label: §44, codex source block7
segments.text: But since this concept always also entails earlier and later existence, the question of descent can almost never be decided from language alone.

segments.label: §44, codex source block8
segments.text: Philosophically, the task is now to investigate what human beings hold to most firmly in language, and what kinds of diversity they enter into more readily or with greater difficulty.

segments.label: §44, muse source block4

segments.label: §44, muse source block5
segments.text: Etymologically, therefore, one has to seek out the different elements of a language and their relation.

segments.label: §44, muse source block8
segments.text: Philosophically it now matters to investigate what in language man holds most firmly to, and what diversity he enters into more easily and more difficultly.

segments.label: §45, de source block1
segments.text: Mit der in dem so eben aufgestellten Grundsatz ausgesprochenen Einheit mehrerer Sprachen ist keinesweges die Einheit einer Ursprache gemeint, sondern die, dass jede irgend ein Element in sich trägt, das auch einer andren angehört, und weil dies der Fall bei Allen ist, alle mittelbar durch einander verändert und betroffen sind.

segments.label: §45, de source block2
segments.text: Die verschiedenen Sprachen, als neben einander bestehende Theile (Mundarten) einer alle umfassenden, nicht als in der Zeit aus einander entstanden anzusehen, ist das Eigenthümliche jener Behauptung, die übrigens gar nicht die Anmassung der Neuheit mit sich führt, sondern nur zum Zweck hat, mit Abschneidung unzeitiger Gleichnisse, die Begriffe fester zu bestimmen, und mehr mit den Thatsachen in Uebereinstimmung zu bringen.

segments.label: §45, de source block3
segments.text: Auch die Zeitfolge der Sprachen darf bei ihrem Studium nicht verabsäumet, sie soll nur nicht unpassend eingemischt werden, und da der Anfang der meisten noch bestehenden Sprachen sich in Dunkel verliert, so tritt bei dieser Unkenntniss ihrer Zeitfolge für uns gewissermassen Gleichzeitigkeit derselben ein.

segments.label: §45, codex source block1
segments.text: The unity of several languages expressed in the principle just established by no means signifies the unity of a primordial language; rather, it means that each contains some element also belonging to another, and that, since this is true of all, all are indirectly modified and affected by one another.

segments.label: §45, codex source block2
segments.text: What is distinctive about that assertion is that it regards the different languages as coexisting parts or dialects of one language embracing them all, rather than as having arisen from one another in time; moreover, it makes no claim to novelty, but aims only, by cutting away inappropriate analogies, to define the concepts more firmly and bring them into closer agreement with the facts.

segments.label: §45, codex source block3
segments.text: The temporal succession of languages must not be neglected in studying them either; it should simply not be introduced inappropriately, and since the beginnings of most languages still existing are lost in darkness, our ignorance of their temporal succession makes them in a sense simultaneous for us.

segments.label: §45, muse source block1
segments.text: By the unity of several languages expressed in the principle just set up, the unity of an original language is by no means meant, but this, that every language carries in itself some element that also belongs to another, and, because this is the case with all, all are mediately altered and affected through one another.

segments.label: §45, muse source block2
segments.text: To regard the different languages as parts (dialects), existing beside one another, of one language embracing all, not as having arisen from one another in time, is the peculiarity of that assertion, which moreover carries with it no pretension to novelty at all, but has only the purpose, by cutting off untimely comparisons, of determining concepts more firmly and bringing them more into accord with the facts.

segments.label: §45, muse source block3
segments.text: The temporal succession of languages too must not be neglected in their study; it is only not to be mixed in unsuitably, and since the beginning of most languages still existing loses itself in darkness, in this ignorance of their temporal succession there arises for us in a certain measure a simultaneity of them.

segments.label: §45, astra source block1
segments.text: The unity of several languages expressed in the principle just established by no means signifies the unity of a primordial language; it means instead that each language contains some element that also belongs to another, and that, since this holds of all, all are indirectly changed and affected by one another.

segments.label: §45, astra source block2
segments.text: What distinguishes this assertion is its treatment of the different languages as coexisting parts—dialects—of a language encompassing them all, rather than as having arisen from one another over time. It makes no claim to novelty, but aims only to dispense with inopportune analogies, determine the concepts more firmly, and bring them into closer agreement with the facts.

segments.label: §45, astra source block3
segments.text: The chronological succession of languages must not be neglected in their study either; it should merely not be introduced inappropriately. Since the beginnings of most languages still in existence are lost in darkness, our ignorance of their chronological succession makes them, in a sense, simultaneous for us.

segments.label: §46, de source block1
segments.text: Eine Ursprache anzunehmen, oder eine Verschiedenheit der Sprachen vor und nach der Vertilgung des grössten Theils des Menschengeschlechts durch eine Flut aufzustellen, scheint mir unnütz und misleitend.

segments.label: §46, de source block2
segments.text: Weder das Gebiet der Thatsachen, noch das reiner Begriffe vermag dahin zu führen.

segments.label: §46, de source block3
segments.text: Es mag Eine, es mag mehrere Ursprachen gegeben haben , im strengsten Verstände, wenn das Menschengeschlecht mehr als Einen geographischen Anfangspunkt hat, in einem weniger strengen, wenn, und dies könnten gerade grosse Fluthen hervorbringen, Völker so vereinzelt worden wären, dass sich alle Spur ihres früheren Zusammenhanges in ihrer Sprache verloren hätte.

segments.label: §46, de source block4
segments.text: Allein schwerlich werden aus den Sprachen zu schöpfende Thatsachen das eine oder das andre beweisen, und schwerlich wird es zur Erklärung von Erscheinungen in der Sprache der einen oder andren Annahme bedürfen.

segments.label: §46, de source block5
segments.text: Den Begriff einer Ursprache, wenn man nur nichts Einzelnes daraus folgern will, kann man indess allerdings ebensowenig, als den irgend eines Anfangs des Menschengeschlechts zurückweisen, und so kann es auch, in Beziehung auf den oben (44.) aufgestellten Grundsatz, sich ereignen, dass ein abgezweigter Volkshaufe sich mit einem solchen vermischt, auf welchen niemals, auch nicht auf die mittelbarste Weise eine der Sprachen eingewirkt hat, die mit dem ersteren in Verbindung stehen.

segments.label: §46, de source block6
segments.text: Zwei solche Völkerstämme würden dann, wenn man die Folge der Geschlechter aufsteigend verfolgt, ihre Sprache allerdings an zwei Ursprachen anknüpfen.

segments.label: §46, codex source block1
segments.text: To assume a primordial language, or to posit a difference between languages before and after the destruction of the greater part of the human race by a flood, seems to me useless and misleading.

segments.label: §46, codex source block2
segments.text: Neither the domain of facts nor that of pure concepts can lead us there.

segments.label: §46, codex source block3
segments.text: There may have been one primordial language, or several: in the strictest sense, if the human race had more than one geographical point of origin; in a less strict sense, if peoples had become so isolated—and great floods in particular could bring this about—that every trace of their earlier connection had been lost in their language.

segments.label: §46, codex source block4
segments.text: Yet facts drawn from languages will scarcely prove either possibility, and explaining phenomena in language will scarcely require either assumption.

segments.label: §46, codex source block5
segments.text: Nevertheless, provided one intends to infer nothing particular from it, the concept of a primordial language can certainly no more be rejected than that of any beginning of the human race; and thus, in relation to the principle established above (44), it may also happen that a group which has branched off from a people intermingles with another group upon which none of the languages connected with the first has ever exercised any influence, even in the most indirect way.

segments.label: §46, codex source block6
segments.text: Two such ethnic stocks would then, if the succession of generations were traced backwards, indeed connect their languages to two primordial languages.

segments.label: §46, muse source block1
segments.text: To assume an original language, or to set up a diversity of languages before and after the extermination of the greatest part of the human race through a flood, seems to me useless and misleading.

segments.label: §46, muse source block2
segments.text: Neither the domain of facts nor that of pure concepts can lead to that.

segments.label: §46, muse source block3
segments.text: There may have been one, there may have been several original languages, in the strictest sense if the human race has more than one geographical starting-point, in a less strict sense if — and precisely great floods could bring this about — peoples had become so isolated that every trace of their earlier connexion had been lost in their language.

segments.label: §46, muse source block4
segments.text: But facts to be drawn from languages will hardly prove the one or the other, and for the explanation of appearances in language one will hardly need either the one assumption or the other.

segments.label: §46, muse source block5
segments.text: The concept of an original language, however, if one does not want to infer anything in particular from it, can indeed as little be rejected as that of any beginning of the human race, and so it can also happen, in relation to the principle set up above (44.), that a branched-off body of a people mixes with one upon which none of the languages standing in connexion with the former has ever acted, not even in the most mediate way.

segments.label: §46, muse source block6
segments.text: Two such tribal stocks would then, if one follows the succession of generations upwards, indeed connect their language to two original languages.

segments.text: If one traced the succession of generations backwards, two such ethnic stocks would then indeed connect their language with two primordial languages.

segments.label: §47, de source block1
segments.text: Ueberall, wo unter den Völkern, auch noch so mittelbar, wirklicher Verkehr der Sprechenden bestanden hat, entspringt Gleichartigkeit ihrer Sprachen aus schon geformter Sprache; und umgekehrt, wenn sich solche aus geformter Sprache entsprungene Gleichartigkeit in Sprachen erkennen lässt, so beweist diese einen solchen Verkehr.

segments.label: §47, de source block2
segments.text: Dies ist wichtig, weil dadurch wenigstens, sollte es auch wenig fruchtbar für die Anwendung seyn, der Grundsatz ausgesprochen ist, nach welchem der geschichtliche Zusammenhang der Sprachen von derjenigen Gleichartigkeit unterschieden werden kann, welche bloss in der Gleichartigkeit der menschlichen Anlagen zu suchen ist.

segments.label: §47, de source block3
segments.text: Denn gesetzt dass die Amerikanischen Nationen einen heimathlichen Ursprung gehabt, und sich bis zur Verbreitung der noch bestehenden Sprachen mit keinen Bewohnern der übrigen Erde vermischt hätten, so wäre kein Nicht-Amerikanischer Laut in Amerika gehört worden, und so könnte es keine Gleichartigkeit zwischen den Amerikanischen und übrigen Sprachen des Erdbodens geben, die durch schon geformte Sprache entstanden wäre.

segments.label: §47, de source block4
segments.text: Dennoch wären die allgemeinen Anlagen des Menschen doch dieselben auch in Amerika, es wäre, man leite sie nun aus einer Abstammung von Einem Menschenpaare, oder aus der Einheit der schaffenden Idee her, dieselbe Einheit des menschlichen Wesens, ohne welche (34.) die Sprache selbst nicht möglich seyn würde, es müsste daher auch daraus nothwendig eine Gleichartigkeit der Sprachen hervorgehen.

segments.label: §47, de source block5
segments.text: In diesem Sinne giebt es nur Eine Sprache, wie es nur Eine Menschengattung giebt, und aller Unterschied der Racen weder den Begriff der Menschheit, noch die Möglichkeit regelmässiger Fortpflanzung aufhebt.

segments.label: §47, de source block6
segments.text: Dies wird noch einleuchtender, wenn man bedenkt, dass auch die auf den Menschen, und mithin auch auf die Sprache einwirkenden Umgebungen der Natur im Grossen dieselben, und die Mittel, deren sich alle Sprachen, als Töne, bedienen, in nicht sehr weiten Gränzen eingeschlossen sind.

segments.label: §47, de source block7
segments.text: Auch in den Sprachen von geschichtlicher Verbindung kommt diese allgemeine Gleichartigkeit, aber nur in den Theilen vor, auf welche die fremd hinzugetretenen Laute nicht eingewirkt haben, jedoch niemals rein, da in der Sprache, die bloss in der Thätigkeit des jedesmaligen Hervorbringens ihr Daseyn hat (40.), jede Einwirkung immer das Ganze durchdringt.

segments.label: §47, de source block8
segments.text: Ob es nun hinlängliche Mittel geben mag, an den Sprachen selbst diese mögliche zwiefache Gleichartigkeit zu unterscheiden, mag für jetzt dahingestellt bleiben, es war aber nothwendig dieselbe, ihrem Begriff nach, genau zu bestimmen.

segments.label: §47, de source block9
segments.text: Wir werden in der Folge sehr ausführlich auf diesen Punkt zurückkommen müssen, da Amerika leichter, als irgend ein Theil der alten Welt (man müsste denn etwa das mittlere Afrika ausnehmen wollen) von jeder Vermischung mit Fremden könnte frei geblieben seyn.

segments.label: §47, codex source block1
segments.text: Wherever actual intercourse between speakers has existed among peoples, however indirectly, likeness in kind between their languages arises from language already formed; conversely, if such likeness in kind arising from formed language can be recognised in languages, it proves such intercourse.

segments.label: §47, codex source block2
segments.text: This is important because it at least states the principle by which the historical connection between languages can be distinguished from the likeness in kind to be sought solely in the likeness in kind of human dispositions, even if the principle should prove of little practical fruitfulness.

segments.label: §47, codex source block3
segments.text: For suppose that the American nations had originated in their own homeland and had not intermingled with any inhabitants of the rest of the earth before the spread of the languages still existing: no non-American sound would then have been heard in America, and there could be no likeness in kind between American languages and the other languages of the earth arising through language already formed.

segments.label: §47, codex source block4
segments.text: Nevertheless, the general human dispositions would still be the same in America too; whether one derived them from descent from a single human pair or from the unity of the creative idea, there would be the same unity of human being without which (34) language itself would be impossible, and a likeness in kind between languages would therefore necessarily have to arise from this too.

segments.label: §47, codex source block5
segments.text: In this sense there is only one language, just as there is only one human species, and no difference of races annuls either the concept of humanity or the possibility of regular reproduction.

segments.label: §47, codex source block6
segments.text: This becomes still more evident when we consider that the natural surroundings acting upon human beings, and consequently upon language too, are broadly the same, and that the means employed by all languages, namely sounds, are confined within limits that are not very wide.

segments.label: §47, codex source block7
segments.text: This general likeness in kind also occurs in historically connected languages, but only in the parts upon which the sounds introduced from outside have not acted, and never in a pure form, since in language, which exists only in the activity of producing it on each occasion (40), every influence always permeates the whole.

segments.label: §47, codex source block8
segments.text: Whether there may be sufficient means of distinguishing these two possible kinds of likeness in the languages themselves may be left undecided for now; but it was necessary to define them precisely in conceptual terms.

segments.label: §47, codex source block9
segments.text: We shall have to return to this point at great length later, since America could more readily have remained free of all intermingling with foreigners than any part of the Old World, unless one wished perhaps to except central Africa.

segments.label: §47, muse source block1
segments.text: Everywhere where real intercourse of speakers has existed among peoples, however mediate it may be, sameness of kind of their languages arises from language already formed; and conversely, if such sameness of kind arising from formed language can be recognized in languages, it proves such an intercourse.

segments.label: §47, muse source block2
segments.text: This is important because thereby at least, even if it should be of little fruitfulness for application, the principle is expressed according to which the historical connexion of languages can be distinguished from that sameness of kind which is to be sought merely in the sameness of kind of human dispositions.

segments.label: §47, muse source block3
segments.text: For suppose that the American nations had had a native origin and, until the spread of the languages still existing, had mixed with no inhabitants of the rest of the earth, then no non-American sound would have been heard in America, and thus there could be no sameness of kind between the American languages and the other languages of the earth that had arisen through language already formed.

segments.label: §47, muse source block4
segments.text: Nevertheless the general dispositions of man would still be the same in America too; there would be, whether one derives them from descent from one human pair or from the unity of the creating idea, the same unity of human being without which (34.) language itself would not be possible; hence a sameness of kind of languages would also necessarily have to proceed from that.

segments.label: §47, muse source block5
segments.text: In this sense there is only One language, as there is only One human genus, and all difference of races abolishes neither the concept of humanity nor the possibility of regular propagation.

segments.label: §47, muse source block6
segments.text: This becomes still more evident if one considers that also the surroundings of nature acting upon man, and therefore also upon language, are in large measure the same, and the means of which all languages make use, as tones, are enclosed within not very wide limits.

segments.label: §47, muse source block7
segments.text: In languages of historical connexion too this general sameness of kind occurs, but only in those parts upon which the foreign sounds that have been added have not acted, yet never purely, since in language, which has its existence merely in the activity of production at any given time (40.), every influence always penetrates the whole.

segments.label: §47, muse source block8
segments.text: Whether there may now be sufficient means of distinguishing in the languages themselves this possible twofold sameness of kind may for now remain undecided; but it was necessary to determine it exactly according to its concept.

segments.label: §47, muse source block9
segments.text: We shall in what follows have to return very fully to this point, since America could more easily than any part of the old world (unless one wanted perhaps to except central Africa) have remained free from every mixture with foreigners.

segments.label: §47, astra source block1
segments.text: Wherever actual contact between speakers has existed among peoples, however indirect, similarity in kind between their languages arises from language already formed; conversely, where such similarity arising from formed language can be recognized in languages, it proves that such contact occurred.

segments.label: §47, astra source block2
segments.text: This is important because it at least states the principle—even if that principle should prove of little practical use—by which the historical connection of languages can be distinguished from the similarity in kind that must be sought solely in the similarity in kind of human dispositions.

segments.label: §47, astra source block3
segments.text: For suppose that the American nations had originated in their own homeland and had not mixed with any inhabitants of the rest of the earth before the spread of the languages still in existence: no non-American sound would then have been heard in America, and no similarity in kind between the American languages and the other languages of the earth could have arisen through language already formed.

segments.label: §47, astra source block4
segments.text: Nevertheless, the general human dispositions would still be the same in America too; there would be the same unity of human essence—whether one derived it from descent from a single human pair or from the unity of the creative idea—without which (34) language itself would not be possible. segments.label: §47, astra source block5
segments.text: In this sense there is only one language, just as there is only one human species, and all differences of race annul neither the concept of humanity nor the possibility of regular reproduction.

segments.label: §47, astra source block6
segments.text: This becomes still more evident when one considers that the natural surroundings that act upon human beings, and consequently upon language, are also broadly the same, and that the means all languages employ as sounds are confined within limits that are not very wide.

segments.label: §47, astra source block7
segments.text: This general similarity in kind also occurs in historically connected languages, but only in those parts upon which sounds added from outside have exerted no influence, and even there never in a pure state: for in language, which exists only in the activity of producing it on each occasion (40), every influence always permeates the whole.

segments.label: §47, astra source block8
segments.text: Whether sufficient means exist to distinguish in languages themselves these two possible kinds of similarity may remain undecided for now; but it was necessary to determine their concepts precisely.

segments.text: We shall have to return to this point in great detail later, since America could more readily have remained free of all mixture with outsiders than any part of the Old World, unless one wished to except central Africa.

segments.text: For suppose that the American nations had originated in their own homeland and had not mixed with any inhabitants of the rest of the earth before the spread of the languages still in existence: no non-American sound would then have been heard in America, and no similarity in kind between the American languages and the other languages of the earth could have arisen through language already formed.

segments.label: §47, revised source block4
segments.text: Nevertheless, the general human dispositions would still be the same in America too; there would be the same unity of human essence—whether one derived it from descent from a single human pair or from the unity of the creative idea—without which (34) language itself would not be possible. A similarity in kind among languages would therefore necessarily have to arise from this too.

segments.label: §47, revised source block5
segments.text: In this sense there is only one language, just as there is only one human species and all differences of race annul neither the concept of humanity nor the possibility of regular reproduction.

segments.label: §47, revised source block6
segments.text: This becomes still more evident when we consider that the natural surroundings acting upon human beings, and consequently upon language too, are broadly the same, and that the means employed by all languages, namely sounds, are confined within limits that are not very wide.

segments.label: §47, revised source block7
segments.text: This general similarity in kind also occurs in historically connected languages, but only in those parts upon which sounds added from outside have exerted no influence, and even there never in a pure state: for in language, which exists only in the activity of producing it on each occasion (40), every influence always permeates the whole.

segments.label: §47, revised source block8
segments.text: Whether sufficient means exist to distinguish in languages themselves these two possible kinds of similarity may remain undecided for now; but it was necessary to determine their concepts precisely.

segments.label: §47, revised source block9
segments.text: We shall have to return to this point in great detail later, since America could more readily have remained free of all mixture with outsiders than any part of the Old World, unless one wished to except central Africa.

segments.label: §48, de source block1
segments.text: In allen Sprachen trifft man daher Gleichartiges an, und die Hoffnung würde vergeblich seyn, in irgend einer etwas durchaus Neues zu finden.

segments.label: §48, de source block2
segments.text: Ich läugne nicht, dass mich die grosse Aehnlichkeit der Europaeischen und mehrerer Asiatischen Sprachen zuerst zu dem Studium der Amerikanischen hingetrieben hat.

segments.label: §48, de source block3
segments.text: Ich glaubte dort auf ein ganz fremdes Gebiet zu kommen, und auf den ersten Anblick und gewissermassen ist es auch so, aber genauere Prüfung zeigt auch da die Erscheinungen minder fremdartig.

segments.label: §48, de source block4
segments.text: Die Aufgabe bei der Untersuchung jeder Sprache ist also das Erkennen des Charakteristischen in der Gleichartigkeit.

segments.label: §48, de source block5
segments.text: Denn da die Sprache immer Eins ist, das heisst, da jedes in Sprache Gedachte immer aus der ganzen Sprache (oder wenn dies deutlicher scheint, der ganzen Sprachfertigkeit) des Individuum in dem jedesmaligen Augenblick hervorgeht, und mithin die ganze Sprache sich in dieser einzelnen Aeusserung ausprägt, so besteht nicht etwa das Gleichartige neben dem Charakteristischen, sondern geht in dasselbe über, das heisst die allgemeine dem ganzen Menschengeschlecht inwohnende Kraft bestimmt sich individuell.

segments.label: §48, de source block6
segments.text: Gleichartigkeit und Individualität können daher nur in der Idee getrennt werden, und man muss, obgleich das Individuelle, als die unmittelbare Thatsache, bloss wahrgenommen, nicht zergliedert für den Verstand dargestellt werden kann, doch soviel als möglich beide in ihrer Einheit auffassen.

segments.label: §48, de source block7
segments.text: Ich wünschte nicht, dass, was ich so eben vom Erscheinen der ganzen Sprache an jedem einzeln Gesprochenen sagte, möchte für eine der Uebertreibungen gehalten werden, welchen man sich in allgemeinen, von Beispielen entblössten Raisonnements leicht zu überlassen Gefahr läuft.

segments.label: §48, de source block8
segments.text: Es soll damit ausgedrückt werden, dass in der Sprache Alles durch Jedes und Jedes durch Alles bestimmt wird, und dies ist buchstäblich wahr.

segments.label: §48, de source block9
segments.text: Man kann an dem einfachsten Satz einen grossen Theil dieses Zusammenhanges sogar factisch nachweisen, wenn man den Satz nach allen Arten bei Sprachen möglicher Zergliederung in seine Elemente zerlegt, jedes Element in alle Kategorieen bringt, die ihm entsprechen, es dort mit den in derselben mit ihm begriffenen, und darauf die Kategorieen selbst unter einander vergleicht, und immer so fortfährt, alle bestimmende Beziehungen der Sprache durchzugehen und zu untersuchen, wie die in jeder geltende Bestimmung auch das Element des gegebenen Satzes bestimmt.

segments.label: §48, de source block10
segments.text: Unendlich Vieles beruht indess freilich auf nicht darstellbaren Analogieen des Sprachgefühls.

segments.label: §48, codex source block1
segments.text: We therefore encounter things alike in kind in all languages, and the hope of finding something entirely new in any one of them would be vain.

segments.label: §48, codex source block2
segments.text: I do not deny that the great similarity between the European and several Asian languages first drove me to study the American languages.

segments.label: §48, codex source block3
segments.text: I thought I would enter an entirely foreign domain there, and at first sight, and in a certain respect, this is indeed so; but closer examination shows the phenomena there too to be less alien.

segments.label: §48, codex source block4
segments.text: The task in investigating each language is therefore to recognise what is characteristic within likeness in kind.

segments.label: §48, codex source block5
segments.text: For since language is always one—that is, since everything thought in language always proceeds from the individual's entire language, or, if this seems clearer, entire proficiency in language, at the particular moment, and consequently the entire language is imprinted in this single utterance—what is alike in kind does not merely exist alongside what is characteristic, but passes into it: that is, the general power dwelling within the whole human race determines itself individually.

segments.label: §48, codex source block6
segments.text: Likeness in kind and individuality can therefore be separated only in the idea; and although the individual, as the immediate fact, can only be perceived, not analysed and presented to the understanding, we must nevertheless grasp the two in their unity as far as possible.

segments.label: §48, codex source block7
segments.text: I should not wish what I have just said about the appearance of the entire language in each particular thing spoken to be taken for one of those exaggerations to which we easily risk surrendering ourselves in general reasonings devoid of examples.

segments.label: §48, codex source block8
segments.text: What it is intended to express is that in language everything is determined by each thing and each thing by everything, and this is literally true.

segments.label: §48, codex source block9
segments.text: Even in the simplest sentence, a large part of this interconnectedness can actually be demonstrated: one divides the sentence into its elements according to every kind of analysis possible in languages, places each element in all the categories appropriate to it, compares it there with the other elements included in the same category, then compares the categories themselves with one another, and continues in this way through all the determining relations of the language, investigating how the determination operative in each also determines the element of the given sentence.

segments.label: §48, codex source block10
segments.text: Admittedly, however, infinitely much rests on analogies of the feeling for language that cannot be presented.

segments.label: §48, muse source block2

segments.label: §48, muse source block3

segments.text: Infinitely much, however, admittedly rests on analogies of linguistic feeling that cannot be presented.

segments.label: §49, de source block1
segments.text: Es ergiebt sich aus dem Vorigen von selbst, dass, obgleich der individuelle Sprachlaut die letzte wirkliche Erscheinung ist, doch die Individualitaet einer Sprache nicht bloss in ihrem Ton, und das Gleichartige etwa in dem Ideellen gesucht werden muss.

segments.label: §49, de source block2
segments.text: Die Individualitaet zeigt sich vielmehr in Allem, und ist eine und eben dieselbe von dem Alphabet bis zu der Weltvorstellung (39.) in der Totalitaet der Sprache.

segments.label: §49, de source block3
segments.text: Wie jene Grundtöne anders gesetzt würden, wäre es auch diese Anschauungsweise, und umgekehrt.

segments.label: §49, de source block4
segments.text: Niemand wird verlangen, dass dies an irgend einer Sprache sollte wirklich dargestellt werden.

segments.label: §49, de source block5
segments.text: Dies ist allerdings unmöglich, aber die Sache ist darum dennoch wahr und wichtig; wahr, weil sie aus der im Vorigen entwickelten Natur des Sprechens und der Sprache nothwendig folgt, wichtig, weil, wenn man von den beiden Grundwahrheiten aller Sprachuntersuchung : dass die Sprache Eins mit dem ganzen Denken und Empfinden des Menschen ausmacht, und dass sie nirgends ein Daseyn hat, als in dem ewig sich wechselseitig erzeugenden Acte des Sprechens und Denkens in Sprache, weil, wenn man, sage ich, von diesen abweicht, man auch das in der That Erkennbare in den wirklichen Sprachen übersieht.

segments.label: §49, de source block6
segments.text: Vorzüglich ist aber die gehörige Erweiterung des Hinblickes auf die Sprachen zu ihrer richtigen Behandlung nothwendig.

segments.label: §49, de source block7
segments.text: Da Alles in der Sprache geistig ist, so hängt es von der Energie und Intelligenz ab, welche sich der Sprache bedient, wie stark und voll sie auf das Denken und Empfinden einwirkt, und jede richtigere Einsicht über sie wird in dem ganzen Menschen in dem reineren Einfluss ihrer Individualität lebendig.

segments.label: §49, de source block8
segments.text: Es tritt aber bei dem eignen Gebrauch auch Alles das in das Gefühl und somit in die Erkenntniss, was durch den zergliedernden Verstand nie darstellbar ist, und so entspringt aus dem durch erweiterten Ueberblick geleiteten Gebrauch auch erweiterte Einsicht.

segments.label: §49, de source block9
segments.text: Was man aber an der eignen Sprache gefühlt hat, ahndet man, wie tief und fein es auch sey, leichter in einer fremden.

segments.label: §49, de source block10
segments.text: So ist es wohl unläugbar, dass, seitdem die hauptsächlichsten Nationen Europas angefangen haben, in ihren Muttersprachen zu schreiben, eine ganz andre Einsicht in den Zusammenhang, welchen jede derselben in sich und mit der Nation hat, als vorher, entstanden ist.

segments.label: §49, de source block11
segments.text: Auch dadurch zeichnet sich diese Epoche aus, die ich für die wichtigste in der Sprachbehandlung halte, und die in unserer Zeit viel mächtiger einwirkt, als es dieselbe Erscheinung bei den Alten that, da bei diesen nur zwei, bei uns aber mehrere Sprachen, und in viel reger wetteifernde Berührung traten.

segments.label: §49, codex source block1
segments.text: It follows of itself from the foregoing that, although the individual speech sound is the ultimate actual manifestation, the individuality of a language must not be sought solely in its sound, with likeness in kind assigned, perhaps, to its ideal content.

segments.label: §49, codex source block2
segments.text: Rather, individuality manifests itself in everything, and is one and the same throughout the totality of the language, from its alphabet to its representation of the world (39).

segments.label: §49, codex source block3
segments.text: If those basic sounds were differently constituted, this manner of apprehension would be different too, and conversely.

segments.label: §49, codex source block4
segments.text: No one will demand that this should actually be demonstrated in any particular language.

segments.label: §49, codex source block5
segments.text: That is certainly impossible, but the proposition is nevertheless true and important: true because it follows necessarily from the nature of speaking and language developed above; important because departing from the two fundamental truths of all linguistic investigation—that language is one with the whole of human thinking and feeling, and that it has no existence anywhere except in the eternally reciprocally productive act of speaking and thinking in language—departing, I say, from these truths also makes us overlook what can actually be known in existing languages.

segments.label: §49, codex source block6
segments.text: Above all, a proper widening of our outlook on languages is necessary for treating them correctly.

segments.label: §49, codex source block7
segments.text: Since everything in language is mental, the strength and fullness of its effect on thinking and feeling depend on the energy and intelligence that employ it; and every more accurate insight into language comes alive in the whole human being through the purer influence of its individuality.

segments.label: §49, codex source block8
segments.text: In one's own use of language, however, everything that can never be presented by the analysing understanding also enters feeling and thus knowledge; hence a use guided by a wider overview also gives rise to wider insight.

segments.label: §49, codex source block9
segments.text: Whatever one has felt in one's own language, however deep and subtle it may be, one more readily divines in a foreign one.

segments.label: §49, codex source block10
segments.text: Thus it is surely undeniable that, since the principal nations of Europe began writing in their mother tongues, an entirely different insight has arisen into the interconnectedness of each language within itself and with its nation.

segments.label: §49, codex source block11
segments.text: This too distinguishes that epoch, which I consider the most important in the treatment of language, and which exercises a much more powerful influence in our time than the same phenomenon did among the ancients, since among them only two languages came into contact, whereas among us several did, and in much more lively rivalry.

segments.label: §49, muse source block1
segments.text: It results of itself from what precedes that, although the individual language-sound is the last real appearance, the individuality of a language must nevertheless not be sought merely in its tone, nor what is of the same kind perhaps in the ideal element.

segments.label: §49, muse source block2
segments.text: Individuality rather shows itself in everything, and is one and the same from the alphabet to the world-representation (39.) in the totality of language.

segments.label: §49, muse source block3
segments.text: As those fundamental tones would be differently posited, so would this mode of viewing also be different, and conversely.

segments.label: §49, muse source block4
segments.text: No one will demand that this should really be presented in any language.

segments.label: §49, muse source block5
segments.text: This is indeed impossible, but the matter is nevertheless true and important on that account; true because it follows necessarily from the nature of speaking and of language developed in what precedes, important because, if one departs from the two fundamental truths of all investigation of language — that language constitutes one whole with the entire thinking and feeling of man, and that it has existence nowhere except in the eternally mutually generating act of speaking and thinking in language — because, if one departs from these, I say, one also overlooks what can in fact be recognized in real languages.

segments.label: §49, muse source block6
segments.text: Pre-eminently, however, the proper widening of the outlook upon languages is necessary for their correct treatment.

segments.label: §49, muse source block7
segments.text: Since everything in language is mental, it depends on the energy and intelligence that makes use of language how strongly and fully it acts upon thinking and feeling, and every more correct insight into it becomes alive in the whole human being in the purer influence of its individuality.

segments.label: §49, muse source block8
segments.text: In one's own use, however, everything also enters into feeling, and thus into knowledge, that can never be presented through the analysing understanding, and so from use guided by a widened survey there also arises widened insight.

segments.label: §49, muse source block9
segments.text: What one has felt in one's own language, however deep and fine it may be, one divines more easily in a foreign one.

segments.label: §49, muse source block10
segments.text: Thus it is probably undeniable that, since the principal nations of Europe began to write in their mother tongues, a wholly different insight has arisen from what existed before into the connexion which each of them has within itself and with the nation.

segments.label: §49, muse source block11
segments.text: This epoch, which I regard as the most important in the treatment of language, is also distinguished by this, and in our time it acts much more powerfully than the same appearance did among the ancients, since among them only two languages, among us, however, several, entered into contact, and into much more actively rivalrous contact.

segments.text: It follows of itself from the foregoing that, although the individual linguistic sound is the ultimate actual manifestation, the individuality of a language must not therefore be sought solely in its sound, and its similarity in kind perhaps in the realm of ideas.

segments.text: Rather, individuality shows itself in everything, and is one and the same throughout the totality of language, from the alphabet to the representation of the world (39).

segments.label: §49, astra source block5
segments.text: That is admittedly impossible, but the matter remains true and important nonetheless: true because it follows necessarily from the nature of speaking and language developed above; important because, if we depart from the two fundamental truths of all investigation of language—that language forms a unity with the whole of human thinking and feeling, and that it exists nowhere except in the act of speaking and thinking in language, which perpetually produce one another—if, I say, we depart from these truths, we also overlook what can in fact be known in actual languages.

segments.label: §49, astra source block6
segments.text: Above all, a proper broadening of our perspective on languages is necessary to treat them correctly.

segments.text: Since everything in language is mental, the strength and fullness of its effect upon thinking and feeling depend on the energy and intelligence that employ it; and every more accurate insight into language comes alive in the whole human being through the purer influence of its individuality.

segments.label: §49, astra source block8
segments.text: In one's own use of language, however, everything that can never be presented by the analysing understanding also enters feeling, and thus knowledge; so use guided by a broader overview also gives rise to broader insight.

segments.label: §49, astra source block9
segments.text: What one has felt in one's own language, however deep and subtle it may be, is easier to intuit in a foreign one.

segments.label: §49, astra source block10
segments.text: Thus it is surely undeniable that, since the principal nations of Europe began writing in their mother tongues, an entirely different insight from that previously available has arisen into the connections within each of these languages and between each language and its nation.

segments.label: §49, astra source block11
segments.text: This too distinguishes that epoch, which I regard as the most important in the treatment of language, and which exerts a much more powerful influence in our time than the same phenomenon did among the ancients: among them only two languages came into contact, whereas among us several did, and in much livelier rivalry.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block1
segments.text: It follows of itself from the foregoing that, although the individual speech sound is the ultimate actual manifestation, the individuality of a language must not be sought solely in its sound, with similarity in kind assigned, perhaps, to the realm of ideas.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block2
segments.text: Rather, individuality shows itself in everything, and is one and the same throughout the totality of language, from the alphabet to the representation of the world (39).

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block3
segments.text: If those basic sounds were differently constituted, this way of viewing would be different too, and conversely.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block4
segments.text: No one will demand that this actually be demonstrated in any particular language.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block5
segments.text: That is admittedly impossible, but the matter remains true and important nonetheless: true because it follows necessarily from the nature of speaking and language developed above; important because, if we depart from the two fundamental truths of all investigation of language—that language forms a unity with the whole of human thinking and feeling, and that it exists nowhere except in the act of speaking and thinking in language, which perpetually produce one another—if, I say, we depart from these truths, we also overlook what can in fact be known in actual languages.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block6
segments.text: Above all, a proper broadening of our perspective on languages is necessary to treat them correctly.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block7
segments.text: Since everything in language is mental, the strength and fullness of its effect upon thinking and feeling depend on the energy and intelligence that employ it; and every more accurate insight into language comes alive in the whole human being through the purer influence of its individuality.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block8
segments.text: In one's own use of language, however, everything that can never be presented by the analysing understanding also enters feeling, and thus knowledge; so use guided by a broader overview also gives rise to broader insight.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block9
segments.text: What one has felt in one's own language, however deep and subtle it may be, is easier to intuit in a foreign one.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block10
segments.text: Thus it is surely undeniable that, since the principal nations of Europe began writing in their mother tongues, an entirely different insight from that previously available has arisen into the connections within each of these languages and between each language and its nation.

segments.label: §49, synthesis source block11

segments.label: §50, de source block1
segments.text: Um aber an der scharfen Begränzung der Begriffe nichts fehlen zu lassen, muss zu dem Vorigen noch hinzugesetzt werden, dass die Individualität einer Sprache auch nur vergleichungsweise eine seyn kann, und dass die wahre Individualität nur in dem jedesmal Sprechenden liegt.

segments.label: §50, de source block2
segments.text: In der That vollendet erst dies den Begriff.

segments.label: §50, de source block3
segments.text: Eine Nation hat freilich im Ganzen dieselbe Sprache, allein schon nicht alle ihre Mitglieder (38.) ganz dieselbe, und geht man noch weiter in das Feinste über, so besitzt jeder Mensch seine eigne.

segments.label: §50, de source block4
segments.text: Keiner denkt bei dem Wort gerade das, was der andre, und die noch so kleine Verschiedenheit zittert, wenn man die Sprache mit dem beweglichsten aller Elemente vergleichen will, durch die ganze Sprache.

segments.label: §50, de source block5
segments.text: Bei jedem Denken und Empfinden kehrt, vermöge der Einerleiheit der Individualitaet, dieselbe Verschiedenheit zurück, und bildet eine Masse aus einzeln Unbemerkbarem.

segments.label: §50, de source block6
segments.text: Alles Verstehen ist daher immer zugleich ein Nicht-Verstehen, eine Wahrheit, die man auch im praktischen Leben trefflich benutzen kann, alle Uebereinstimmung in Gedanken und Gefühlen zugleich ein Auseinandergehen.

segments.label: §50, de source block7
segments.text: Dies wird nur da nicht sichtbar, wo es sich unter der Allgemeinheit des Begriffs und der Empfindung verbirgt; wo aber die erhöhete Kraft die Allgemeinheit durchbricht, und auch für das Bewusstseyn schärfer individualisirt, da tritt es deutlich ans Licht.

segments.label: §50, de source block8
segments.text: So wird niemand jedem bedeutenden Schriftsteller seine eigene Sprache absprechen.

segments.label: §50, de source block9
segments.text: Zwar lässt sich entgegnen, dass man unter Sprache nur eben jene Allgemeinheit der Formen, Wörter und Regeln versteht, welche gerade verschiedenartiger Individualitaet Raum erlaubt, und dies ist allerdings vollkommen wahr.

segments.label: §50, de source block10
segments.text: Indess lässt sich darum doch die angeregte Ansicht nicht aus dem Gebiete auch der allgemeinsten Sprachuntersuchung verbannen.

segments.label: §50, de source block11
segments.text: Denn es giebt mehrere Stufen, auf denen die Allgemeinheit der Sprachformen sich auf diese Weise individualisirt, und das individualisirende Princip ist dasselbe : das Denken und Sprechen in einer bestimmten Individualität.

segments.label: §50, de source block12
segments.text: Dadurch entsteht die Verschiedenheit in der Sprache der Einzelnen, wie der Nationen.

segments.label: §50, de source block13
segments.text: Es ist überall nur ein Mehr oder Weniger.

segments.label: §50, de source block14
segments.text: Man muss daher bis zur letzten Stufe herabsteigen.

segments.label: §50, de source block15
segments.text: Man könnte zwar die Gränze da finden wollen, wo die Sprache, wenn auch individuell nuancirt, sich doch derselben Laute bedient.

segments.label: §50, de source block16
segments.text: Aber auch dies ist schon bei den verschiedenen Classen einer Nation nicht ganz der Fall, und auch der Einzelne braucht einige vorzugsweise, bedient sich andrer, gleichsam als ihm fremder, schliesst noch andre ganz aus, und bildet sich dadurch, auch ausser den Abweichungen in der Bedeutung, sein eignes Wörterbuch.

segments.label: §50, codex source block1
segments.text: To leave nothing wanting in the precise delimitation of concepts, however, we must add to the foregoing that the individuality of a language can itself be individuality only comparatively, and that true individuality lies only in the person speaking on each occasion.

segments.label: §50, codex source block2
segments.text: In fact, only this completes the concept.

segments.label: §50, codex source block3
segments.text: A nation certainly has, on the whole, the same language; yet not even all its members have precisely the same one (38), and if we proceed further into the finest detail, each human being possesses a language of his own.

segments.label: §50, codex source block4
segments.text: No one thinks exactly what another does on hearing a word, and the difference, however small, trembles through the entire language, if we may compare language with the most mobile of all the elements.

segments.label: §50, codex source block5
segments.text: In every act of thinking and feeling, the same difference recurs by virtue of the sameness of the individuality, forming a mass out of things individually imperceptible.

segments.label: §50, codex source block6
segments.text: All understanding is therefore always at the same time a not-understanding—a truth that can also be put to excellent use in practical life—and all agreement in thoughts and feelings is at the same time a divergence.

segments.label: §50, codex source block7
segments.text: This remains invisible only where it hides beneath the generality of concept and feeling; but where heightened power breaks through that generality and individualises more sharply even for consciousness, it comes clearly to light.

segments.label: §50, codex source block8
segments.text: Thus no one will deny that every significant writer has a language of his own.

segments.label: §50, codex source block9
segments.text: It may admittedly be objected that by language we mean precisely that generality of forms, words and rules which allows room for diverse individuality, and this is certainly perfectly true.

segments.label: §50, codex source block10
segments.text: Nevertheless, the view raised here cannot on that account be banished even from the domain of the most general investigation of language.

segments.label: §50, codex source block11
segments.text: For there are several levels at which the generality of linguistic forms is individualised in this way, and the individualising principle is the same: thinking and speaking within a particular individuality.

segments.label: §50, codex source block12
segments.text: This gives rise to diversity in the language of individuals as of nations.

segments.label: §50, codex source block13
segments.text: Everywhere it is only a matter of more or less.

segments.label: §50, codex source block14
segments.text: We must therefore descend to the final level.

segments.label: §50, codex source block15
segments.text: One might admittedly wish to find the boundary where language, though individually nuanced, nevertheless employs the same sounds.

segments.label: §50, codex source block16
segments.text: But even among the different classes of a nation this is not entirely the case; and the individual too uses some preferentially, employs others as though they were foreign to him, excludes still others altogether, and thereby forms his own dictionary, quite apart from divergences in meaning.

segments.label: §51, de source block1
segments.text: Vorzüglich aber ist nothwendig, auf die Modificirung der Sprache in jedem Individuum aufmerksam zu machen, um die Gewalt des Menschen über die Sprache zu beweisen, so wie wir im Vorigen (42. 43.) ihre Macht über ihn dargestellt haben.

segments.label: §51, de source block2
segments.text: Diese kann man (wenn man den Ausdruck auf geistige Kräfte anwenden will) als ein physiologisches Wirken ansehen, jene ist ein rein dynamisches, in dieser liegt die Natur der wirkenden Kräfte der Sprache, in jener das Princip ihrer Freiheit.

segments.label: §51, de source block3
segments.text: Denn es kann im Menschen etwas aufsteigen, dessen Grund kein Verstand in den vorhergehenden Zuständen aufzufinden vermag, und man würde die Natur der Sprache verkennen, und gerade die geschichtliche Wahrheit ihrer Entstehung und Umänderung verletzen, wenn man die Möglichkeit solcher unerklärbaren Erscheinungen von ihr ausschliessen wollte.

segments.label: §51, de source block4
segments.text: Wenn aber auch die Freiheit unbestimmbar und unerklärbar ist, so lassen sich, nur innerhalb eines gewissen Spielraums, ihre Gränzen erkennen, und die Sprachuntersuchung muss die Erscheinung der Freiheit erkennen und ehren, aber ihren Gränzen sorgfältig nachspüren, um nicht in den Sprachen durch Freiheit für möglich zu halten, was es nicht ist.

segments.label: §51, codex source block1
segments.text: Above all, however, attention must be drawn to the modification of language in each individual, in order to demonstrate human power over language, just as we presented its power over human beings above (42, 43).

segments.label: §51, codex source block2
segments.text: The latter may be regarded as a physiological operation, if one wishes to apply the expression to mental powers; the former is a purely dynamic operation: in the latter lies the nature of the operative powers of language, in the former the principle of their freedom.

segments.label: §51, codex source block3
segments.text: For something may arise in a human being whose ground no understanding can discover in preceding states; and we would misunderstand the nature of language, and violate precisely the historical truth of its genesis and transformation, if we sought to exclude from it the possibility of such inexplicable phenomena.

segments.label: §51, codex source block4
segments.text: Yet although freedom cannot be determined or explained, its limits can be recognised, albeit only within a certain latitude; linguistic investigation must recognise and honour the manifestation of freedom, but carefully trace its limits, so as not to regard as possible in languages through freedom what is not possible.

segments.label: §51, muse source block1
segments.text: Pre-eminently, however, it is necessary to draw attention to the modification of language in every individual in order to prove the power of man over language, just as in what precedes (42. 43.) we have presented its might over him.

segments.label: §51, muse source block2
segments.text: The latter can be regarded (if one wants to apply the expression to mental powers) as a physiological working; the former is a purely dynamical one; in the latter lies the nature of the working powers of language, in the former the principle of its freedom.

segments.label: §51, muse source block3
segments.text: For something can arise in man whose ground no understanding can discover in preceding states, and one would misconceive the nature of language, and precisely violate the historical truth of its origin and alteration, if one wanted to exclude the possibility of such inexplicable appearances from it.

segments.label: §51, muse source block4
segments.text: But even if freedom is indeterminable and inexplicable, its limits can be recognized, though only within a certain latitude, and investigation of language must recognize and honour the appearance of freedom, but carefully trace its limits, so as not to regard as possible through freedom in languages what is not so.

segments.label: §51, astra source block1
segments.text: Above all, however, it is necessary to draw attention to the modification of language in each individual in order to demonstrate human power over language, just as we have presented its power over human beings above (42, 43).

segments.label: §51, astra source block2
segments.text: Language's power over human beings can be regarded—if one is willing to apply the expression to mental powers—as a physiological operation; human power over language is purely dynamic. In the former lies the nature of language's operative powers, in the latter the principle of its freedom.

segments.label: §51, astra source block3
segments.text: For something can arise within a human being whose ground no understanding can discover in the preceding states; and we would misconceive the nature of language, and violate precisely the historical truth of its emergence and transformation, if we sought to exclude from it the possibility of such inexplicable phenomena.

segments.label: §51, astra source block4
segments.text: But although freedom cannot be determined or explained, its limits can be recognized, though only within a certain range; and the investigation of language must recognize and honour the manifestation of freedom, while carefully tracing its limits, so as not to regard as possible through freedom in languages what is not possible.

segments.label: §51, synthesis source block1
segments.text: Above all, however, it is necessary to draw attention to the modification of language in each individual in order to demonstrate human power over language, just as we have presented its power over human beings above (42, 43).

segments.label: §51, synthesis source block2
segments.text: Language's power over human beings can be regarded—if one is willing to apply the expression to mental powers—as a physiological operation; human power over language is purely dynamic. In the former lies the nature of language's operative powers, in the latter the principle of its freedom.

segments.label: §51, synthesis source block3
segments.text: For something can arise within a human being whose ground no understanding can discover in the preceding states; and we would misconceive the nature of language, and violate precisely the historical truth of its emergence and transformation, if we sought to exclude from it the possibility of such inexplicable phenomena.
