A Sanskrit grammatical text attributed to Pāṇini is available. No precise date, rule count or claim about Humboldt’s intended grammatical scope is inferred.

evidence.locator: https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/speech-and-language; How do speech and language develop?; What are the milestones for speech and language development?
evidence.statement: Both relevant complete sections read through web tool Development varies between children and depends on exposure; developmental timetables do not warrant a universal narrow age under every circumstance. No diagnosis or clinical advice is offered.

evidence.excerpt: Humboldt is describing the limits of his knowledge, not denying that India had a grammatical tradition. Pāṇini’s *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is a Sanskrit grammatical text; see its [opening rules](https://sanskritdocuments.org/doc_z_misc_major_works/aShTAdhyAyI.html?lang=iast).
evidence.statement: Prevent the qualification about knowledge from becoming a claim of an absent tradition.

evidence.excerpt: The English takes intellectual activity as establishing the domain of sounds. The nearer German subject, articulated sound, is also possible; the hypothetical beginning may qualify that establishment or the whole account of producing articulated sound.
evidence.statement: Disclose the ambiguous agent and scope of the hypothetical beginning.

evidence.excerpt: “Noise” here means the audible physical component of speech, contrasted with articulation; it need not mean an unwanted or disorderly sound. See the terminology guide on sound and articulation.
evidence.statement: Avoid the modern everyday evaluative sense of Geräusch.

evidence.excerpt: “Deaf-mute” is Humboldt’s historical label. His account considers lip-reading, writing and taught speech; a natural sign language such as ASL is a complete visual language with its own grammar, not merely a set of signs for spoken sounds. See [NIDCD, American Sign Language](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/american-sign-language), especially “What is ASL?” and “How does ASL compare with spoken language?”
evidence.statement: Qualify the account of language access without erasing the historical argument.

evidence.excerpt: Passage21 separates articulation from audible noise; here Humboldt nevertheless restricts articulation in its essential nature to hearing. His restriction does not accommodate natural sign languages, whose grammar is expressed visually; see the preceding note on deaf people and language.
evidence.statement: Expose both the local conceptual tension and the unsupported sensory restriction.

evidence.excerpt: Air is needed to carry sound, but light can travel through a vacuum. The image here combines these different kinds of propagation; see [NASA, “Anatomy of an Electromagnetic Wave”](https://science.nasa.gov/ems/02_anatomy/), on mechanical and electromagnetic waves.
evidence.statement: Correct a substantive physical claim while retaining Humboldt’s image.

evidence.excerpt: Birds are not the only animals that sing: male humpback whales also produce complex songs. See [NOAA’s account of humpback whale song](https://hawaiihumpbackwhale.noaa.gov/science/research/whale-behavior.html), “Understanding the function of humpback whale song”.
evidence.statement: Correct the explicit exclusivity claim.

evidence.excerpt: “So-called savages” preserves Humboldt’s qualified historical label. His immediate point is that these languages contain expressive resources beyond practical need, rather than being impoverished systems for obtaining help.
evidence.statement: Make the rhetorical function of a historical classification clear.

evidence.excerpt: “Brings much to a close” follows the printed verb *abschliesst*, whose force here is uncertain: it may mean completing or closing off. “Wears much away” would fit the contrast with what remains fixed, but would require a different German reading; the checked print has not been altered.
evidence.statement: Expose a consequential uncertain verb rather than silently emending it.

evidence.excerpt: The distinction is between “we, including you” and “we, excluding you”: often called inclusive and exclusive *we*. Humboldt invokes different grammatical forms for these meanings, without giving a language-specific example here.
evidence.statement: Explain an unfamiliar grammatical contrast in ordinary English.

evidence.excerpt: The English reads the parenthesis as “not just … but also”, including both emergence as such and emergence in each act of speaking. The print has an uneven “not … but also” construction; the inclusive reading follows “also”, but a strictly literal rendering leaves the relation unclear.
evidence.statement: Disclose a syntactic interpretation that changes the scope of origin.

evidence.excerpt: The broad developmental pattern does not warrant the claim about all children under the most varied circumstances. Children differ in timing, and access to language matters; see [NIDCD, “Speech and Language Developmental Milestones”](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/speech-and-language), the opening two sections.
evidence.statement: Qualify the universal narrow-timing inference, not merely its dated wording.

evidence.excerpt: The proposed inherited destiny for a particular language is Humboldt’s inference, not something established by the examples offered here. He names no individual case in this passage; attachment to a familiar language does not by itself distinguish inheritance from experience. The German may instead mean that an original destiny was shifted onto another language; distinguish either reading from the descent of languages in43–47.
evidence.statement: Identify the missing discriminating evidence without introducing unsupported modern genetic claims.

evidence.excerpt: Humboldt gives no name or example that identifies this variety precisely. “The language of the Incas” here should therefore not be silently equated with a particular modern language; the point of the example is its joint association with family descent and social rank.
evidence.statement: Retain the identification limit for a historical example.

evidence.excerpt: Mr Klaproth already makes this observation in *Asia polyglotta*, p. [43.]
evidence.statement: Translate the sole source footnote in full; the bracketed page reference belongs to the print.

evidence.excerpt: This qualifies the earlier emphasis on sound in29: here individuality extends throughout a language, and50 places “true individuality” in the individual speaker. The changes in level—from a language’s audible identity to its entire character and then its speakers—should remain visible rather than being harmonized into one unchanging claim.
evidence.statement: Flag an apparent shift while distinguishing its bearers.

evidence.excerpt: The claim concerns differences within understanding, not its complete impossibility: even speakers who agree do not attach precisely identical content to a word. The qualification develops the differences introduced in50 rather than retracting the possibility of communication argued for earlier.
evidence.statement: Prevent the compressed paradox from erasing its degree qualification.

evidence.excerpt: “Physiological” describes language’s inherited power over its users; “dynamic” describes their power to act upon it. Humboldt expressly marks the physiological term as an analogy applied to mental powers, not a claim about a measured bodily mechanism.
evidence.statement: Resolve the demonstratives and explain the historically specific contrast.

evidence.excerpt: The English takes “within a certain latitude” to qualify how far freedom’s limits can be recognized. It may instead describe the latitude within which freedom itself operates;52 uses the same word for the scope left to an individual.
evidence.statement: Expose the consequential scope ambiguity instead of hiding it in a literal English comma frame.

evidence.excerpt: “In that influence” takes the compressed German pronoun to refer to national influence: individual treatments appear there in the aggregate. “In the individual” is grammatically possible, but fits the contrast between collective influence and individual activity less well.
evidence.statement: Expose a consequential pronoun choice.

evidence.excerpt: The shared pattern of the mental process described in16–20, abstracting from circumstances that give particular languages their character. It is not a classification such as “inflecting” or “agglutinating”.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: This unit uses “mind”, “soul” and “inner life” to keep these recurring German terms recoverable. They overlap in reference; the wording does not impose a system of three separate faculties. The earlier English147 used “mind” for some instances of Seele and remains preserved.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: A representation is what the mind presents to itself; a concept is its articulated determination in the argument. “Reality” translates Wesenheit where a thought acquires standing as an object for a subject, not necessarily material substance.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Articulation is the shaping of sound into thought-bearing elements and combinations. Ton and Laut overlap and can both require “sound”; “speech sound” marks Laut where useful. Geräusch is “noise” in the specific contrast of21–22, without the implication of unwanted sound. “Alphabet” in29 and33 ranges over speech sounds rather than merely written letters.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: “Power of language” keeps the recurring Sprachkraft visible; “capacity for language” renders Sprachvermögen. These are contextual contrasts, not names for two independently established mechanisms. Empfindung is “feeling” in the thinking/feeling contrast and “sensation” where bodily or animal responsiveness is at issue. Gewalt and Macht can also require “power”; their German identity remains available in the source. In51 the crucial contrast is who acts upon whom, made explicit in the English, rather than three independently established kinds of mechanism. Gefühl also requires “feeling”; the German words overlap here rather than naming universally separate domains.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Individuality is a distinctive way of being, said of languages, nations and persons at different levels; similarity in kind is what makes them comparable. The bearer and comparison matter. Sound’s privileged role in29 is qualified by49–50, as the local note explains.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Weltansicht in39 is “view of the world”: a standpoint and manner of apprehending things, not merely an explicit set of opinions. Weltvorstellung in49 is “representation of the world”; the English retains the change of German term. This does not by itself make every member of a nation hold identical beliefs;50 explicitly returns to individual differences.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Descent may concern people or languages; the argument distinguishes these. “Stock” retains the historical grouping metaphor, including regional groups such as the Florentines in29, without making it a modern biological taxon. “Primordial language” belongs to the explicitly qualified origin discussion in45–47. In43 “mother language” is a supposed parent language; “mother tongues” in49 are people’s native languages.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Rede concerns connected speech or discourse, rather than a stock of words. In55 the distinction is between words as matter and their combination into discourse as form, explicitly not simply sounds versus rules. “Material” renders Stoff where the inherited language is contrasted with its living production. “Dead” material means the inherited stock considered apart from its living use; it need not be an extinct language.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: The repeated Intellectualitaet in52 and54 is “intellectual life”: the sphere towards which national activity is directed, with a role for language. It does not mean measured intelligence or modern national test scores. Geistig and intellectuell can also overlap as “mental” or “intellectual”; the English does not posit two exclusive faculties from that lexical difference.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: These name the human communities in the argument, not automatically modern sovereign states. Humboldt places dialects, social groups and individual ways of speaking within them, and describes their historical formation through separation and cohesion.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: In31 the word is contrasted with things and then becomes an object for a thinking subject;39 distinguishes an external object’s impression from the word’s own effect. “Object” can translate either German noun where the context supports it. Gegenstand does not invariably mean a physical thing:31 also calls I and he different Gegenstände.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

text_version.body: In jeder Sprache wiederholt sich unläugbar derselbe geistige Process; Kräfte, Mittel und Erfolge sind einander so gleich und ungleich, als die menschlichen körperlichen und geistigen Sprachanlagen Verschiedenartigkeit innerhalb der von der Natur gesteckten Gränzen erlauben. Wo man nun einzelne Sprachen zu schildern versucht, muss man von dem allgemeinen Typus dieses Processes ausgehen und dahin zurückkehren, weil es sonst durchaus an dem nothwendigen Vergleichungspunkt fehlen würde. Die Allgemeinheit dieses Typus besteht darin, dass Alles, was von ihm auszusagen ist, nur durch den reinen Begriff der Sprache bedingt und von allen andren Umständen abgesehen wird, die, aus den übrigen menschlichen Anlagen und den auf sie einwirkenden Verhältnissen entspringend, in der Wirklichkeit den allgemeinen Typus individualisiren.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §16 — checked German

text_version.body: The same mental process undeniably recurs in every language; its powers, means and results resemble and differ from one another as much as the diversity of human bodily and mental dispositions for language permits within the limits set by nature. Whenever one attempts to describe particular languages, one must therefore start from the general type of this process and return to it, since otherwise the necessary point of comparison would be entirely lacking. The generality of this type consists in everything that can be said of it being determined solely by the pure concept of language, with all other circumstances left aside: circumstances which arise from the other human dispositions and the conditions acting upon them, and which in reality individualise the general type.

text_version.body: In every language the same mental process undeniably repeats itself; powers, means and results are as like and unlike one another as the human bodily and mental dispositions for language permit diversity within the limits set by nature. Where one now attempts to describe individual languages, one must start from the general type of this process and return to it, because otherwise the necessary point of comparison would be entirely lacking. The generality of this type consists in this, that everything that is to be asserted of it is conditioned only by the pure concept of language and that abstraction is made from all other circumstances which, arising from the remaining human dispositions and from the conditions acting upon them, individualize the general type in reality.

text_version.body: The same mental process undeniably recurs in every language; its powers, means and results resemble and differ from one another to the extent that human bodily and mental dispositions for language permit diversity within the limits set by nature. When attempting to describe individual languages, we must therefore begin with the general type of this process and return to it, since otherwise we would entirely lack the necessary point of comparison. The generality of this type consists in everything that can be said of it being determined solely by the pure concept of language, while all other circumstances are disregarded: circumstances that arise from the remaining human dispositions and the conditions acting upon them, and that individualize the general type in reality.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §16 — revised English, nature of language

text_version.body: Was man bisher in diesem Sinn, unter dem Namen der allgemeinen Grammatik, ausgearbeitet hat, erschöpft den Begriff bei weitem nicht, sondern bleibt bei einem kleinen Theile desselben stehn. Diese Wissenschaft, von der wir leider noch nicht wissen, ob sie schon bei den Indischen Grammatikern Fortschritte gemacht hatte, die aber von den Griechischen in einigen Punkten zu einer Vollendung gebracht war, die wenig mehr hinzuzufügen erlaubte, beschäftigt sich eigentlich nur mit der logischen Zergliederung der Rede und der Untersuchung der zur Verknüpfung der Gedanken in dieser nöthigen Wortformen ; also zunächst mit einem Erzeugniss der Sprache und daher nur mit einem Theile von dieser. Man hat zwar hie und da dem Begriff der allgemeinen Grammatik eine grössere Ausdehnung gegeben, nirgends aber, soviel mir bekannt ist, hat man, wie hier gefordert wird, eine Analyse des Verfahrens der Sprache in seinem ganzen Zusammenwirken versucht. Da sie sich auch vorzüglich mit der Betrachtung der grammatischen Formen, als der Bestandtheile der Rede, im Einzelnen beschäftigt, so fällt sie, nach der hier versuchten ganz andren Eintheilung der Sprachanalyse, grossentheils in den folgenden Abschnitt, und kann auf keine Weise uns des Geschäftes überheben, das Allgemeine, was zur Vergleichung des Besondren erfordert wird, aus eigner Ideenentwicklung hier von neuem aufzustellen, so viel besser es auch wäre, sich, bei der Schilderung einer Gattung bestimmter Sprachen, auf ein schon anderwärts aufgeführtes, und bewährtes allgemeines Lehrgebäude der Sprache beziehen zu können.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §17 — checked German

text_version.body: What has so far been developed in this sense under the name of general grammar falls far short of exhausting the concept, stopping instead at a small part of it. This discipline, which we unfortunately do not yet know whether the Indian grammarians had already advanced, but which the Greek grammarians brought in some respects to a perfection that left little to add, is actually concerned only with the logical analysis of discourse and the investigation of the word forms needed to connect thoughts within it; thus, in the first instance, with a product of language, and consequently with only a part of language. Here and there, admittedly, the concept of general grammar has been given a wider scope; but nowhere, to my knowledge, has anyone attempted what is required here: an analysis of the procedure of language in the full interplay of its operations. Since general grammar is also chiefly concerned with examining grammatical forms individually as the components of discourse, it falls largely within the following section under the quite different division of linguistic analysis attempted here, and can in no way relieve us of the task of establishing afresh, through the development of our own ideas, the general principles needed to compare particulars, however much better it would be, when describing a class of particular languages, to be able to refer to an established and tested general system of linguistic doctrine already constructed elsewhere.

text_version.body: What has hitherto been worked out in this sense, under the name of general grammar, by no means exhausts the concept, but stops at a small part of it. This science, of which we unfortunately do not yet know whether it had already made progress among the Indian grammarians, but which had been brought by the Greek grammarians in some points to a perfection that allowed little more to be added, is really concerned only with the logical analysis of speech and with the investigation of the word-forms necessary in it for connecting thoughts; thus in the first instance with a product of language and therefore only with a part of language. A greater extension has indeed here and there been given to the concept of general grammar, but nowhere, so far as I know, has an analysis of the procedure of language in its whole joint working been attempted, as is required here. Since it is also chiefly concerned in detail with considering the grammatical forms as the constituents of speech, it falls, according to the wholly different division of the analysis of language attempted here, for the most part into the following section, and can in no way relieve us of the task of setting up anew here, from our own development of ideas, the general element required for comparison of the particular, however much better it would be, in describing a genus of determinate languages, to be able to refer to a general system of doctrine concerning language already erected and proved elsewhere.

text_version.body: Denn es ist schon sonst dargethan, und kann wohl, als unbestritten, angenommen werden, dass die Sprache nicht bloss die Bezeichnung des, unabhängig von ihr geformten Gedanken, sondern selbst das bildende Organ des Gedanken ist. Die intellectuelle Thätigkeit, durchaus geistig, durchaus innerlich, und gewissermassen spurlos vorübergehend, wird durch den Ton in der Rede äusserlich und wahrnehmbar für die Sinne, und erhält durch die Schrift einen bleibenden Körper. Das auf diese Weise Erzeugte ist das Gesprochene und Aufgezeichnete aller Art, die Sprache aber der Inbegriff der Laute, welche die bestimmte intellectuelle Thätigkeit, welcher sie angehört, auf diesem Wege hervorzubringen vermag, und der nach Gesetzen (die wiederum aus der Natur der intellectuellen Thätigkeit und des ihr entsprechenden Tonsystems hervorgehn) möglichen Verbindungen und Umgestaltungen derselben. Die intellectuelle Thätigkeit und die Sprache sind daher Eins und unzertrennlich von einander; man kann nicht einmal schlechthin die erstere als das Erzeugende, die andre als das Erzeugte ansehen. Denn obgleich das jedesmal Gesprochene allerdings ein Erzeugniss des Geistes ist, so wird es doch, indem es zu der schon vorher vorhandenen Sprache gehört, ausser der Thätigkeit des Geistes, durch die Laute und Gesetze der Sprache bestimmt, und wirkt, indem es gleich wieder in die Sprache überhaupt übergeht, wieder bestimmend auf den Geist zurück. Die intellectuelle Thätigkeit ist an die Nothwendigkeit geknüpft, eine Verbindung mit dem Ton einzugehen, das Denken kann sonst nicht zur Deutlichkeit gelangen, die Vorstellung nicht zum Begriff werden. Den Ton erzeugt sie aus freiem Entschluss und formt ihn durch ihre Kraft, denn vermöge ihrer Durchdringung wird er zum articulirten Laut (wenn es möglich wäre, einen Anfang aller Sprache zu denken), begründet ein Gebiet solcher Laute, das selbständig, bestimmend und beschränkend, auf sie zurückwirkt.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §20 — checked German

text_version.body: For it has already been demonstrated elsewhere, and may surely be accepted as undisputed, that language is not merely the designation of thought formed independently of it, but is itself the formative organ of thought. Intellectual activity, wholly mental, wholly inward, and in a sense passing without a trace, becomes outward and perceptible to the senses through sound in speech, and acquires an enduring body through writing. What is produced in this way is everything spoken and recorded; language, however, is the totality of the sounds that the particular intellectual activity to which it belongs can produce by this means, together with their possible combinations and transformations according to laws which in turn arise from the nature of intellectual activity and its corresponding sound system. Intellectual activity and language are therefore one and inseparable from each other; one cannot even regard the former simply as what produces and the latter as what is produced. For although what is spoken on any occasion is certainly a product of the mind, it nevertheless belongs to a language already in existence, and is therefore determined not only by the mind's activity but also by the sounds and laws of that language; and as it immediately passes back into language as a whole, it acts back upon the mind, determining it in turn. Intellectual activity is bound by the necessity of entering into a connection with sound; otherwise thinking cannot attain distinctness, nor can a representation become a concept. It produces sound by a free decision and shapes it through its power, for sound becomes articulated sound through being permeated by intellectual activity; and it establishes a domain of such sounds which acts back upon it independently, determining and limiting it—if it were possible to conceive of a beginning of all language.

text_version.body: For it has already been shown elsewhere, and may well be assumed as undisputed, that language is not merely the designation of thought formed independently of it, but is itself the formative organ of thought. Intellectual activity, wholly mental, wholly inward, and in a certain measure passing without trace, becomes outward and perceptible to the senses through tone in speech, and receives through writing an enduring body. What is produced in this way is what is spoken and recorded of every kind; language, however, is the totality of the sounds which the determinate intellectual activity to which it belongs is able to produce by this path, and of the combinations and transformations of them that are possible according to laws which in turn proceed from the nature of the intellectual activity and of the system of tones corresponding to it. Intellectual activity and language are therefore one and inseparable from each other; one cannot even simply regard the former as what produces and the other as what is produced. For although what is spoken at any given time is indeed a product of the mind, it is nevertheless, inasmuch as it belongs to the language already existing beforehand, determined, besides by the activity of the mind, by the sounds and laws of the language, and, inasmuch as it at once passes again into language in general, reacts in a determining way upon the mind. Intellectual activity is bound to the necessity of entering into a combination with tone; otherwise thinking cannot attain distinctness, nor representation become concept. It produces tone from free resolve and forms it by its power, for by virtue of its penetration of it tone becomes articulated sound (if it were possible to think a beginning of all language), and establishes a domain of such sounds which, independent, determining and limiting, reacts upon it.

text_version.body: For it has already been demonstrated elsewhere, and may surely be accepted as undisputed, that language does not merely designate thought formed independently of it, but is itself the formative organ of thought. Intellectual activity, wholly mental, wholly inward, and passing, in a sense, without a trace, becomes external and perceptible to the senses through sound in discourse, and receives a lasting body through writing. What is produced in this way is everything spoken and recorded; language, however, is the totality of the sounds that the particular intellectual activity to which it belongs can produce by this means, together with their possible combinations and transformations according to laws that arise, in turn, from the nature of intellectual activity and its corresponding system of sounds. Intellectual activity and language are therefore one and inseparable; we cannot even regard the former simply as what produces and the latter as what is produced. For although what is spoken on any occasion is certainly a product of the mind, it belongs to a language already in existence, and is therefore determined not only by the mind's activity but also by the sounds and laws of that language; and, immediately passing back into language as a whole, it in turn acts upon and determines the mind. Intellectual activity is bound by the necessity of entering into a connection with sound; otherwise thinking cannot attain distinctness, nor can a representation become a concept. It produces sound by a free decision and shapes it through its power—for sound becomes articulated sound through being permeated by intellectual activity (if it were possible to conceive a beginning of all language)—and establishes a domain of such sounds that independently acts back upon it, determining and limiting it.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §20 — revised English, nature of language

text_version.body: Dasjenige, wessen das Denken in der Sprache bedarf, ist nicht eigentlich das dem Ohre wirklich Vernehmbare, oder um es anders auszudrücken, wenn man den articulirten Laut in die Articulation und das Geräusch zerlegt, nicht dieses, sondern nur jene. Die Articulation beruht auf der Gewalt des Geistes über die Sprachwerkzeuge, sie zu einer Behandlung des Tons zu nöthigen, welche der Form seines Wirkens entspricht. Dasjenige, worin sich diese Form und die Articulation, wie in einem verknüpfenden Mittel begegnen, ist, dass beide ihr Gebiet in Grundtheile zerlegen, deren Zusammenfügung lauter solche Ganze bildet, welche das Streben in sich tragen, Theile neuer Ganze zu werden. Ausser jener Gewalt ist aber auch in dem Geiste ein, sich den Sprachwerkzeugen selbst mittheilender Drang, von ihnen einen solchen Gebrauch zu machen, und auf jener Gewalt und diesem Drange beruht die Erzeugung der Sprache sogar unabhängig von dem Ohre vernehmbarem Geräusch. Dass die Sprache wirklich ganz innerlich ist, und auch ohne Lauthervorbringung und Vernehmung möglich bleibt, lehrt das Beispiel der Taubstummen. Durch das Ohr ist jeder Zugang zu ihnen verschlossen, sie lernen aber das Gesprochene an der Bewegung der Sprachwerkzeuge des Redenden und an der Schrift verstehen, sie sprechen selbst, indem man die Lage und Bewegung ihrer Sprachwerkzeuge lenkt. Dies kann nur durch das, auch ihnen beiwohnende Articulationsvermögen geschehen, indem sie durch den Zusammenhang ihres Denkens mit ihren Sprachwerkzeugen im Andern aus dem einen Gliede, der Bewegung seiner Sprachwerkzeuge, das andre, sein Denken, errathen lernen. Der Ton, den wir hören, offenbart sich ihnen durch die Lage und Bewegung der Organe, sie vernehmen seine Articulation ohne sein Geräusch. Es mag diesem auch in ihnen etwas Sinnliches, vielleicht etwas von ihrer Phantasie dem Mangelnden untergeschobenes entsprechen, wovon wir keinen Begriff haben, aber immer geht bei ihnen eine merkwürdige Zerlegung des articulirten Lautes vor. Sie verstehen wirklich die Sprache, da sie alphabetisch lesen und schreiben, und selbst reden lernen, nicht bloss den Gedanken durch Zeichen oder Bilder. Sie erlernen dies, nicht bloss dadurch, dass sie Vernunft, wie andre Menschen, sondern ganz eigentlich dadurch, dass sie auch Sprachfähigkeit besitzen, Uebereinstimmung ihres Denkens mit ihren Sprachwerkzeugen, und Drang beide zusammenwirken zu lassen, das eine und das andre wesentlich gegründet in der menschlichen, wenn auch von einer Seite verstümmelten Natur.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §21 — checked German

text_version.body: What thinking requires in language is not, strictly speaking, what is actually audible to the ear; or, to put it differently, if articulated sound is divided into articulation and noise, it requires only the former, not the latter. Articulation rests on the mind's power over the organs of speech, compelling them to handle sound in a way corresponding to the form of its own operation. The point at which this form and articulation meet, as in a connecting medium, is that both divide their domain into basic parts whose combination produces nothing but wholes that carry within themselves the striving to become parts of new wholes. Besides this power, however, the mind also contains an impulse to make such use of the organs of speech, an impulse which communicates itself to those organs; and the production of language rests on this power and this impulse even independently of noise audible to the ear. The example of deaf-mute people teaches us that language really is wholly inward and remains possible even without the production and perception of sound. Every avenue of access to them through the ear is closed, yet they learn to understand what is spoken through the movements of the speaker's organs of speech and through writing; they themselves speak when the position and movement of their organs of speech are guided. This can happen only through the capacity for articulation that they too possess: because of the connection between their thinking and their organs of speech, they learn to infer in another person one member of the connection, his thinking, from the other, the movement of his organs of speech. The sound we hear reveals itself to them through the position and movement of the organs; they perceive its articulation without its noise. Something sensory of which we have no conception may correspond to this noise in them too, perhaps something their imagination supplies in place of what is missing; but in any event, a remarkable separation of the components of articulated sound takes place in them. They really understand language, since they learn to read and write alphabetically and even to speak, rather than merely understanding thought through signs or pictures. They learn this not merely because they possess reason like other human beings, but quite specifically because they also possess a capacity for language: a correspondence between their thinking and their organs of speech, and an impulse to make the two work together, both essentially grounded in human nature, even though it is mutilated in one respect.

text_version.body: That of which thinking has need in language is not really what is actually audible to the ear, or, to express it differently, if one resolves articulated sound into articulation and noise, it is not the latter, but only the former. Articulation rests on the power of the mind over the organs of speech, compelling them to a treatment of tone which corresponds to the form of its working. That in which this form and articulation meet, as in a connecting means, is that both resolve their domain into fundamental parts whose joining together forms nothing but wholes of such a kind as carry within themselves the striving to become parts of new wholes. Besides that power, however, there is also in the mind an urge, communicating itself to the organs of speech themselves, to make such use of them, and on that power and this urge rests the production of language even independently of noise audible to the ear. That language is really wholly inward, and remains possible even without the production and hearing of sound, is taught by the example of deaf-mutes. Every access to them through the ear is closed; but they learn to understand what is spoken from the movement of the organs of speech of the person speaking and from writing, and they themselves speak when the position and movement of their organs of speech are guided. This can happen only through the faculty of articulation dwelling in them also, in that, through the connexion of their thinking with their organs of speech, they learn in another person to divine the one member, his thinking, from the other member, the movement of his organs of speech. The tone that we hear reveals itself to them through the position and movement of the organs; they perceive its articulation without its noise. Something sensible may also correspond to the latter in them, perhaps something supplied by their imagination in place of what is lacking, of which we have no concept, but always a remarkable resolution of articulated sound takes place in them. They really understand language, since they read and write alphabetically and themselves learn to speak, not merely thought through signs or pictures. They learn this not merely because they possess reason, like other human beings, but quite properly because they also possess a capacity for language, a correspondence of their thinking with their organs of speech, and an urge to let both work together, the one and the other essentially grounded in human nature, even if mutilated on one side.

text_version.body: Die Articulation (deren Begriff ich hier nur nach ihrer Wirkung, als diejenige Gestaltung des Lautes nehme, welche ihn zum Träger von Gedanken macht) ist jedoch im Vorigen nur nach ihrer logischen, oder wenigstens nur nach ihrer intellectuellen Natur geschildert worden. In ihrer wesentlichen hängt sie aber gerade von dem Ton, als Geräusch, oder vielmehr von derjenigen Lufterschütterung ab, durch welche die Sprachwerkzeuge in die Ferne wirken. Sie lässt sich daher auch nie unmittelbar auf andre Sinne, als das Ohr, anwenden, und wie man es versuchte, würde man immer nur Zeichen von Tönen, nicht unmittelbar von elementarisch zerlegbaren Wörtern hervorbringen. Dies beruht darauf, dass gerade die einem fremden Ohre vernehmbare Lufterschütterung durch die, von dem Gedanken bestimmten Organe mit der menschlichen Natur unzertrennlich, und nothwendig zu ihrer Entwicklung, verbunden ist.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §22 — checked German

text_version.body: In the foregoing, however, articulation—whose concept I take here only in terms of its effect, as the shaping of sound that makes it a vehicle of thoughts—has been described only in its logical, or at least only in its intellectual, nature. In its essential nature, however, it depends precisely on sound as noise, or rather on the vibration of the air through which the organs of speech act at a distance. It can therefore never be applied directly to any sense other than hearing; however one attempted this, one would always produce only signs of sounds, not direct signs of words divisible into elementary parts. This rests on the fact that precisely the vibration of the air, audible to another's ear and produced by organs determined by thought, is inseparably connected with human nature and necessary to its development.

text_version.body: Das Denken ist eine geistige Handlung, wird aber durch sein Bedürfniss nach Sprache ein Antrieb zu einer körperlichen. Es ist ein fortschreitendes Entwicklen, eine blosse innere Bewegung, in der nichts Bleibendes, Stätiges, Ruhendes angenommen werden kann, und zugleich eine Sehnsucht aus dem Dunkel nach dem Licht, aus der Beschränkung nach der Unendlichkeit. In dem, aus zwiefacher Natur in Eins zusammengeschmolzenen menschlichen Wesen geht dies Streben auch nach aussen, und findet, durch die Vermittlung der Sprachwerkzeuge, in der Luft, dem feinsten und am leichtesten bewegbaren aller Elemente, dessen scheinbare Unkörperlichkeit dem Geiste auch sinnlich entspricht, einen ihm wundervoll angemessenen Stoff, in dem, bei der menschlichen aufrechten Stellung, die Rede frei und ruhig von den Lippen zum Ohre strömt, der das Licht der Gestirne herbeiführt, und sich, ohne sichtbare Schranken, in die Unendlichkeit ausdehnt.

text_version.body: Thinking is a mental act, but through its need for language it becomes an impulse towards a bodily act. It is a progressive unfolding, a purely inward movement in which nothing enduring, constant or at rest can be assumed, and at the same time a longing to pass from darkness into light, from limitation into infinity. In the human being, whose twofold nature is fused into one, this striving also turns outwards and, through the mediation of the organs of speech, finds a material wonderfully suited to it in air, the finest and most easily moved of all the elements, whose apparent incorporeality corresponds to the mind even in sensory terms: a material in which, given the human upright posture, speech flows freely and calmly from the lips to the ear, which brings us the light of the stars, and which extends without visible bounds into infinity.

text_version.body: Indem auf diese Weise das geistige Streben sich Bahn durch die Lippen bricht, kehrt das Erzeugniss desselben zum eignen Ohre zurück; die subjective innere Handlung wird als äussres Object wieder aufgenommen. Dadurch theilt und befördert die Sprache das innerste Wesen des Denkens, das beständige Uebergehen des Subjects und Objects in einander. Denn keine Gattung der Vorstellungen kann als ein reines Beschauen eines schon vorhandenen Gegenstandes betrachtet werden. Die Thätigkeit der Sinne muss sich mit der inneren Handlung des Geistes synthetisch verbinden, und aus dieser Verbindung reisst sich die Vorstellung los, wird, der subjectiven Kraft gegenüber, zum Object, und kehrt, als solches aufs neue wahrgenommen, in jene zurück. Ohne daher irgend auf die Mittheilung zwischen Menschen und Menschen zu sehn, ist das Sprechen eine nothwendige Bedingung des Denkens des Einzelnen in abgeschlossener Einsamkeit. In der Erscheinung entwickelt sich jedoch die Sprache nur gesellschaftlich. Denn der Mensch versteht sich selbst nur, indem er die Verstehbarkeit seiner Worte an Andren versuchend geprüft hat.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §25 — checked German

text_version.body: As mental striving thus breaks a path through the lips, its product returns to one's own ear; the subjective inward act is received again as an outward object. Language thereby shares in and furthers the innermost essence of thinking: the constant passage of subject and object into each other. For no kind of representation can be regarded as the mere contemplation of an object already present. The activity of the senses must unite synthetically with the inward act of the mind; the representation breaks free from this union, becomes an object confronting the subjective power, and returns to that power when perceived anew as such an object. Thus, quite apart from any communication between one human being and another, speaking is a necessary condition of the individual's thinking in secluded solitude. In its actual manifestation, however, language develops only socially. For a human being understands himself only after experimentally testing the intelligibility of his words on others.

text_version.body: Wenn der unarticulirte Laut, wie immer bei den Thieren, und bisweilen beim Menschen, die Stelle der Sprache vertritt, so entpresst ihn entweder, wie bei widrigen Empfindungen, die Noth, oder es liegt ihm Absicht zum Grunde, indem er lockt, warnt, zur Hülfe herbeiruft, oder er entströmt, ohne Noth und Absicht, dem frohen Gefühle des Daseyns, dem Gefallen am Schmettern der Töne. Das Letzte ist das Poetische, ein aufglimmender Funke in der thierischen Dumpfheit. Diese verschiedenen Arten der Laute sind unter den mehr oder minder stummen und klangreichen Geschlechtern der Thiere sehr ungleich vertheilt, und verhältnissmässig wenigen ist die höhere und freudigere Gattung geworden. Es wäre auch für die Sprache belehrend, aber vielleicht unmöglich, zu ergründen, woher diese Verschiedenheit stammt. Dass die Vögel allein den Gesang besitzen, liesse sich vielleicht daraus erklären, dass sie freier, als alle andre Thiere, in dem Elemente des Tons, und in seinen reineren Regionen leben, wenn nicht so viele Gattungen derselben, gleich den auf der Erde wandelnden Thieren, an wenige einförmige Laute gebunden wären.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §26 — checked German

text_version.body: When unarticulated sound takes the place of language, as it always does in animals and sometimes in human beings, either distress forces it out, as with painful feelings; or it has an intention behind it, as when it lures, warns or calls for help; or, without distress or intention, it pours forth from the joyful feeling of existence, from pleasure in the pealing of sounds. The last is the poetic element, a spark flaring up in animal dullness. These different kinds of sound are distributed very unequally among the more or less silent or richly vocal kinds of animal, and comparatively few have been granted the higher and more joyful kind. To discover the source of this difference would be instructive for language too, but perhaps impossible. The fact that birds alone possess song might perhaps be explained by their living more freely than all other animals in the element of sound, and in its purer regions, were it not that so many kinds of bird, like the animals that walk on the earth, are restricted to a few monotonous sounds.

text_version.body: When unarticulated sound takes the place of language, as always in animals and sometimes in man, either need wrings it out, as in adverse feelings, or intention underlies it, in that it lures, warns or calls hither for help, or it streams forth, without need and intention, from the glad feeling of existence, from delight in the loud ringing out of tones. The last is the poetic element, a spark glimmering up in animal dullness. These different kinds of sounds are very unequally distributed among the more or less mute and richly sounding genera of animals, and to relatively few has the higher and more joyful kind fallen. It would also be instructive for language, but perhaps impossible, to fathom whence this diversity stems. That birds alone possess song could perhaps be explained from the fact that they live more freely than all other animals in the element of tone and in its purer regions, if so many genera of them were not, like the animals that walk on the earth, bound to a few uniform sounds.

text_version.body: In die Sprache gehen dieselben antreibenden Ursachen über: Noth, Absicht und Gefallen an der Rede. Aber das letzte bezieht sich in ihr auch, und hauptsächlich, auf den Gedanken, und dadurch kommt eine vierte Ursach hinzu, das Bedürfniss der Mittheilung und Entwicklung der Ideen und Empfindungen durch Gespräch. Es gehört gewiss zu den irrigsten Behauptungen, die Entstehung der Sprachen vorzugsweise dem Bedürfniss gegenseitiger Hülfsleistung zuzuschreiben. Der Mensch im Naturstande ist nicht so bedürftig, und dazu hätten, wie man an den Thieren sieht, unarticulirte Laute ausgereicht. Die Sprache ist, auch in ihren Anfängen, durchaus menschlich. Auch die Sprachen der sogenannten Wilden, und gerade sie, besitzen eine überall über das Bedürfniss überschiessende Fülle und Mannigfaltigkeit von Ausdrücken, und es giebt wohl in keiner Einöde eine wandernde Familie, die nicht ihre Lieder besässe, denn der Mensch, als Thiergattung, ist wesentlich ein singendes Geschöpf, nur Ideen mit den Tönen verbindend. Der viel wesentlichere Entstehungsgrund der Sprache ist das Gefallen am Sprechen, und daher ist es auf die Bildung der Sprachen von so wichtigem Einfluss, wie schweigsam oder geschwätzig ein Volk ist.

text_version.body: The same impelling causes pass into language: distress, intention and pleasure in discourse. But in language the last also refers, and chiefly, to thought, and this adds a fourth cause: the need to communicate and develop ideas and feelings through conversation. It is surely among the most erroneous assertions to attribute the origin of languages chiefly to the need for mutual assistance. text_version.title: Grundzüge §27 — revised English, nature of language

text_version.body: Man muss den Menschen, auch in seinen edelsten Bestrebungen, immer in seiner ganzen Natur, deren eine Seite er mit der Thierheit theilt, betrachten, und daher auch in der Sprache nicht das blosse Tönen übersehen, wodurch gleichsam der thierische Laut in den articulirten übergeht. Hierbei ist nun zunächst das Verhältniss dieses Tönens zur Ideenbezeichnung bemerkbar. Es kann dies mit dem Colorit in der Malerei verglichen werden. Die Sprachen sind darin bald reicher, bald dürftiger, bald freier von schmetterndem Geräusch, bald mehr damit überladen. Es geschieht aber auch, dass Sprachen überhaupt, oder auf gewissen Bildungsstufen mehr oder weniger ideenloses Schmettern der wirklichen Sprache beimischen, Sylben und selbst Wörter gebrauchen ohne bestimmte Einwirkung auf den Sinn, fast nur zur Ausfüllung des Tones. Ein gewisses Gefühl mag sich freilich mit allen dieser Art verbinden, dies aber ist auch bei dem unarticulirten Laute möglich. Durch die Cultur der Sprache fallen nun entweder diese blossen Ausfüllungsworte hinweg, oder werden im günstigeren Falle, durch künstlichere Bearbeitung, Zeichen feiner Nuancen der Ideen oder ihrer Verbindungen.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §28 — checked German

text_version.body: Even in their noblest endeavours, human beings must always be considered in their whole nature, one side of which they share with animality; hence we must not overlook in language the mere sounding through which animal sound passes, as it were, into articulated sound. What first deserves attention here is the relation of this sounding to the designation of ideas. It may be compared with colouring in painting. Languages are sometimes richer, sometimes poorer in it, sometimes freer from pealing noise, sometimes more overloaded with it. But languages also sometimes, either generally or at certain stages of development, mix more or less thoughtless pealing into actual language, using syllables and even words without any definite effect on the meaning, almost solely to fill out the sound. Some feeling may admittedly attach to everything of this kind, but that is possible with unarticulated sound too. As language is cultivated, these mere filler words either disappear or, in the more favourable case, become signs of fine nuances of ideas or their connections through more skilful elaboration.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §28 — revised English, nature of language

text_version.body: In der Natur des Tones, als solchen, liegt endlich allein die wahre Individualitaet jeder Sprache. Was man thun und versuchen mag, ihre Eigenthümlichkeiten zu schildern, so bestimmt man nur immer näher und näher die Gattung, welcher sie angehört ;als diese und keine andere Sprache spricht sie sich nur selbst vor dem Ohre aus. Obgleich das Alphabet der ganzen Menschheit von gewissen, nicht einmal sehr weiten Gränzen umschlossen ist, so hat doch jedes Volk mit eigner Sprache auch sein eignes Lautsystem in der Ausschliessung gewisser Töne, der Vorliebe für andre, der Bestimmung der verschiedenen zur Bezeichnung verschiedener Begriffe, der Behandlung der Töne in ihren Verbindungen u. s. f. Man kann dies mit dem verschiedenartigen Geschrei und den Tonarten der Thiergattungen vergleichen. Es ist darin, wenn auch die fortschreitende Entwicklung viel abschliesst, doch etwas Festes, Stammartiges, tief in den Modificationen der Sprachwerkzeuge und dem Tongefühle Gegründetes. Es unterscheidet aber noch mehr die Stämme, als die Sprachen, da in derselben Sprache einzelne Stämme von allen übrigen durchaus abweichende Töne haben, wie z. B. die Florentiner den hauchenden Kehllaut. Allein abgesehen von solchen Einzelnheiten, die für die Sprache an sich zufällig erscheinen, hat das Lautsystem auf die wesentlichsten Theile einer jeden den bedeutendsten Einfluss; es ist das erste, worin man sich durchaus fest setzen muss. Freilich führt dies in eine mühvolle, oft ins Kleinliche gehende Elementaruntersuchung, es sind aber auch lauter in sich kleinliche Einzelnheiten, auf welchen der Totaleindruck der Sprachen beruht, und nichts ist mit dem Studium derselben so unverträglich, als bloss in ihnen das Grosse, Geistige, Vorherrschende aufsuchen zu wollen. Genaues Eingehen in jede grammatische Subtilitaet, und Spalten der Wörter in ihre Elemente ist durchaus nothwendig, wenn man sich nicht in allen Urtheilen über den Bau und selbst über die Abstammung Irrthümern blossstellen will.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §29 — checked German

text_version.body: Ultimately, the true individuality of each language lies solely in the nature of sound as such. Whatever one does or attempts in describing its peculiarities, one only defines more and more closely the class to which it belongs; as this language and no other, it expresses itself only by sounding itself before the ear. Although the alphabet of all humanity is confined within certain limits, which are not even very wide, every people with a language of its own nevertheless also has its own sound system: in excluding certain sounds, preferring others, assigning different sounds to designate different concepts, handling sounds in their combinations, and so forth. This may be compared with the different cries and vocal modes of the kinds of animal. Although progressive development brings much to completion, there is nevertheless something fixed and characteristic of a stock in this, deeply grounded in modifications of the organs of speech and in the feeling for sound. It distinguishes stocks even more than languages, however, since within the same language particular stocks have sounds entirely different from those of all the others, as the Florentines, for example, have their aspirated guttural. Yet apart from such details, which seem accidental to language in itself, the sound system has the most significant influence on the most essential parts of every language; it is the first thing in which one must establish a thoroughly firm footing. Admittedly, this leads into laborious elementary investigation, often descending to minutiae; but the total impression of languages rests entirely on details that are minute in themselves, and nothing is more incompatible with studying languages than wanting to seek in them only what is great, mental and predominant. Close attention to every grammatical subtlety, and the splitting of words into their elements, are absolutely necessary if one is to avoid exposing every judgement about structure, and even about descent, to error.

Although the alphabet of the whole of mankind is enclosed by certain limits that are not even very wide, yet every people with a language of its own also has its own system of sounds in the exclusion of certain tones, preference for others, determination of the different ones for the designation of different concepts, treatment of the tones in their combinations, and so forth. One can compare this with the diverse crying and the kinds of tone of the animal genera. There is in it, even if progressive development rounds much off, something firm, tribal in kind, deeply grounded in the modifications of the organs of speech and in the feeling for tone. It distinguishes, however, tribes even more than languages, since in the same language individual tribes have tones wholly deviating from all the rest, as for example the Florentines have the breathing guttural sound. But apart from such details, which appear accidental for language in itself, the system of sounds has the most significant influence on the most essential parts of every language; it is the first thing in which one must establish oneself thoroughly. This does indeed lead into a laborious elementary investigation often descending into the petty, but it is also nothing but details petty in themselves on which the total impression of languages rests, and nothing is so incompatible with the study of them as wanting to seek out in them merely what is great, mental and predominant. Exact attention to every grammatical subtlety, and splitting words into their elements, is thoroughly necessary if one does not want to expose oneself to errors in all judgements about structure and even about descent.

text_version.body: Die wichtigste Ursach, aus welcher die Sprache, vermittelst des Tones, der Wirkung nach aussen bedarf, ist die Geselligkeit, zu welcher der Mensch durch seine Natur unbedingt hingewiesen wird. Es liegt in derselben aber ein zwiefaches, obgleich in einem dritten Höheren eng Verbundenes: einmal dass alle menschlichen Kräfte sich nur gesellschaftlich vollkommen entwickeln, dass es etwas Gemeinsames in dem ganzen menschlichen Geschlechte giebt, von dem jeder Einzelne eine, das Verlangen nach Vervollständigung durch die andren in sich tragende Bestimmung besitzt. Beides ist gerade bei der Sprache besonders wichtig. Denn je grösser und bewegter das gesellige Zusammenwirken auf sie ist, je mehr gewinnt sie unter übrigens gleichen Umständen, und auf jenem eben erwähnten Gemeinsamen beruht die Möglichkeit alles Verständnisses.

text_version.body: The most important reason why language needs to act outwards through sound is sociability, towards which human beings are unconditionally directed by their nature. text_version.body: Auch die Geselligkeit lässt sich ohne Einseitigkeit nicht aus dem blossen Bedürfniss ableiten. Sie beruht nicht einmal in den Thieren darauf. Keines ist leicht so sich in seiner Stärke alleingenügend, als der gerade vorzugsweise in Heerden lebende Elephant. Auch in den Thieren entspringt daher die bei einigen Gattungen grössere, bei andren geringere Neigung zur Geselligkeit aus viel tiefer in ihrem Wesen liegenden Ursachen. Es ist nur uns unmöglich, dieselben zu ergründen, weil wir uns gar keinen Begriff von der doch nicht abzuläugnenden Fähigkeit der Thiere machen können, wahrzunehmen, zu empfinden und Wahrnehmungen zu verknüpfen. Im Menschen aber ist das Denken wesentlich an gesellschaftliches Daseyn gebunden, und der Mensch bedarf, abgesehen von allen körperlichen und Empfindungsbeziehungen, zum blossen Denken eines dem Ich entsprechenden Du , der Begriff erreicht seine Bestimmtheit und Klarheit erst durch das Zurückstrahlen aus einer fremden Denkkraft. Er wird erzeugt, indem er sich aus der bewegten Masse des Vorstellens losreisst, und dem Subject gegenüber zum Object bildet. Es genügt jedoch nicht, dass diese Spaltung in dem Subjecte allein vorgeht, die Objectivität ist erst vollendet, wenn der Vorstellende den Gedanken wirklich ausser sich erblickt, was nur in einem andren, gleich ihm vorstellenden und denkenden Wesen möglich ist. Zwischen Denkkraft und Denkkraft aber ist die einzige Vermittlerin die Sprache, und so entsteht auch hier ihre Nothwendigkeit zur Vollendung des Gedanken. Es liegt aber auch in der Sprache selbst ein unabänderlicher Dualismus, und alles Sprechen ist auf Anrede und Erwiederung gestellt. Das Wort ist kein Gegenstand, vielmehr den Gegenständen gegenüber etwas Subjectives, nun aber soll es im Geiste des Denkenden doch ein Object, von ihm erzeugt und auf ihn zurückwirkend seyn. Damit es sich nun von einem blossen Scheinobjecte, einem Traumbilde, unterscheide, muss es Wesenheit in einem Hörenden und Erwiedernden gewinnen. Diesen Urtypus aller Sprachen drückt das Pronomen durch die Unterscheidung der zweiten Person von der dritten aus. Ich und Er sind wirklich verschiedne Gegenstände, und mit ihnen ist eigentlich Alles erschöpft, denn sie heissen mit andren Worten Ich und Nichtich. Du aber ist ein dem Ich gegenübergestelltes Er. Indem Ich und Er auf innrer und äusserer Wahrnehmung beruhen, liegt in dem Du Spontaneitaet der Wahl. Es ist auch ein Nicht-Ich, aber nicht, wie das Er, in der Sphäre aller Wesen, sondern in einer andren, der eines durch Einwirkung gemeinsamen Handelns. In dem Er selbst liegt nun dadurch, ausser dem Nicht-Ich, auch ein Nicht-Du, und es ist nicht bloss einem von ihnen, sondern beiden entgegengesetzt. Dass dieselbe Pronominalform durch alle Sprachen durchgeht, zeigt, dass, nach dem Gefühl aller Völker, das Sprechen in seinem Wesen voraussetzt, dass der Sprechende, sich gegenüber, einen Angeredeten von allen Andren unterscheidet. In mehreren Amerikanischen Sprachen zeigt sich sogar darin eine besondre Sorgfalt die zweite Person herauszuheben, dass sie auch in der ersten des Plurals durch verschiedene Formen andeuten, ob der Angeredete darunter begriffen, oder ausgeschlossen ist.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §31 — checked German

text_version.body: Sociability too cannot be derived from mere need without one-sidedness. It does not rest on need even in animals. Scarcely any animal is so self-sufficient in its strength as the elephant, which nevertheless lives predominantly in herds. Thus in animals too, the greater inclination towards sociability in some kinds and the lesser inclination in others arise from causes lying much deeper in their being. It is simply impossible for us to fathom these causes, because we can form no conception at all of animals' nevertheless undeniable ability to perceive, to feel and to connect perceptions. In human beings, however, thinking is essentially bound to social existence; quite apart from all bodily relations and relations of feeling, a human being needs, simply in order to think, a You corresponding to the I: a concept attains its definiteness and clarity only by being reflected back from another power of thought. It is produced by breaking free from the moving mass of representation and forming itself into an object confronting the subject. Yet it is not enough for this division to take place within the subject alone; objectivity is complete only when the person forming representations actually sees the thought outside himself, which is possible only in another being that forms representations and thinks as he does. But language is the sole mediator between one power of thought and another, and so here too its necessity for the completion of thought becomes apparent. There is also an unalterable dualism within language itself, and all speaking is directed towards address and reply. The word is not a thing; rather, in relation to things it is something subjective, yet in the mind of the thinker it is nevertheless to be an object, produced by him and acting back upon him. To distinguish itself from a merely apparent object, a dream image, it must acquire substantial reality in someone who hears and replies. The pronoun expresses this original type of all languages by distinguishing the second person from the third. I and He are genuinely different objects, and in fact they exhaust everything, for in other words they mean I and Not-I. You, however, is a He placed opposite the I. Whereas I and He rest on inward and outward perception, You involves spontaneity of choice. It too is a Not-I, but unlike He it lies not in the sphere of all beings, but in another sphere, that of action made common through influence. He itself thereby comes to contain, besides Not-I, also Not-You, and is opposed not merely to one of them but to both. The fact that the same pronominal form runs through all languages shows that, according to the feeling of all peoples, speaking essentially presupposes that the speaker distinguishes, opposite himself, an addressee from everyone else. Several American languages even show particular care in singling out the second person by indicating, through different forms in the first-person plural as well, whether the addressee is included or excluded.

text_version.body: Sociability too cannot without one-sidedness be derived from mere need. It does not even in animals rest on that. No animal is easily so sufficient to itself in its strength as the elephant, which lives precisely pre-eminently in herds. In animals too, therefore, the inclination to sociability, greater in some genera and lesser in others, arises from causes lying much deeper in their being. It is only impossible for us to fathom them, because we can form no concept at all of the capacity of animals, which is nevertheless not to be denied, to perceive, to feel and to combine perceptions. In man, however, thinking is essentially bound to social existence, and man needs, apart from all bodily and feeling relations, for mere thinking a Thou corresponding to the I; the concept attains its determinateness and clarity only through being reflected back from a foreign power of thought. It is produced in that it tears itself loose from the moved mass of representing and forms itself, over against the subject, into an object. It is not sufficient, however, that this division takes place in the subject alone; objectivity is only completed when the representing person really beholds the thought outside himself, which is possible only in another being representing and thinking like him. Between power of thought and power of thought, however, the sole mediatress is language, and so here too its necessity for the completion of thought arises. But there also lies in language itself an unalterable dualism, and all speaking is set upon address and reply. The word is not an object; rather, over against objects, it is something subjective, but now in the mind of the thinking person it is nevertheless to be an object, produced by him and reacting upon him. In order that it may now distinguish itself from a mere apparent object, a dream-image, it must gain real being in a person hearing and replying. The pronoun expresses this original type of all languages through the distinction of the second person from the third. I and He are really different objects, and with them everything is really exhausted, for in other words they are called I and Non-I. Thou, however, is a He placed over against the I. Whereas I and He rest on inner and outer perception, in the Thou there lies spontaneity of choice. It too is a Non-I, but not, like He, in the sphere of all beings, but in another sphere, that of a common acting through mutual influence. In the He itself there now thereby lies, besides the Non-I, also a Non-Thou, and it is opposed not merely to one of them, but to both. That the same pronominal form runs through all languages shows that, according to the feeling of all peoples, speaking in its essence presupposes that the speaker distinguishes, over against himself, a person addressed from all others. In several American languages a special care to single out the second person even shows itself in this, that they also indicate in the first person of the plural through different forms whether the person addressed is included under it or excluded from it.

text_version.body: Was sich auf diese Weise ergiebt, wenn man den einfachen Act des Denkens zu zergliedern versucht, das wiederholt sich im geistigen Leben des Menschen unaufhörlich; die gesellige Mittheilung gewährt ihm Ueberzeugung und Anregung. Die Denkkraft bedarf etwas ihr Gleiches und doch von ihr Geschiedenes. Durch das Gleiche wird sie entzündet, durch das von ihr Geschiedne erhält sie einen Prüfstein der Wesenheit ihrer innern Erzeugungen. Denn der Mensch kann in seiner veränderlichen Beschränktheit die Wahrheit, als das schrankenlos Feste, nur als ausser sich Liegendes ansehn, und sein ganzes geistiges Streben ist ein Anringen an sie, und das mächtigste Mittel ihr nahe zu kommen, seinen Abstand von ihr zu messen, ist die gesellige Vereinigung. So ist die Sprache ein nothwendiges Erforderniss zur ersten Erzeugung des Gedanken, und zur fortschreitenden Ausbildung des Geistes.

text_version.body: What emerges in this way when we attempt to analyse the simple act of thinking repeats itself unceasingly in human mental life; social communication affords conviction and stimulation. The power of thought needs something like itself and yet distinct from itself. It is kindled by what is like itself, while what is distinct from it supplies a touchstone for the substantial reality of its inward productions. For in his changeable limitation, the human being can regard truth, as what is boundlessly fixed, only as something lying outside himself; all his mental striving is a struggle towards it, and social association is the most powerful means of approaching it and measuring his distance from it. Language is thus a necessary requirement both for the first production of thought and for the progressive development of the mind.

text_version.body: Die geistige Mittheilung setzt, von dem Einen zum Andren übergehend, in diesem etwas ihm mit jenem Gemeinsames voraus. Man versteht das gehörte Wort nur, weil man es selbst hätte sagen können. Es kann in der Seele nichts, als durch eigne Thätigkeit vorhanden seyn, und das Verstehen ist ebensowohl, als das Sprechen, selbst eine Anregung der Sprachkraft, nur in ihrer innern Empfänglichkeit, wie dieses in seiner äusseren Thätigkeit, daher es dem Menschen auch so natürlich ist, das eben Verstandene gleich wieder auszusagen. Es liegt daher in jedem Menschen die Sprache in ihrem ganzen Umfange, was aber nichts anders sagen will, als dass jeder ein durch eine bestimmt modificirte Kraft, anstossend und beschränkend, geregeltes Streben besitzt, die ganze Sprache, wie es äussere oder innere Veranlassung herbeiführt, nach und nach hervorzubringen, oder hervorgebracht zu verstehen. Diese Kraft ist, wie jede, natürlich eine individuelle, aber nach allen den Gattungsbegriffen individualisirt, vermöge welcher jede Gattung gegen eine allgemeinere höhere als Individuum genommen werden kann. Sie ist mithin die allgemeine Sprachkraft, bestimmt durch den Völkerstamm, die Nation, die Mundart, dann in ihren Lautzeichen feststehend, in der Art des Gebrauches bestimmt durch alle so mächtig auf das Gemüth einwirkenden inneren Beschaffenheiten und äusseren Zufälligkeiten, dass die Wirkung in der Sprache fühlbar wird, endlich durch die in keine allgemeinere Kategorie mehr zu bringende Individualität. Jede dieser bis zum Allgemeinsten aufsteigenden Stufen bildet eine Sprachsphäre, die durch das allem unter ihr Begriffenen Gemeinsame, und durch das von dem ausser ihr Befindlichen Verschiedne bestimmt wird. Bei jeder allgemeinen Sprachuntersuchung wird es daher zur nothwendigen Aufgabe, bei den verschiedenen in Betrachtung kommenden Punkten, z. B. beim Alphabet, die Gränzen der menschlichen Sprache überhaupt aufzusuchen, in diesem weiten Gebiete die kleineren, wieder in einander begriffenen der einzelnen Sprachgattungen abzusondern, und überall dahin zu sehen, ob diese den Begriff, von welchem aus die Eintheilung gemacht ist, erfüllen, mithin in ihrem geschichtlichen Daseyn ein durch die Idee gegebenes Ganzes bilden.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §33 — checked German

text_version.body: Mental communication, in passing from one person to another, presupposes in the latter something he has in common with the former. We understand a word we hear only because we could have said it ourselves. Nothing can be present in the soul except through its own activity, and understanding, just as much as speaking, is itself a stimulation of the power of language, only in its inward receptivity, as speaking is in its outward activity; hence it is also so natural for human beings immediately to say again what they have just understood. Language therefore lies within every human being in its entire extent; but this means nothing other than that everyone possesses a striving, regulated through the prompting and limiting action of a specifically modified power, gradually to produce the whole language, or to understand it when produced, as inward or outward occasions arise. Like every power, this is naturally an individual one, but it is individualised according to all those concepts of classes by virtue of which each class can be taken as an individual in relation to a higher, more general class. It is thus the general power of language, determined by the ethnic stock, the nation and the dialect; then, with its sound signs fixed, determined in its manner of use by all the inward qualities and outward contingencies that act upon the mind so powerfully that their effect becomes perceptible in language; and finally determined by the individuality that can no longer be brought under any more general category. Each of these levels, ascending to the most general, forms a linguistic sphere determined by what is common to everything included within it and by what distinguishes it from everything outside it. In every general investigation of language it therefore becomes necessary, at the various points under consideration—for example, the alphabet—to seek the limits of human language in general, to distinguish within this wide domain the smaller, again mutually nested domains of particular classes of language, and everywhere to consider whether these fulfil the concept from which the division was made, and thus form in their historical existence a whole given by the idea.

text_version.body: Jede Vielfachheit des in sich Gleichartigen führt diese Aufgabe mit sich, und vorzugsweise bei Untersuchungen, die, wie die die Sprache betreffenden, nicht bloss historisch zu erkennen und darzustellen, sondern teleologisch auf die Sprache und den Menschen bildend zurückzuwirken geführt werden. Den allgemeinen Zusammenhang der Sprachen erklärt nun zwar allerdings die Gleichartigkeit der menschlichen Natur, in der ähnliche Kräfte nach gleichen Gesetzen wirken. Eine tiefere Untersuchung und vollere Würdigung der Sprache scheint mir aber noch viel weiter und auf einen Punkt zu führen, zu dem ich bis jetzt nur durch leichtere Betrachtungen den Weg habe bahnen wollen, und auf dem keine weitere Erklärung möglich ist, wie denn keine metaphysische d. h. auf die Ergründung des Seyns an sich gegründete Untersuchung weiter als an das Ende des zu Erklärenden zu leiten vermag. Mir nun — denn ich spreche dies lieber in dem Tone innerer Ueberzeugung, als mit der Zuversicht allgemeiner Behauptung aus — scheint das Wesen der Sprache verkannt, der geistige Process ihrer Entstehung (nicht der an sich, sondern auch der im jedesmaligen Sprechen und Verstehen) nur scheinbar erklärt, und ihre mächtige Einwirkung auf das Gemüth unrichtig gewürdigt zu werden, wenn man das Menschengeschlecht als zahllose zu derselben Gattung gehörende Naturen, und nicht vielmehr als Eine in zahllose Individuen zerspaltene betrachtet, eine Ansicht, zu der man auch in ganz andren Beziehungen, als in der der Sprache, und von ganz anderen Punkten aus gelangt. Die Verschiedenheit der beiden einander gegenüber gestellten Behauptungen ist einleuchtend, da die innere Verwandtschaft des Menschengeschlechts nach der letzteren auf der Einheit des Wesens desselben, nach der ersteren nur auf der Einheit der Idee beruht, welche dasselbe, betrachtend oder schaffend, zusammenfasst.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §34 — checked German

text_version.body: Every multiplicity of things alike in kind brings this task with it, especially in investigations which, like those concerning language, are conducted not merely to gain and present historical knowledge, but teleologically to act back formatively upon language and human beings. The general interconnectedness of languages is certainly explained by the likeness in kind of human nature, in which similar powers operate according to the same laws. Yet a deeper investigation and fuller appreciation of language seem to me to lead much further, to a point towards which I have so far sought to prepare the way only through less demanding reflections, and at which no further explanation is possible; for no metaphysical investigation—that is, one grounded in fathoming being in itself—can lead beyond the point where what is to be explained ends. To me—for I prefer to express this in the tone of inward conviction rather than with the assurance of a universal assertion—the essence of language seems to be misunderstood, the mental process of its genesis—not that in itself, but also that in each act of speaking and understanding—only seemingly explained, and its powerful influence on the mind incorrectly appreciated, if the human race is regarded as countless natures belonging to the same species, rather than as one nature divided into countless individuals: a view reached in quite other connections than that of language, and from quite different starting points. The difference between the two opposed assertions is evident, since on the latter view the inward kinship of the human race rests on the unity of its being, whereas on the former it rests only on the unity of the idea that encompasses it, whether in contemplation or in creation.

text_version.body: Every multiplicity of what is in itself of the same kind brings this task with it, and pre-eminently in investigations which, like those concerning language, are conducted not merely in order historically to know and present, but teleologically so as to react formatively upon language and man. The general connexion of languages is indeed explained by the sameness of kind of human nature, in which similar powers act according to the same laws. A deeper investigation and fuller appreciation of language seems to me, however, to lead much further, and to a point to which I have hitherto wished only to clear the way through easier considerations, and at which no further explanation is possible, just as no metaphysical investigation, that is, one grounded on fathoming being in itself, can lead further than to the end of what is to be explained. Now to me — for I utter this preferably in the tone of inner conviction rather than with the confidence of general assertion — the essence of language seems to be misconceived, the mental process of its origin (not that in itself, but also that in each act of speaking and understanding) only apparently explained, and its powerful effect on the inner mind incorrectly appreciated, if one regards the human race as countless natures belonging to the same genus, and not rather as One nature split into countless individuals, a view to which one also arrives in wholly other relations than that of language, and from wholly other points. The difference between the two assertions placed opposite each other is evident, since the inner relationship of the human race according to the latter rests on the unity of its being, according to the former only on the unity of the idea which, contemplating or creating, comprehends it.

text_version.body: In der Art dieser Verwandtschaft liegt das Geheimniss der menschlichen Individualität verschlossen, das man zugleich als das des menschlichen Daseyns ansehen kann. Es ist der Punkt, in dem sich in einem auf den irdischen folgenden Zustande vorzüglich eine Verschiedenheit erwarten lässt, die dann, wenn Bewusstseyn beide Zustände verknüpfte, zugleich eine durchgängige Umänderung aller bisherigen Ansichten hervorbringen würde. Erklären und ergründen lässt sich dies Geheimniss nicht, aber zur richtigen Erklärung der Erscheinungen und zur Richtung des intellectuellen Strebens muss man sich hüten, das wahre Wesen jener Verwandtschaft der menschlichen Individualität zu verkennen, es bloss aus logischen und discursiven Begriffen [zu] schöpfen, und es nicht vielmehr aus der Tiefe des inneren Gefühls, und in einem die Untersuchung bis zu ihren Endpunkten verfolgenden Nachdenken aufzufassen. Man gewinnt daher schon, wenn man die im Vorigen als die richtige angegebene Ansicht auch nur als geahndete Möglichkeit stehen lässt, sich nicht in die entgegengesetzte zu verschliessen.
